$doc: The data contract: the introspected schema merged with the authored sidecars and the engine registry snapshot. Generated — do not edit; `npm run contract:check` fails on drift.

analysis_kinds.tier_name: project-independent, versioned by vintage rather than by project
analysis_kinds.grain: One row per analysis kind: which LEVEL of the graph it reads. The one place that is stated — `analysis_get_or_start` reads it to choose the hash a run is keyed on, so a price edit does not invalidate a centrality. What each kind's parameters mean is stated in `analysis_runs.contract.yaml`'s catalog; `analysisKindsParity.test.ts` fails when the two disagree about which kinds exist.

governance.note: Reference data authored in a migration and read by everyone; no API role writes it. Not project-scoped. Not audited: a change to a kind's scope is a migration, and the migration is the record.

columns.name: kind
columns.meaning: The analysis kind, as `analysis_runs.analysis_kind` names it.

columns.name: input_scope
columns.meaning: The level whose hash keys a run of this kind: `product`, `process`, `firm`, `simulation` (the tables the engine reads — WP 11.2), or `all` (the composite). Which hash names each is stated once, in `_scope_hash_key`.

columns.name: fallback_scope
columns.meaning: The level used instead when `fallback_rule` holds — today only `network_metrics`, which reads the lane graph (process level) when the deep tier is incomplete. NULL for a kind with no fallback.

columns.name: fallback_rule
columns.meaning: When the fallback applies. `deep_tier_incomplete`: the project has no `network_nodes` or no `network_edges` — the same condition the analyzer used to test itself, now stated once and returned to it as `input_scope`.

columns.name: description
columns.meaning: What the kind computes, over which table.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was first written.

analysis_results.tier_name: derived — a pure function of tier 2
analysis_results.grain: One entity's metrics from one run. `metrics` is jsonb rather than a column per measure on purpose: the set of measures is the analysis's business and adding one must not be a migration — which is the same argument the open `analysis_kind` enum makes, applied to the output side.

governance.note: Read follows the parent run's project reachability. No write policy and no user-facing write path: rows arrive only through `analysis_complete_run`. APPEND-ONLY AS A PROPERTY OF THE SCHEMA — `analysis_results_are_immutable` refuses every UPDATE, because a result that can be rewritten makes its run's key a lie: the key says these inputs and this code produced this answer. DELETE is not refused, and that is deliberate rather than an omission: rows cascade from `analysis_runs` and thence from `projects`, and refusing DELETE would make deleting an analysed project fail. Deleting a project is retention, not mutation of a result.

policies.name: analysis_results_select
policies.using: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.analysis_runs r WHERE r.id = analysis_results.run_id AND public.has_project_access(r.project_id))
policies.with_check: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.analysis_runs r WHERE r.id = analysis_results.run_id AND public.has_project_access(r.project_id))

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate row identifier. Carries no meaning.

columns.name: run_id
columns.meaning: The run that computed this. Every result reaches its dataset, its parameters and its code version through here — which is what makes a stored metric reproducible (T4) instead of a number with no provenance.

columns.name: entity_type
columns.meaning: What kind of thing the metrics are about — `node`, `project`, and whatever a later `analysis_kind` declares. Shape-checked only, for the same reason `analysis_kind` is: the catalog belongs in the contract, not in a CHECK.

columns.name: entity_id
columns.meaning: The entity's own id within the project, as the analysis names it (a node `uid`, a project id). TEXT because the analyses disagree about what an entity is and forcing one type here would force a migration the first time a new kind lands.

columns.name: metrics
columns.meaning: What was computed for this entity. jsonb so a new measure is not a migration. IMMUTABLE — see the governance note; recomputing means a NEW run, which is the point of the key.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: Row insert time, maintained by the database.

analysis_runs.tier_name: derived — a pure function of tier 2
analysis_runs.grain: One execution of one analysis for one project, identified by the world it ran against (`input_hash`), the parameters it ran with (`params_hash`) and the code that ran (`code_version`). Two runs carrying the same five-part key ARE the same run by definition, which is what makes serving a stored answer sound rather than a bet on how recently a timestamp moved.

governance.note: Read follows project reachability (`has_project_access`), uuid-only since WP 3.0. `write: null` is a STATEMENT, not an omission: there is no user-facing write path and there must not be one. Every write goes through `analysis_get_or_start`, `analysis_complete_run` and `analysis_fail_run`, each of which takes the actor as a PARAMETER and routes it through `assert_writer_may_act` — so the audit trigger names a person rather than recording `actor_known: false` (G4). There is deliberately NO write policy on this table, which makes `no-tier-skip` (I2) a property of the schema here rather than of today's callers. The RPCs AUTHENTICATE and do not AUTHORIZE: `20260917000005` removed a role gate from the shared preamble after it was found to refuse an organization admin on a live path, and making `min_project_role` load-bearing is D66 and WP 6.2's.

constraints.name: analysis_runs_actor_user_id_fkey
constraints.definition: FOREIGN KEY (actor_user_id) REFERENCES public.approved_users(id) ON DELETE SET NULL

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate row identifier. Carries no meaning — the IDENTITY of a run is the five-column natural key, not this.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this analysis ran for. Referenced by uuid and never by a displayable name (`uuid-identity`, G1); cascades on project delete, which is retention rather than mutation of a result.

columns.name: analysis_kind
columns.meaning: WHICH analysis ran. Open enum — the CHECK constrains the shape to a lowercase identifier and the catalog of values is the `analysis_kinds` block above, so a new kind costs a sidecar edit and not a migration.

columns.name: input_hash
columns.meaning: WP 4.1's `current_graph_hash(project_id)` at the moment the run was claimed: the world this answer is about. This is the anchor invariant `input-hash` (I5) is about — and I5 is NOT met by this table alone, because I5 is about the DERIVED ROW carrying it. WP 4.3 stamps the same value onto the tier-3 rows the analyzers already write.

columns.name: params_hash
columns.meaning: SHA-256 of `params` as canonical `jsonb` text. Over jsonb and never over the text a caller sent, because jsonb normalises key order and duplicate keys — so the same parameters written two ways are one cache key rather than two.

columns.name: code_version
columns.meaning: WHICH code produced the answer. Part of the key so that a changed analyzer does not serve its predecessor's numbers, and so two versions can coexist on one input hash and be compared (§11's fourth exit check).

columns.name: params
columns.meaning: The parameters as sent, beside the hash of them, so a run can be read without reversing a digest. Immutable: re-pointing a stored run at different parameters would re-attribute an answer to a question it never answered.

columns.name: status
columns.meaning: `running`, `succeeded` or `failed`. Only a `succeeded` run is ever served as a hit — a `running` row is a claim somebody else is still working on and holds no results, and handing it back would render an empty analysis as a complete one. `failed` sits OUTSIDE the unique index on purpose (see `natural_key_unique`): otherwise the first crash would own that cache key forever and the analysis could never be retried on that input.

columns.name: started_at
columns.meaning: When the key was claimed. Part of the run's frozen identity, not of its state.

columns.name: finished_at
columns.meaning: When the run reached `succeeded` or `failed`. Null while running.

columns.name: duration_ms
columns.meaning: Wall-clock milliseconds from claim to finish. Reporting only — nothing keys on it, and a staleness rule that compared it to anything would be the timestamp comparison D12 is about.
columns.note: Nothing reads it, deliberately. It is here so a slow analysis is VISIBLE rather than inferred from two timestamps, and the moment anything keys on it we are back to asking whether a clock moved instead of whether the data changed — which is exactly D12.

columns.name: row_counts
columns.meaning: What the run produced, by entity type. Reporting and the Trust Report's input (A3); WP 4.4 assembles it.

columns.name: warnings
columns.meaning: The run's own account of its blind spots, carried with the result rather than left in a log — transparency commitment T3, which says every report states the known limits of its own computation.

columns.name: actor_user_id
columns.meaning: WHO asked for this run. Required when the run is CREATED — a BEFORE INSERT trigger, `analysis_runs_actor_required`, refuses a run that cannot name its actor, the same stance `assert_writer_may_act` takes for the RPC writers (`20260917000005`). NULL only afterwards, when that person's account is deleted: the key is `ON DELETE SET NULL` and the identity guard admits exactly that change, so the run is kept and its actor becomes unknown (WP 7.2 (a), §4 D213). Until `20260930000007` the column was NOT NULL with no ON DELETE rule, so nobody who had ever run an analysis could be deleted. Note what attribution means here: the application authenticates against `approved_users` and not Supabase Auth, so the id is CLIENT-ASSERTED (D28) — the database refuses a write into a project the user cannot reach, which is a real constraint, but it is not proof of identity.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: Row insert time, maintained by the database.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: Last lifecycle change. The IDENTITY columns are frozen by `analysis_runs_identity_is_immutable`; only status, finish and reporting columns move, which is the line between what a run IS and what it is DOING.

columns.name: input_scope
columns.meaning: Which LEVEL of the graph `input_hash` is the hash of — `product`, `process`, `firm`, `simulation` (the scope the engine reads, WP 11.2), or `all` (the composite). Resolved by `analysis_get_or_start` from `analysis_kinds`, the one place each kind's scope is stated, including `network_metrics`'s fallback to the process level when the deep tier is incomplete (WP 10.1, §4 D235). Every run before WP 10.1 is `all`.

columns.name: dataset_version_id
columns.meaning: The graph version this run computed over (WP 10.1). Taken through `snapshot_dataset` at claim time, which returns the existing version of the current content, so this names "Graph vN" rather than a hash a person cannot read. NULL on every run before WP 10.1.

columns.name: level_version_id
columns.meaning: The VERSION of the level the run keyed on ("Firm graph v5") — the `graph_level_versions` row whose content is `input_hash` (WP 11.2, §4 D261). Filled by `analysis_get_or_start` from the level row the claim's snapshot has just registered; NULL for scope `all`, whose version is the snapshot (`dataset_version_id`). History learnt it from its own scope and hash where the project's level ever froze that content.

weighted.meaning: Weight edges by `relative_revenue` rather than treating the graph as unweighted.

graph.meaning: The graph measured: the Product-level view's four echelons, built by `_shared/productGraph.ts` from `supply_chain_data`'s flat lanes — the function the page draws with, so a node in the table is a node on the canvas.

weighted.meaning: Edge weight for the weighted measures: the lane's weekly flow, normalised to the largest edge.

exact.meaning: Betweenness from every source and a shifted eigenvector iteration, rather than `network_metrics`' 50-source sample and plain power iteration, which does not converge on this layered (bipartite) graph.

product_metrics.note: Keyed on the PROCESS level, not the product level: `supply_chain_data` is rebuilt from `bom_multi_level`, which the product-level hash does not cover. Store only — no entity mirror. Read by `get_product_level_metrics`.

config.meaning: The caller's `ProminenceConfig` — the four weights and the two caps. It is part of the key because two configs produce two different scores over one graph. `null` means the analyzer's `defaultConfig`, which the function fills in before the digest is taken, so a stored run always records the config it actually used rather than the word "default".

plant_name.meaning: The plant filter the request carried, or null for every row of the project. It is part of the key because two plants of one project are two different analyses over two different row sets. NOTE that `plant_name` is NOT project-scoped, which is why the function derives the project from the rows it loaded and refuses a set spanning two.

critical_nodes.note: NO `topology_digest`, and the absence is a statement: this analyzer reads `supply_chain_data`, which is `combine-project`'s output over the eleven tier-2 tables `current_graph_hash` already covers. Its inputs ARE in the anchor. The `threshold` parameter this block used to declare DOES NOT EXIST — `predictCriticalNodes` takes no threshold and the entry was authored from the plan rather than from the code. Removed in WP 4.3 rather than carried: an undeclared default is `declared-fallback` (I6) broken, and a DECLARED parameter that no code reads is the same defect pointing the other way.

process_structure.note: For every level-1 node of the process network, the nodes it reaches downstream and upstream, transitively, over `supply_chain_data_multi_tier`. Computed where the data is; the process page reads it instead of walking the graph in the browser on every selection (§4 D239).

feature_spec_version.meaning: Which feature definition the run computed. Part of the key, so a changed definition is a new run over the same graph rather than a stale hit.

feature_spec.note: The structural features a surrogate reads per Graph Version (blueprint §11.3): over `inbound_logistics`, out-degree and weekly-volume-weighted out-degree per supplier (`entity_type` supplier), suppliers per material (`material`), and one `graph`/`summary` row with the counts, means, the single-sourced count and the multi-source rate. Keyed on the PRODUCT level hash, so it is computed once per sourcing network and a revert is the first run again (`rehearsal/620`). No model is trained.

scenario.meaning: The shared scenario, `scsim.stress.nexus.NEXUS_SCENARIO` as the engine exported it (start week, durations, effect, measure). Part of the key.

scenario_hash.meaning: sha256 of `scenario`; the publish refuses rows computed under another.

replications.meaning: Replications per cell, each paired with the undisrupted run on the same seeds.

run_settings.meaning: The horizon, seed, CRN, confidence level and adopted warm-up, read from the Validated Model's protocol by the job.

model_validation_id.meaning: Written by `analysis_start_nexus_stress`, with `model_hash`, `policy_version_id`, `policy_hash`, `dataset_version_id`, `graph_hash` and `hash_inputs` — the server's binding, over anything the caller sent.

nexus_stress.note: The nexus battery (§4 D310): every supplier and supplied material disrupted alone; one result row per target with its lost sales in € per duration and the Average it ranks by. Keyed on the SIMULATION scope (`hash_inputs`) of the data version it ran on, opened only on an active Validated Model, published whole (`analysis_publish_nexus_stress`), read by `get_nexus_stress_results` (`rehearsal/900`).

combine_etl.computed_by: combine-project (migrated in WP 4.3, as §11 names it)
combine_etl.note: REGISTERED BUT NEVER SKIPPED. `combine_etl`'s output is rows in `supply_chain_data`, not entries in `analysis_results`, so "already computed" means "those rows are still there" — which the store cannot see, and a row deleted by hand would make a hit skip an ETL the project needs. WP 4.3 records the run for its identity; WP 4.4 owns staleness and is the package that may turn a hit into a skip.

approved_users.grain: One person who may sign in. This is the authentication table: the product does not use Supabase Auth for its own users, so a row here IS an account — credential, role, tenant and profile in one.

governance.note: READ THE POLICIES BEFORE TRUSTING THIS ROW. The table carries two policies and they contradict each other: "Users can check their own login credentials" is `FOR SELECT USING (true)`, and "No direct access - use RPCs" is `FOR ALL TO authenticated, anon USING (false)`. Postgres policies are PERMISSIVE unless declared RESTRICTIVE, and permissive policies are OR'd — so the deny-all does not deny anything, and the intended rule ("no direct access") is not the enforced one. Whether that is reachable depends on the table GRANTs Supabase applies outside `supabase/migrations/`, which no static replay can see and which PLAN.md §15 is the way to settle. Recorded as D28 and assigned to WP 2.4, which owns the RESTRICTIVE-policy decision for the whole schema; it is named here because a reader of this page must not take `rls_enabled: true` for "reads are restricted".

policies.name: Users can check their own login credentials

constraints.name: approved_users_avatar_color_check
constraints.definition: CHECK ( avatar_color IS NULL OR avatar_color IN ( 'slate', 'red', 'orange', 'amber', 'green', 'teal', 'blue', 'indigo', 'violet', 'pink'))

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: The user's identity, and the value every other governance table joins on — `organization_members.user_id`, `projects.modeler_id`, the `_user_id` argument of `capabilities_for_user()` and of `get_current_user_org_id()`.

columns.name: name
columns.meaning: The account holder's full name, as entered when the account was approved. Their identity for accountability: its owner cannot change it (§4 D209) — `update_own_profile` has no parameter for it — and only the administrator paths write it. `first_name` / `last_name` are a reading of it.

columns.name: email
columns.meaning: The sign-in address, UNIQUE. Also a second identity path: the fallback branch of `get_current_user_org()` and `get_current_approved_user()` locate the row by `auth.jwt() ->> 'email'` when the session GUC is unset.

columns.name: password_hash
columns.meaning: The bcrypt hash of the account's password. A credential, and the reason the contradiction recorded in `governance.note` above is a security finding rather than an untidiness.

columns.name: role
columns.meaning: The account's global role — `admin`, `modeler`, `user` or `super_admin`. GLOBAL, not per-project and not per-organization: it is the left-most input to `capabilities_for_user()`'s role -> org -> user merge, and `super_admin` short-circuits that merge to grant everything.

substitutions.when: an account is created without a role
substitutions.visible_as: the column default; the admin user list renders the resulting role verbatim

ingest.validate: one of the app_role enum values

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the account was approved. Server-stamped.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When the row was last modified. Server-stamped.

columns.name: organization
columns.meaning: The user's tenant, as a string. This is the value `get_current_user_org()` returns, and it was the left-hand side of every access comparison in the schema until WP 2.1.

substitutions.when: an account is created without an organization
substitutions.visible_as: nowhere — and that is the defect. The string is a real tenant name to every comparison that reads it, so accounts that fall to the default share one tenant with each other without any surface saying so.

columns.note: Half of D13. A displayable, editable, non-unique string used as a join key. It is kept, not dropped: `organization_id` is nullable and the rows D27 left unstamped have nothing else to authorize on. Every live comparison now goes through `org_is_current_user_org(uuid, text)`, so when §15 confirms the backfill at 100 % the text branch is removed from one function body rather than from 107 call sites.

columns.name: display_name
columns.meaning: The name the user chose for themselves, overriding `name` in the UI — labelled "User name" on /profile, and the one name its owner can change (§4 D209). It never replaces `name` as the account holder's identity.

columns.name: avatar_url
columns.meaning: URL of a profile image uploaded to the `avatars` bucket. RETIRED by §4 D206: the upload was refused for every `anon` caller by its storage policies, and the owner chose an avatar colour instead, so no RPC reads or writes this column any more. Kept rather than dropped so nothing uploaded before is destroyed.

columns.name: phone
columns.meaning: Contact number. Not used for authentication or for any second factor.

columns.name: password_changed_at
columns.meaning: When the password was last set. Server-stamped.

columns.name: password_expires_at
columns.meaning: When the current password expires — `now() + password_max_age()` (90 days) when the password was last set. Expiry does not refuse a sign-in: it sends the user to /profile and closes every other page until the password is changed (`RoleGuard`, reading `get_my_profile`'s server-computed `password_expired`; §4 D206). Rows that predate `20260527011429` were stamped by that migration's column default, not by a real password change.

substitutions.value: password_max_age() (90 days) after the row is written
substitutions.visible_as: the column default; the account pages render the resulting date

columns.name: force_password_change
columns.meaning: Whether the user must set a new password before continuing. Set when an administrator creates or resets an account; cleared by `change_own_password`. Enforced by `RoleGuard`, which could not see it until §4 D206.

columns.name: is_active
columns.meaning: Whether the account may sign in. Enforced by the SERVER since `20260929000002` (§4 D205): `authenticate_approved_user` returns no row for a suspended account and records `auth.sign_in_failed` with the reason, and `_assert_super_admin` refuses a suspended super admin. The browser also checks it through `get_my_profile` at login and on every reload — a check that, until §4 D206, raised for every user and was ignored, so before these two changes the column was set and never read. It is not consulted by any RLS policy, so between reloads a suspended user's open session is not revoked (D28's client-asserted identity).

columns.name: organization_id
columns.meaning: The account's ACTIVE organization, by uuid — the one it is working in now, the same organization `organization` names, and the plane that survives a rename. What `get_current_user_org_id(_user_id)` returns, and therefore what every org-scoped RLS policy reads and what a new project is stamped with. Since §4 D210 an account may BELONG to several organizations (`organization_members`, the authority for membership) and this column is always one of them — NULL exactly when it belongs to none. Setting it adds the membership if missing; the account changes it itself through `switch_my_organization`, and sign-in moves it to a current membership when the active one's access period has ended. Since §4 D216 sign-in first moves it to the account's DEFAULT organization (`organization_members.is_default`, set by a super admin) when that one is within its period, and leaving the active organization re-points to the default before the earliest membership. The `organization` text copy follows it (`trg_approved_users_track_active_org`).
columns.note: NULLABLE, and rows are genuinely NULL here. It was added and backfilled once by `20260709000002`; WP 2.1 re-ran the backfill matching on `name` OR `slug` and leaving ambiguous matches alone rather than picking one. A row whose text org matches no organization — `'default_org'`, or a tenant renamed and re-typed — stays NULL and keeps working on the text branch. How many is a §15 question; no work-package session can reach the database.

columns.name: avatar_color
columns.meaning: The colour of the user's initial on their avatar — one token of a fixed palette, CHECK-constrained; the page maps each token to its fill (`src/lib/avatarColors.ts`, pinned to the CHECK by `avatarColors.test.ts`). §4 D206.

substitutions.when: the user has not chosen a colour (NULL)
substitutions.visible_as: the "Default" swatch, selected, on /profile

ingest.validate: one of the palette tokens in the CHECK

columns.name: first_name
columns.meaning: The first word of `name` (§4 D209), derived by the `approved_users_derive_name_parts` trigger on every write that names `name` or either part, so a value written into it directly is overwritten. Shown read-only on /profile; changed only by an administrator changing `name`.

substitutions.when: always — the column is derived, never authored
substitutions.visible_as: the read-only First name field on /profile

columns.name: last_name
columns.meaning: `name` after its first word (§4 D209); NULL when the name is one word. Derived with `first_name` by the same trigger, read-only on /profile.

substitutions.when: always — the column is derived, never authored
substitutions.value: everything in `name` after its first word (`split_person_name`)
substitutions.visible_as: the read-only Last name field on /profile

approved_users.note: The table WP 1.4 found existed in production but in no migration — the authentication table, untracked for a year, discovered by the orphan rule (D4). `20250815000000_approved_users_base.sql` now builds it on a fresh database, and the parts of that file which are reconstruction rather than evidence are marked as such in it. This sidecar describes the table as the migrations now define it. DELETING A ROW (`admin_delete_user`, `20260930000007`, WP 7.2 (a)): memberships, delegations, AI permissions and capabilities CASCADE; every actor column that records what the person did — `ingest_files.uploaded_by`, `ingest_runs`' two, `analysis_runs.actor_user_id`, `supply_chain_data.uploaded_by` and the rest — is `ON DELETE SET NULL`, so the fact stays and its actor becomes unknown; `audit_logs.actor_user_id` carries no key and keeps the uuid (§4 D161, D213).

audit_logs.grain: One recorded action, on one plane. `admin` is what a super admin did, `data` is a tier transition — a write to tier 2, 3 or 4 — and `access` is a governed decision such as an export being allowed or refused.

governance.note: Two SELECT policies, and they are PERMISSIVE on purpose. A super admin reads every plane; an admin of the SAME ORGANIZATION as the actor reads that org's `data` and `access` rows. They grant DISJOINT slices, so the OR that D28 makes unavoidable is the intended union here rather than an accidental escape hatch — which is worth stating, because the same shape on `approved_users` IS the defect. There is no write policy: rows arrive from SECURITY DEFINER functions and from statement-level triggers, never from a client, so RLS denying writes by default is the enforcement (WP 2.2's pattern). `audited: false` on the audit table is not a joke — nothing records reads of it. What changed in `20260929000001` (§4 D185, D186): no reader in this application can satisfy those policies — the browser calls as `anon` and carries no GUC — so `/admin/audit` reads through `admin_audit_log_read`, which names its reader and requires a super admin, as every /admin RPC does. And the table is WRITE-ONCE and HASH-CHAINED: `audit_logs_guard` refuses DELETE, TRUNCATE and every UPDATE but the sealer's, and `admin_audit_log_verify` names the first edited, re-linked or missing row. A deletion now leaves a trace — except by a table owner who disables the guard and rewrites the chain from some row onward or cuts its tail, which only a chain head recorded OUTSIDE the database can reveal. The page shows the head for that reason.

policies.name: audit: org admins read their own org's data and access rows
policies.using: plane IN ('data','access') AND EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.approved_users me JOIN public.approved_users actor ON actor.id = audit_logs.actor_user_id WHERE me.id = public.get_current_user_id() AND me.role = 'admin'::public.app_role AND me.organization_id IS NOT NULL AND me.organization_id = actor.organization_id )
policies.with_check: plane IN ('data','access') AND EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.approved_users me JOIN public.approved_users actor ON actor.id = audit_logs.actor_user_id WHERE me.id = public.get_current_user_id() AND me.role = 'admin'::public.app_role AND me.organization_id IS NOT NULL AND me.organization_id = actor.organization_id )

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: The row's identity. Returned by the emit functions so a caller can cite what it wrote.

columns.name: actor_user_id
columns.meaning: Who did it. NULLABLE, and the null carries meaning: a service-role write with no session context has no attributable actor.
columns.note: NO FOREIGN KEY since `20260929000001` (§4 D186). It was `REFERENCES approved_users ON DELETE SET NULL`, which is an UPDATE of a sealed row the moment a person who acted is deleted — so the key is gone, the row keeps the uuid, and the person's name and email leave with their `approved_users` row (the page says "deleted user"). THE HONEST LIMIT OF THIS TABLE. `audit_tier_write()` reads `get_current_user_id()`, which resolves only when the caller set `app.current_user_id`. The ingest and ETL edge functions run as the service role and do not, so their rows say WHAT changed and WHEN and record `actor_known: false` in `after` rather than inventing a WHO. That is worth having and it is not attribution; closing it means those functions setting user context, which is their change to make (§16, WP 2.3).

columns.name: action
columns.meaning: What happened. Admin-plane rows use the existing dotted vocabulary (`org.update`, `api_key.revoke`); data-plane rows use the SQL operation (`insert`, `update`, `delete`); access-plane rows use `export.allowed` / `export.refused`, and since `20260929000001` `auth.sign_in` / `auth.sign_in_failed`, written by `authenticate_approved_user` after the database has checked the password (throttled to one per person per minute; a failed attempt names the ACCOUNT as target and no actor). Three vocabularies in one column, which is a cost of one table and is recorded here rather than discovered by a reader.

columns.name: target_type
columns.meaning: What kind of thing was acted on — a table name on the data plane, an entity name on the others.

columns.name: target_id
columns.meaning: Which one, as text. NULL on data-plane rows: a statement-level trigger records a STATEMENT, and a statement that touched 5,000 rows has no single id.

columns.name: before
columns.meaning: The prior state, where the writer knows it. Admin RPCs capture it; data-plane trigger rows do NOT — a statement-level trigger has the transition tables but writing 5,000 prior rows into one jsonb would make the log unreadable and unbounded. Their row COUNT is in `after` instead.

columns.name: after
columns.meaning: The resulting state, or — on a data-plane row — the shape of the statement: `tier`, `rows_after`, `rows_before`, `actor_known` and (since `20260929000001`) `projects`, the distinct `project_id`s it touched, at most 20. On an access-plane row it carries the decision and what was asked for.

columns.name: ip
columns.meaning: Caller IP where the writer recorded one. Never set by the triggers, which run inside the database.

columns.name: user_agent
columns.meaning: Caller user agent where the writer recorded one. As with `ip`, absent on trigger-written rows.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When it happened. Server-stamped — since `20260929000001` the guard overwrites whatever an INSERT supplies with now(), so a row cannot be back-dated — and the column the plane index orders by.

columns.name: plane
columns.meaning: Which plane the action belongs to — `admin`, `data` or `access`, CHECK-constrained. Added by WP 2.3; every row that predates it is `admin` by construction, because the only writer was `log_admin_action()`, which refuses anyone who is not a super admin.

substitutions.when: a row is written without naming a plane
substitutions.visible_as: the column default, which is also what makes the `admin_audit_logs` compatibility view writable for callers that have not moved yet

columns.name: seq
columns.meaning: The row's position in the hash chain (§4 D186), 1-based and gapless. NULL until `audit_log_seal()` chains the row, which it does right after the insert unless another transaction is sealing, in which case the next seal picks it up. Unique, so a fork is an error rather than a second chain.

columns.name: prev_hash
columns.meaning: The `row_hash` of the row at `seq - 1` (64 zeros for the first). What makes a deleted or replaced row visible: the next row stops pointing at anything real.

columns.name: row_hash
columns.meaning: sha256, hex, over `prev_hash`, `seq` and every content column (`audit_log_digest`). An edited row no longer matches it. The newest one is the chain HEAD, which is what must be recorded outside the database to detect a rewrite or a cut tail.

audit_logs.note: Coverage on the data plane is by TRIGGER, not by instrumented RPCs, and the difference is the point. WP 2.3's gap check measured 22 live SQL functions writing tier 2/3/4 with none emitting an audit row, plus six more write paths in edge functions running as the service role. Editing the 22 would have been the obvious reading of "emit on every tier transition" and would have missed all six, and would have missed the twenty-third function somebody writes next month. A statement-level trigger on each of the twelve tier 2/3/4 tables catches every writer that exists and every writer added later.

bom_multi_level.tier_name: canonical — the only tier humans edit
bom_multi_level.grain: One child-to-parent line of a deep bill of materials: this material is consumed by this higher-level component, at this level of the tree. Collapsed to effective product-to-material arcs before the engine sees it. UNIQUE on `natural_key_intended` since WP 3.3 (`20260916000018`), and the index is NULLS NOT DISTINCT because a ROOT line has no parent — without that clause the constraint would hold every line except the roots (D5 closed).

governance.note: `write` names the capability that exists today. WP 2.2 splits `data_editing` into `data_edit_inputs` (tier 2) and `data_edit_policies` (tier 4); this row becomes `data_edit_inputs` then, and all twelve sidecars change together.

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate row identifier. Carries no meaning and joins to nothing.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this row belongs to. Every read is scoped by it.

engine.transform: filter, never read as a value

ingest.validate: set from the selected project, never from the CSV

columns.name: plant_name
columns.meaning: The focal plant this row belongs to, by NAME. A displayable string used as a join key — the thing invariant G1 forbids; WP 2.1/3.3 replace it with a uuid.

ingest.validate: must equal the project's plant_name — a trigger raises otherwise

columns.name: material_id
columns.meaning: The material this line is about — the CHILD in the parent/child pair.

engine.transform: str(); multi-level rows are folded into product->material arcs

ingest.validate: non-empty after trim — this ingest function is the correct pattern to copy

columns.name: level
columns.meaning: Depth in the BOM tree. Level 1 is directly under the finished product; higher numbers are deeper.

engine.transform: int()

ingest.validate: integer >= 0 — level 0 is a root component, which both live parsers admit and always have (WP 3.2 §16)

resolution.note: Depth in the BOM tree is structure, not measurement.

columns.name: higher_level_component_id
columns.meaning: The parent this material feeds. Empty at the top of the tree, where the parent is the finished product itself.

engine.transform: str(); NULL means 'the product'

ingest.validate: may be blank only at the root level

columns.name: consumption_rate
columns.unit: units of material per unit of parent
columns.meaning: How many units of this material one unit of the parent consumes. An engineering fact, never estimated (WP 1.3).

engine.transform: float(); multiplied down the tree when collapsing; a falsy value becomes 1.0

resolution.note: estimable_from is EMPTY and that is a positive statement, not an omission. This is an engineering or commercial fact that someone knows exactly — it is written on a drawing, in a contract, or on a machine's nameplate. Fitting a distribution to it would produce a number with error bars around something that has no error, and the error bars would be believed. A future estimator reading this contract must refuse this field. Same rule as bom_single_level.consumption_rate, and more important here: multi-level rates multiply down the tree, so an estimate at level 3 propagates into every product above it.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When the row last changed. Server-set.

columns.name: ingest_run_id
columns.meaning: The ingestion run that last wrote this row (WP 3.3), and through it the project, the source kind and who approved the promotion. NULL for every row that predates the CSV landing path, and for rows whose run has since been deleted — a null here means the provenance is UNKNOWN, never that there was none. capabilities.grain: One thing a user may or may not be permitted to do — a page they may open or a feature they may use. The CATALOG: it says what rights exist, never who holds them. The four grant tables answer that.

governance.note: Read is open — every client needs the catalog to render a permissions screen, and the rows contain no tenant data. Writes are service-role only, and in practice happen in migrations: a capability is introduced by the feature that needs it, not by an administrator at runtime.

columns.name: key
columns.meaning: The capability's identity, and the string every grant table and every call site names. Page keys are ROUTES (`/policies`); feature keys are snake_case verbs (`data_edit_inputs`). The convention is not enforced by a CHECK.

columns.name: kind
columns.meaning: `page` or `feature`, CHECK-constrained. The resolver aggregates the two separately and returns them under separate keys, so the distinction is load-bearing rather than descriptive.

columns.name: label
columns.meaning: The human name shown on permission screens.

columns.name: description
columns.meaning: One sentence on what holding it lets you do. Nullable.

columns.name: sort_order
columns.meaning: Display order on permission screens. Presentation only.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the capability was added to the catalog. Server-stamped.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When its metadata last changed. Server-stamped.

capabilities.note: THE CATALOG IS DUPLICATED IN TYPESCRIPT. `src/lib/capabilities.ts` carries the same keys as a union type and a list, because the client needs them without a round trip. Two hand-maintained copies of one fact is an I1 violation waiting to drift — `projectMembership.test.ts` asserts the WP 2.2 keys agree, but nothing checks the whole catalog, and the honest count is that the DB has grown keys the TS list learned about only when someone noticed. Generating one from the other is the fix and it belongs with the contract's other generators, not here.

customers.tier_name: canonical — the only tier humans edit
customers.grain: One customer of one project — the demand-side counterpart of `suppliers`. The key is the customer's identifier AS THE SOURCE FILE SPELLS IT, scoped to the project, so the same company appearing in two projects is two rows and stays two rows.

governance.note: Adopted with RLS enabled and no `anon` policy. The logistics lanes carry an `*_anon_read` policy because the public network pages render them (D28, a standing decision); nothing reads this table at all, so there was no reader to keep working and no reason to widen that exposure. `audited: true` was NOT the first draft. The adoption was written with the three WP 2.3 triggers left off — the table had had no migration when they were written, so it had never had them — and `dataPlaneAudit.test.ts` failed on the same commit that put the table in the contract. Its rule is derived from the contract's own tier, not from a list, so a tier-2 table without its triggers is a failure by construction. The triggers are in `20260916000003_adopt_customers_drop_product_code_map.sql` and R9 holds this field to them.

constraints.definition: FOREIGN KEY (project_id) REFERENCES public.projects(id) ON DELETE CASCADE

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this customer belongs to. Scoping is what makes `customer_id` a key: the same company in two projects is two rows, and merging them would merge two customers' models.

columns.name: customer_id
columns.meaning: The customer's identifier as the source file spells it. Joins to `outbound_logistics.customer_id`, which is the only place the identifier is used today — and the join is by string, untrimmed, which is D8's shape. IT IS ALSO THE UPLOAD KEY since WP 6.2 (§4 D108): the same string the outbound file spells, so a customer row and its lanes meet on the value the user typed rather than on a normalisation neither file performed.

columns.name: name
columns.meaning: The customer's display name. Nullable; never a join key (G1).

columns.name: segment
columns.meaning: The customer's service segment, the axis the customer-echelon allocation policies tier on (`P-C.x`, blueprint §4.2 and Appendix A). NOT a closed vocabulary yet — there is no CHECK, because the set a CHECK would name is the user's own segmentation and inventing it before anybody can write the table is how a column gets a constraint nobody can satisfy.

engine.consumed_by: P-C.2 customer_allocation — Customer.segment, the axis `sla_tiers` keys its fill floors by, and what the `fill_rate_segment_<segment>` KPIs are named after
engine.missing_default: "default" (Customer.segment's own default) — every customer in one segment, so no `sla_tiers` key can match and every declared floor resolves to 0.0

ingest.validate: optional; any string. Blank lands NOTHING and the column's own DEFAULT 'default' stands in — which is a value and not an absence, so the landing reports it as a substitution rather than leaving the cell silent (T2).

columns.note: DEFAULT 'default' is production's own default, adopted rather than chosen. It is a value, not an absence, and a later reader must not treat it as "unsegmented" without saying so at the point of display (§5 T2). DECLARED IN WP 6.2 (§4 D94), which is what closed the blank above rather than the trace alone. `p_c2_customer_allocation.data_requirements` named one field — `outbound_logistics.volume` — while reading this column and `priority_weight` on every run, so `consumed_by: null` here had nothing to contradict it. The requirement is declared now, at level `defaulted` because `Customer` carries a default, and the gate that fell out of it is the inverse of the one `contract:generate` already enforces: an IMPLEMENTED policy's declared data requirement may not be `consumed_by: null` in the sidecar. TRACED IN WP 6.2 (§4 D69). This is the column whose absence was silent in a second way: `P-C.2`'s `sla_tiers` guarantees a fill floor PER SEGMENT, and the mapper gave every customer the entity default `"default"`, so no tier could ever match and every floor was 0.0. The engine already warned (`unknown_sla_segment` in P-C.2's feasibility) — the warning named the symptom while nothing named the cause, because the segments it compared against were a constant.

columns.name: priority_weight
columns.meaning: Relative allocation priority when demand exceeds supply. Dimensionless and relative — only the RATIO between two customers means anything, so a row at 1.0 is not "one unit" of anything.

engine.consumed_by: P-C.2 customer_allocation — Customer.priority_weight, the default priority of each of the customer's rows under the `priority` and `sla_tier` rules wherever the `priority_weights` param does not name the customer and no Customer-row override (`row_priority`, WP 14.3) does
engine.missing_default: 1.0 (Customer.priority_weight's own default) — every customer equal, so the `priority` rule cannot order anything

ingest.validate: optional; >= 0. ZERO IS ALLOWED AND MEANS SOMETHING: only the ratio between two customers matters, so 0 is the lowest priority there is — served last, and only out of what is left. `exclusive_min` would reject a value the engine reads correctly. Blank lands nothing and the DEFAULT 1.0 stands in, which makes the `priority` rule inert for that customer.

columns.note: TRACED IN WP 6.2 (§4 D69), AND THE PREVIOUS NOTE'S REASON WAS FALSE. It read: "`scsim` has no customer-priority concept today … none of [the `P-C.x` policies] is implemented". `p_c2_customer_allocation` is `status: implemented` in the registry export and has always read `Customer.priority_weight`. What was true is the CONSEQUENCE — nothing reached it — but the cause was the mapper never loading this table, not an absent policy, and the stated reason sent the next reader to the blueprint instead of to `project_map.py`. The blank was still correct while it lasted: `from_project_data` built `Customer(id=c, name=c)` from the outbound arcs, so every customer arrived at 1.0 whatever this column held. The mapper now reads it. AND IT IS DECLARED SINCE WP 6.2 (§4 D94). The mapper reading a column is the hop; the registry DECLARING it is what every tool deriving "what the engine reads" was missing — this sidecar, `project_map`'s requirement list and WP 6.1's resolution-chain door 1 were all blind to a field the engine consumes on every run.

columns.name: sla_fill_floor_pct
columns.meaning: The minimum fill rate the customer is contracted to receive, as a percentage. NULLABLE, and the null means "no contracted floor" — not zero. A reader that coerces it to 0 turns "unconstrained" into "no service required", which is D17's error in the other direction.

engine.consumed_by: project_map.py::_build_customers -> Customer.sla_fill_floor_pct; P-C.2 customer_allocation — each of the customer's rows' default service target under the `sla_tier` rule
engine.transform: clamped 0-100 (warned); a Customer-row override on /policies (`sla_fill_floor_pct`) beats it for that row
engine.missing_default: no floor — the segment's `sla_tiers` floor applies, else none

ingest.validate: optional; 0-100 (a percentage of the row's demand). Blank lands nothing — no floor, not 0

columns.note: CONSUMED SINCE PLAN.md §24 WP 14.3 (§4 D284 c). The floor is per CUSTOMER × PRODUCT ROW now, not per segment, so this column is the default service target of each of the customer's rows under `sla_tier`, and the segment's `sla_tiers` floor applies only where it is empty. The question that kept it out — two customers of one segment disagreeing — has no answer to invent once the floor belongs to the row. UPLOADABLE SINCE WP 14.3 too: the customers template withheld it on purpose while nothing read it (§4 D18), and offers it now that the engine does. Before WP 14.3: NOT TRACED — `Customer` had no field for it and the per-segment param could not hold a per-customer floor (§4 D69, D94).

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When the row was last modified. Server-stamped.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was first inserted. Server-stamped.

columns.name: ingest_run_id
columns.meaning: The ingestion run that last wrote this row (WP 6.2, §4 D108), and through it the file, the uploader and who approved the promotion. NULL for every row that predates the CSV landing path — and on THIS table that is every row written before `20260919000001`, because until then nothing in the product wrote it at all: the only way a row got here was a hand at the database. A null means the provenance is unknown, never that there was none.

columns.name: source_row_id
columns.meaning: The tier-1 staged row this was promoted from (WP 6.2). Its `source_row_number` is the physical line of the uploaded file, header = line 1, so a person can be shown the LINE rather than told a file name. `ON DELETE SET NULL` and DEFERRABLE, because staging dies with its run and a customer belongs to the project rather than to the run.

customers.note: ADOPTED IN PHASE 3 / WP 3.0 (D43). This table existed in the production database with six rows and no creating migration, and it was invisible to the `no-orphan-table` gate for a reason worth keeping: R4 catches tables the CODE READS that no migration creates, and nothing has ever read this one. §15's schema probe — which keys on "production has it" rather than "the code reads it" — is what found it, and that probe now fails the verification run rather than reporting. TWO OF ITS COLUMNS ARE READ SINCE WP 6.2 (§4 D69): `segment` and `priority_weight` reach `P-C.2 customer_allocation`, because the mapper now loads this table instead of synthesizing `Customer(id=c, name=c)` from the outbound arcs. The sentence that stood here — "NOTHING READS IT YET, and the sidecar says so in every `consumed_by: null`" — was true of the outcome and wrong about the cause, and it gave that wrong cause twice more in the column notes below. It is not dead: its columns are the inputs of the customer-echelon policies (`P-C.x`), which is why it was adopted rather than dropped the way `product_code_map` was in the same migration. What it still lacks is a WRITER and a CSV template, and that gap is now BINDING rather than tidy: two of its columns reach the engine and no surface in this product writes them, so the values deciding who is served when supply is short can only arrive by hand in the database (§4 D94).

dataset_versions.tier_name: derived — a pure function of tier 2
dataset_versions.grain: One frozen snapshot of a project's tier-2 data, with the hash that identifies it. The trust anchor: a run that names a dataset_version can be reproduced, and one that does not cannot.

governance.note: Written by the `_build_dataset_snapshot` database function, never by a page — that is the INTENT, and `write: null` records it. **And since WP 11.1 the database enforces it** (§4 D265): from WP 2.4 to WP 11.1 the live policy `dataset_versions_insert_all` was `FOR INSERT ... WITH CHECK (true)` with an INSERT grant to `anon` and `authenticated`, pinned by `governanceEnforcement.test.ts` rather than changed. No path inserted a row directly, and from WP 11.1 a planted row would also have minted level versions, so the policy is dropped and the grant revoked; `snapshot_dataset` (SECURITY DEFINER) and the service role are the writers. Reads stay open to every API role (`dataset_versions_read_all`, part of D28's pinned list).

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate identifier for the version. Referenced by runs.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this snapshot is of.

engine.transform: filter, never read as a value

columns.name: label
columns.meaning: A human-chosen name for this version, so a user can say which one they mean.
columns.note: Display only. Not read by the engine and deliberately not part of the hash — renaming a version must not change its identity.

columns.name: snapshot
columns.meaning: The frozen tier-2 rows themselves, as JSON. What the run actually ran against, not a pointer to rows that may since have changed.

engine.consumed_by: sim-command -> the dataset a run is pinned to
engine.transform: built by _build_dataset_snapshot from the project's tier-2 tables

columns.note: `schema_version: 2` since WP 4.1 (`20260917000002`), and the shape changed with it: the tables now sit under two keys, `inputs` (what a SIMULATION reads) and `network` (what the multi-tier ANALYSES read), where v1 held them at the top level. A row written before that migration still holds the v1 shape and always will — nothing rewrites a frozen version — so any reader of this column handles both. `verifiableExports.ts` does. The rule for WHAT is in it changed too, and that is the point: v1 mirrored `datamap.py` by hand and missed three things as the engine moved on (D11, D67). v2 hashes every VALUE column of every tier-2 input table — everything but the surrogate `id`, `project_id`, the audit timestamps, the ingestion provenance and the cosmetic `name` — and `graphHashCoverage.test.ts` fails when a tier-2 value column is missing from it.

columns.name: graph_hash
columns.meaning: The fingerprint of the snapshot. Two runs with the same graph_hash saw the same world; two with different hashes did not.

engine.consumed_by: sim-command and the run-identity reuse check -> simulation_runs.graph_hash
engine.transform: hashed from the snapshot by _build_dataset_snapshot

columns.note: D11 and D67 CLOSED by WP 4.1: the snapshot now covers `bom_multi_level` (which `datamap.py` PREFERS over the single-level table), `lead_time_unit`, `demand_min`/`demand_max` and `customers`, and every row ordering is the table's UNIQUE natural key rather than a hand-picked prefix, so the same data cannot hash two ways (D68). Equal hashes now prove equal inputs for every tier-2 table the contract describes; what they still do not cover is the four DERIVED network tables, which are WP 4.2's and deliberately out — a derived artifact inside the identity of its own inputs is the confusion I5 exists to prevent. COMPOSITE since WP 4.1: SHA-256 over `{schema_version, hash_inputs, hash_network}`, so it decomposes into the two columns beside it and `supabase/rehearsal/110` fails if it stops doing so. The name and the place in `simulation_runs` are unchanged on purpose (§11) — a rename is a migration across every reader.

columns.name: author_user_id
columns.meaning: Who froze this version.
columns.note: Governance, not a parameter — and the closest thing the data plane has to the actor-naming audit row I-G4 requires. WP 2.3 generalises it.

columns.name: author_email
columns.meaning: The author's email, denormalized so the version survives the user record.
columns.note: Governance display. A displayable name stored beside the uuid — acceptable here precisely because `author_user_id` is the join key and this is not (G1).

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the version was frozen. Server-set.

columns.name: hash_inputs
columns.meaning: SHA-256 over the `inputs` domain of the snapshot — the tier-2 tables a SIMULATION reads. When this moves, a run stamped with the old composite cannot be reproduced.

engine.consumed_by: current_hash_inputs() -> staleness display; not read by the engine
engine.transform: sha256 over snapshot->'inputs', computed inside snapshot_dataset

columns.note: NULL on every version frozen before WP 4.1 and NOT BACKFILLABLE: a v1 snapshot has no `inputs` key and the rows it was built from have moved on. A NULL here means "this version predates the split", never "this version has no inputs", and a reader that treats the two as the same is reporting an absence as a fact.

columns.name: hash_network
columns.meaning: SHA-256 over the `network` domain — `tier2_suppliers`, `tier3_suppliers`, `multi_tier_supply_chain`, and since `schema_version` 3 the deep-tier topology itself: the six columns the two prominence RPCs return from `network_nodes` and `network_edges`. When this moves a multi-tier or deep-tier ANALYSIS is stale; no simulation changes.

engine.consumed_by: current_hash_network() -> staleness display; not read by the engine
engine.transform: sha256 over snapshot->'network', computed inside snapshot_dataset

columns.note: THIS TEXT SAID THREE TABLES UNTIL WP 5.2f, AND `20260917000009` HAD ADDED TWO MORE. WP 5.3 folded the deep-tier topology in to close §4 D75 — a re-uploaded network was being served the previous graph's centralities as a cache hit, because the anchor could not see the tables the two centrality analyzers read. The sidecar was not updated with the migration, and the manual renders this sentence, so the drift would have been published. The original three source tables hold ZERO rows in production (§15); the two deep-tier tables do not, so the domain is no longer the digest of an empty set on every project. NULL before WP 4.1, and not backfillable, for the same reason as `hash_inputs`.

columns.name: hash_product
columns.meaning: SHA-256 over the PRODUCT level (WP 10.1, §4 D235): suppliers, materials, products, customers, the single-level BOM and the inbound / outbound lanes — every column the `inputs` domain hashes except the multi-level BOM. A projection of facts already hashed; the composite does not include it, so adding it moved no `graph_hash`. NULL never — computed for every snapshot that has `inputs`.

columns.name: hash_process
columns.meaning: SHA-256 over the PROCESS level (WP 10.1): `bom_multi_level` and `multi_tier_supply_chain` whole, plus the endpoints and quantities — not the prices — of the single-level BOM and the lanes, and the product ids. Exactly what `rebuild_supply_chain_lanes` builds the two lane graphs from, so the derived lane tables never enter an identity. NULL on a pre-v2 snapshot, which has no `network` domain.

columns.name: hash_firm
columns.meaning: SHA-256 over the FIRM level (WP 10.1): the deep-tier topology (`network_nodes(uid, revenue)`, `network_edges(src_uid, dst_uid, relative_revenue)`) and the tier-2 / tier-3 supplier tables. NULL on a snapshot older than `schema_version` 3, which did not hash the deep tier — a level computed from it would hash an absence, which is not a fact.

columns.name: version_no
columns.meaning: "Graph v7" — one number per CONTENT (`graph_hash`) per project, in order of first appearance, assigned by a BEFORE INSERT trigger (WP 10.1, §4 D234). Since WP 10.1 `snapshot_dataset` returns the OLDEST version of a content, so a reverted edit is the earlier number again; rows that predate that and share a hash share the number.

columns.name: product_version_id
columns.meaning: This snapshot's PRODUCT level version — the `graph_level_versions` row whose content is this row's `hash_product` ("Product graph v3"). With its two siblings it is the snapshot's TUPLE: a snapshot IS its level versions (WP 11.1, §4 D258). Written by the registration trigger the moment the row is frozen.
columns.note: NULL only where `hash_product` is NULL — a snapshot frozen before WP 4.1, whose level the snapshot cannot support. Never defaulted.

columns.name: process_version_id
columns.meaning: This snapshot's PROCESS level version — the `graph_level_versions` row whose content is this row's `hash_process` ("Process graph v3"). With its two siblings it is the snapshot's TUPLE: a snapshot IS its level versions (WP 11.1, §4 D258). Written by the registration trigger the moment the row is frozen.
columns.note: NULL only where `hash_process` is NULL (a snapshot frozen before WP 4.1).

columns.name: firm_version_id
columns.meaning: This snapshot's FIRM level version — the `graph_level_versions` row whose content is this row's `hash_firm` ("Firm graph v3"). With its two siblings it is the snapshot's TUPLE: a snapshot IS its level versions (WP 11.1, §4 D258). Written by the registration trigger the moment the row is frozen.
columns.note: NULL where `hash_firm` is NULL — every snapshot older than `schema_version` 3, which did not hold the deep-tier topology. A NULL here means the snapshot cannot say, never that the project had no deep tier.

columns.name: simulation_version_id
columns.meaning: This snapshot's SIMULATION scope version — the `graph_level_versions` row whose content is this row's `hash_inputs`, the tables the engine reads (WP 11.2, §4 D259, D264). The fourth element of the tuple; what a Validated Model and RunKey v2 bind. NULL where `hash_inputs` is (a snapshot frozen before WP 4.1).

delegation_grants.grain: One temporary, subtractive grant of project access from one person to another. `subtractive-delegation` (§2.1 G3) made real: a grant may never exceed what the grantor holds, and it always ends.

governance.note: `write: null` again literal. SELECT is limited to the grantor, the grantee and super admins; there is NO write policy, so RLS denies writes and `grant_project_delegation()` / `revoke_project_delegation()` are the only way in. That is forced rather than chosen: subtraction has to be CHECKED against the grantor's own level, and a PERMISSIVE policy cannot subtract (D28) — it can only add another OR'd way to say yes. `audited: false` is the uncomfortable one: a privilege grant that writes no audit row is exactly what `audit-actor` (§2.1 G4) exists to prevent, and WP 2.3 owns it. Recorded here rather than left to be noticed. One further writer since D212: `admin_transfer_project` sets `revoked_at` on the live delegations the previous owner granted (the grantor no longer holds a level to subtract from) and, on an organization change, on those held by accounts outside the target organization — logged in its `admin_audit_logs` row.

policies.name: delegation_grants: read own
policies.using: grantor_user_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR grantee_user_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR public.current_is_super_admin()
policies.with_check: grantor_user_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR grantee_user_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR public.current_is_super_admin()

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate identifier for the grant. What revoke takes.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project the grant applies to. A delegation is never org-wide.

columns.name: grantor_user_id
columns.meaning: Who gave it. Their effective project role at the moment of granting is the ceiling on what the grant may contain.

columns.name: grantee_user_id
columns.meaning: Who received it.

columns.name: project_role
columns.meaning: The level granted. Rejected by the RPC if it outranks the grantor's own — the subtractive rule, enforced in one place.

ingest.validate: one of owner / editor / analyst / viewer, and no higher than the grantor's own level

columns.name: expires_at
columns.meaning: When it stops granting. NOT NULL, and the RPC additionally refuses a time already past. A delegation without an end is a membership, and the product has a table for those.

columns.name: rationale
columns.meaning: Why the elevation exists. NOT NULL and non-empty, unlike on `project_members`: a temporary grant of someone else's access is exactly the thing a reviewer will later ask the reason for.

columns.name: revoked_at
columns.meaning: When it was withdrawn early, if it was. Revocation SETS this rather than deleting the row — who held what, and when, survives the withdrawal.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the grant was made. Server-stamped.

delegation_grants.note: Expiry and revocation are both applied inside `effective_project_role()` rather than by each caller, so "did you remember to check expires_at" is not a question any future reader has to answer. Verified against a live PostgreSQL in WP 2.2: a grant exceeding the grantor's level is rejected, one with no expiry is rejected, and a grant whose expiry passes stops granting (PLAN.md §16).

demand_forecasts.tier_name: canonical — the only tier humans edit
demand_forecasts.grain: One forecast BUCKET of one customer × product row: from `period_start`, for one week or one calendar month, this customer is expected to take `quantity` of this product (PLAN.md §24 WP 14.2, ADR 0002 decisions 2 and 7). A series is the row's buckets in date order. The plan reads it as the centre of the row's weekly demand; the simulated world draws actual demand around it.

governance.note: RLS with NO `anon` policy: §4 D28's list of unconditional policies is meant to shrink, and nothing needs one. The run reads through the snapshot (SECURITY DEFINER), the worker as service role, and /policies and the Data map through `get_project_demand_forecasts`, which names its caller. Writes: the project's modeler or an admin, as on `customers`. The three WP 2.3 audit triggers and the WP 10.1 graph-state triggers are created with the table.

policies.name: Demand forecasts: modifiers only
policies.using: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = demand_forecasts.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) AND (p.modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR (SELECT user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1) = 'admin'))
policies.with_check: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = demand_forecasts.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) AND (p.modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR (SELECT user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1) = 'admin'))

constraints.name: demand_forecasts_time_unit_check
constraints.definition: CHECK (time_unit IS NULL OR lower(time_unit) IN ('week', 'month'))

constraints.name: demand_forecasts_source_row_fk
constraints.definition: FOREIGN KEY (source_row_id) REFERENCES public.ingest_staged_rows(id) ON DELETE SET NULL DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate row identifier. Carries no meaning and joins to nothing.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this bucket belongs to. Every read is scoped by it.

engine.transform: filter, never read as a value

ingest.validate: set from the selected project, never from the CSV

columns.name: customer_id
columns.meaning: The customer, spelled as `outbound_logistics.customer_id` spells it — the bucket belongs to that outbound row.

engine.consumed_by: datamap.py::forecast_series -> OutboundArc.forecast of the matching (product, customer) row
engine.transform: str()

columns.name: product_id
columns.meaning: The finished product, spelled as `outbound_logistics.product_id` spells it.

engine.consumed_by: datamap.py::forecast_series -> OutboundArc.forecast of the matching (product, customer) row
engine.transform: str()

columns.name: period_start
columns.meaning: The first day of the bucket. The project's EARLIEST `period_start` is simulated week 0; simulated week w is the seven days starting w·7 days later.

engine.consumed_by: datamap.py::forecast_series -> which simulated weeks the bucket covers
engine.transform: days since the project's earliest period_start

columns.name: time_unit
columns.meaning: How long the bucket is: `week` or `month` (a calendar month from `period_start`). Blank means week. Kept AS UPLOADED — unlike a lane's `time_unit` it is not rewritten at promotion, because it is the bucket's length and the spread below needs it.

ingest.validate: week or month; blank means week

columns.name: quantity
columns.meaning: How much the customer is forecast to take over the WHOLE bucket — 1 000 for a month is 1 000 over that month. Spread evenly over the bucket's days at promotion (decision 7) into `weekly_quantity`; nothing reads this column as a rate.

resolution.note: A forecast is the user's statement of what they expect; it is not estimated here. History-based forecasting (P-F.1) is out of scope for Phase 14 (design doc §8).

columns.note: `unit_source: column` with NO `normalize_at_promotion`, deliberately. The generic `rate` conversion rewrites the unit column to `week`, which would erase the bucket's length; the conversion this column needs is the calendar spread `demand_forecast_spread()` applies in the promoting statement, which writes `period_end` and `weekly_quantity` and leaves `time_unit` as uploaded.

columns.name: period_end
columns.meaning: The bucket's EXCLUSIVE end: `period_start` + 1 week, or + 1 calendar month. Server-computed at promotion; never uploaded.

engine.consumed_by: datamap.py::forecast_series -> which days the bucket covers

columns.name: weekly_quantity
columns.meaning: The bucket's quantity spread evenly over its own days, as a weekly rate: quantity × 7 / days in the bucket (decision 7). A 30-day month of 1 000 units is 233.33 per week. Server-computed at promotion; the only quantity the run reads.

engine.consumed_by: datamap.py::forecast_series -> the daily rate weekly_quantity / 7 over the bucket's days
engine.transform: summed per simulated week over the days that week shares with the bucket

columns.name: ingest_run_id
columns.meaning: The ingestion run that last wrote this row, and through it the file, the uploader and who approved the promotion. Set by `ingest_apply_run` and by nothing else.

columns.name: source_row_id
columns.meaning: The tier-1 staged row this was promoted from; its `source_row_number` is the physical line of the uploaded file. `ON DELETE SET NULL`, DEFERRABLE.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was inserted. Server-set.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When the row last changed. Server-set.

disruption_scenario_effects.grain: One effect for one profile: WHAT the disruption does to whatever it hits. A capacity reduction or a time delay, with a magnitude and the unit that magnitude is in.

governance.note: Tier 4 — the DECISION plane. Audited from WP 6.4.

policies.name: Scenario effects: organization access view
policies.using: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.disruption_scenario_profiles sp JOIN public.projects p ON p.id = sp.project_id WHERE sp.id = disruption_scenario_effects.profile_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) )
policies.with_check: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.disruption_scenario_profiles sp JOIN public.projects p ON p.id = sp.project_id WHERE sp.id = disruption_scenario_effects.profile_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) )

policies.name: Scenario effects: project access modify
policies.using: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.disruption_scenario_profiles sp JOIN public.projects p ON p.id = sp.project_id WHERE sp.id = disruption_scenario_effects.profile_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) AND (p.modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR ( SELECT g.user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() g LIMIT 1 ) = 'admin') )
policies.with_check: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.disruption_scenario_profiles sp JOIN public.projects p ON p.id = sp.project_id WHERE sp.id = disruption_scenario_effects.profile_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) AND (p.modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR ( SELECT g.user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() g LIMIT 1 ) = 'admin') )

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key. The natural key is below; this is what the child rows reference.

columns.name: profile_id
columns.meaning: The profile this effect belongs to. ON DELETE CASCADE.

columns.name: effect_type
columns.meaning: `capacity_reduction` or `time_delay`, as the `disruption_effect_type` enum. It decides which units `unit` may legally carry, and `validate_disruption_effect` enforces that on write.

columns.name: magnitude
columns.meaning: How much. Its meaning depends entirely on `effect_type` and `unit`: a capacity reduction is a percentage, a time delay a count of time. NOT NULL, so an effect always states a size.
columns.note: Reaches no engine field directly: the scenario runner reads it with `effect_type` and `unit`, which together decide what the number means. `validate_disruption_effect` is what keeps the three consistent on write, and it is the only such trigger in this group.

columns.name: unit
columns.meaning: The unit `magnitude` is in. A TEXT column rather than the canonical `UNIT_DAYS` vocabulary that governs tier-2 lead times, because a decision's unit is whatever the person chose and is converted where it is read — `normalize-at-promotion` (I3) governs observations, not decisions.

columns.name: organization
columns.meaning: The tenant's DISPLAY NAME, carried on every row of this vintage. `uuid- identity` (G1) says a displayable name is never a join key: nothing joins on this, and `organization_id` is the identity. Kept because the rows exist.

columns.name: created_by
columns.meaning: The user who created the row, as a uuid. Client-asserted — this application authenticates against `approved_users` rather than Supabase Auth (D28) — so it names who the client said acted, which is why the audit row added by WP 6.4 is the record that matters.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was created. Server-stamped, never the client's clock.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When it was last changed. Server-stamped by the `update_*_updated_at` trigger.

disruption_scenario_effects.note: THE ONLY TABLE IN THIS GROUP WHOSE PAYLOAD IS VALIDATED. `validate_disruption_effect` fires BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE and checks `magnitude` and `unit` against `effect_type` — so an effect cannot carry a unit its type does not admit. `_targets` has the same discriminator shape and no such trigger, which is worth noticing when reading the two side by side.

disruption_scenario_profiles.grain: One disruption profile for one project — the HEADER of the normalised disruption model. What it hits lives in `_targets`, what it does in `_effects`, and how it is simulated in `_settings`; all three cascade from this row.

governance.note: Tier 4 — the DECISION plane. Audited from WP 6.4. The three child tables cascade from this row's id, so a DELETE here is four tables' worth of decision disappearing on one statement — which is exactly why the audit row naming the actor matters more here than on a table that loses one row.

policies.name: Scenario profiles: organization access view
policies.using: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = disruption_scenario_profiles.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) )
policies.with_check: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = disruption_scenario_profiles.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) )

policies.name: Scenario profiles: project access modify
policies.using: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = disruption_scenario_profiles.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) AND (p.modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR ( SELECT g.user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() g LIMIT 1 ) = 'admin') )
policies.with_check: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = disruption_scenario_profiles.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) AND (p.modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR ( SELECT g.user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() g LIMIT 1 ) = 'admin') )

constraints.name: disruption_scenario_profiles_project_id_fkey
constraints.definition: FOREIGN KEY (project_id) REFERENCES projects(id) ON DELETE CASCADE

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key. The natural key is below; this is what the child rows reference.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this row belongs to.

columns.name: plant_name
columns.meaning: The plant this scenario belongs to, by display name. A project has one plant_name, so this is a denormalised copy of `projects.plant_name` rather than a second identity.

columns.name: scenario_name
columns.meaning: What the person called this profile. Not unique — two profiles may share a name, and the surrogate id is the key.

columns.name: status
columns.meaning: `draft`, `active` or `archived`, as the `disruption_status` enum. CHECKed by the type rather than by a constraint, so an unknown value is refused at cast time.

columns.name: description
columns.meaning: Free text the person wrote. Never parsed.

columns.name: tags
columns.meaning: Free-form labels. No vocabulary and no validation — a tag is whatever was typed.

columns.name: organization
columns.meaning: The tenant's DISPLAY NAME, carried on every row of this vintage. `uuid- identity` (G1) says a displayable name is never a join key: nothing joins on this, and `organization_id` is the identity. Kept because the rows exist.

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key. The natural key is below; this is what the child rows reference.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this row belongs to.

columns.name: plant_name
columns.meaning: The plant this scenario belongs to, by display name. A project has one plant_name, so this is a denormalised copy of `projects.plant_name` rather than a second identity.

columns.name: node_id
columns.meaning: The node the disruption is applied to, by its display id — the same string the network pages use. Not a uuid and not a foreign key: a scenario may name a node that no longer exists in the graph, and deleting it silently would lose the decision.

columns.name: scenario_name
columns.meaning: What the person called this scenario. Not unique — see `natural_key_unique` below, which is the surrogate id and nothing else.

columns.name: capacity_reduction_percent
columns.meaning: How much of the node's capacity the scenario removes. A PERCENT, not a fraction: the column name says so and the default of 0 means 'no reduction'.
columns.note: Reaches no engine field. `project_map.py` builds the engine's world from the tier-2 tables and the policy bundle; a disruption is applied by the SIMULATOR at run time from `sim_payload`, not by the mapper from this column. So the value a person types here is read by the scenario runner and by nothing the data contract traces (§5 T1: the number has a source, and that source is this row).

columns.name: time_delay_days
columns.meaning: Additional delay the scenario imposes at this node. DAYS, and it is NOT normalised at promotion the way a tier-2 lead time is — this is a decision the user typed, not an observation, so it is stored as entered and converted where it is read.
columns.note: Reaches no engine field, for the same reason as `capacity_reduction_percent`. Note the unit is in the COLUMN NAME rather than in a unit column — the opposite of the tier-2 convention `lead_time`/`lead_time_unit` that `normalize-at-promotion` (I3) governs. That is defensible for a decision (there is one unit and it cannot vary) and it is worth stating, because a reader who has learned the tier-2 rule will look for the companion column.

columns.name: description
columns.meaning: Free text the person wrote. Never parsed.

columns.name: created_by
columns.meaning: The user who created the row, as a uuid. Client-asserted — this application authenticates against `approved_users` rather than Supabase Auth (D28) — so it names who the client said acted, which is why the audit row added by WP 6.4 is the record that matters.

columns.meaning: The tenant's DISPLAY NAME, carried on every row of this vintage. `uuid- identity` (G1) says a displayable name is never a join key: nothing joins on this, and `organization_id` is the identity. Kept because the rows exist.
