columns.name: sim_payload
columns.meaning: The scenario as the simulator receives it, frozen at save time. A denormalised copy of the columns above plus whatever the caller added; nothing reads it back into the columns, so a divergence between the two is possible and unnoticed.

columns.name: from_network
columns.meaning: Whether the scenario was created by clicking a node on a network page (true) or entered by hand. Defaults true, so a row written by any other path claims a provenance it may not have.

disruption_scenarios.note: TWO DISRUPTION MODELS ARE LIVE AT ONCE AND NEITHER READS THE OTHER. This table is the 2025-08-26 shape — one row per node, capacity and delay inline. The `disruption_scenario_profiles`/`_targets`/`_effects`/`_settings` group is the 2025-08-27 redesign that normalises the same idea. Nothing migrated the rows and nothing deprecates either, so a project can hold disruptions in both and a reader of one sees half the picture. Naming that is this sidecar's job; deciding it is not, and it belongs with WP 6.4's gap check.

docs_faq.grain: One question and its prepared answer, shown on the manual's Questions & answers page. Authored by super admins from /admin/docs; readers only read.

governance.note: RLS on and NO policy, deliberately: an unpublished answer, or one about a section the reader may not open, must not be one PostgREST query away. Readers go through `docs_list_faq(p_user_id)`, which applies the Q&A section's audience AND the audience of the section each answer is about; super admins through `admin_list_docs_faq`. Writes are `admin_save_docs_faq` / `admin_delete_docs_faq`, each writing an `admin_audit_logs` row. The reader id is client-asserted (§4 D28), so the filter is as strong as this application's sign-in. An answer should LINK to the page that owns a fact rather than restate it (PLAN.md §6.1 rule 2) — `check:docs` cannot see database content.

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate id, `gen_random_uuid()`.

columns.name: question
columns.meaning: The question as a reader would ask it. Non-blank, and unique — the natural key, which also lets the seed re-run without duplicating.

columns.name: answer
columns.meaning: The prepared answer, as Markdown rendered with raw HTML disabled. Links into the manual are written `/docs/<slug>`.

columns.name: section_key
columns.meaning: The manual section the question is about, by registry section key, or NULL for a general question. That section's audience applies on top of the Q&A section's own, so an answer about a confidential section stays confidential.

columns.name: related_slugs
columns.meaning: Manual pages the answer points readers to, by slug. Presentation only; an unknown slug is ignored by the reader page.

columns.name: sort_order
columns.meaning: Display order within the list. Presentation only.

columns.name: is_published
columns.meaning: Whether readers may see it at all. A draft is listed only to super admins.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the entry was created. Server-stamped.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When the entry last changed. Server-stamped by the writer.

columns.name: created_by
columns.meaning: The super admin who created it; NULL for the seeded answers.

columns.name: updated_by
columns.meaning: The super admin who last changed it; NULL for the seeded answers.

docs_section_releases.grain: One section of the /docs manual and who may read it. A row per registry section KEY; a section with no row is read as confidential by the database and the client alike, so a section added later is closed until a super admin opens it.

governance.note: Read is open to anon and authenticated — the /docs gate needs it BEFORE sign-in to know whether a public section may render, and a row says only which sections are open, whose titles are already in the bundle. There is no write policy; the one writer is `admin_set_docs_section_audience`, which asserts an active super admin and writes an `admin_audit_logs` row naming them. `audited: false` means no data-plane trigger, which this tier-G table does not carry; the admin audit row is the record. What an audience protects is presentation, not secrecy: page bodies are compiled into the app bundle (PLAN.md §6.5).

columns.name: section_key
columns.meaning: The registry's stable section key (`DocGroup.key` in `src/components/docs/registry.ts`), not §6.3's section number, so renumbering a section cannot hand its audience to another. CHECK-constrained to a lowercase slug shape; the key SET is the registry's, and `docsRelease.test.ts` compares the seed against it.

columns.name: audience
columns.meaning: `public` (anyone, signed in or not), `internal` (any signed-in account) or `confidential` (super admins and accounts holding the `docs_confidential` capability). CHECK-constrained; no DEFAULT, so a row always states its audience.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When the audience last changed. Server-stamped by the writer.

columns.name: updated_by
columns.meaning: The super admin who last changed it. NULL for the seeded rows and after that account is deleted.

experiments.tier_name: results — pinned to dataset + policy + engine version
experiments.grain: One designed experiment over a project: a name, a design (full factorial or Latin hypercube), the factors and levels it varies, and the `scenarios` it cloned — one per design row — to run. A design a person authors, grouping runs that were MADE to be compared. UNREACHABLE TODAY: the only screen that writes or reads it, `ExperimentDesigner.tsx`, is mounted by no route (§4 D115), so although `useExperiments` reads and writes the table, no page a user can open reaches that code.

governance.note: `write: simulation_lab`, not `null`, because the table's one policy, `experiments_auth_all` (`FOR ALL TO authenticated USING (true) WITH CHECK (true)`), has no predicate, and `governanceEnforcement.test.ts` refuses a `null` write claim on a table any grant-holder may write. The capability is the one that gates designing and running simulations, which is what the unmounted designer does. §4 D154 lists `experiments` among the eleven tables probe 0.8 measured as writable by `anon`, and that listing deserves a qualifier: the probe intersects `anon`'s GRANT with "a write policy that refuses nothing" without asking which ROLES that policy names, and the only policy the migrations give this table is `TO authenticated`. So as far as the repository can see, `anon` holds the grant and RLS refuses it; whether production carries an `anon` policy no migration declares is D158's class of question and only `pg_policies` can answer it. Either way it is D28's standing decision and WP 7.1's to close. `min_project_role` is `viewer` because nothing enforces a role here today, not because a viewer ought to design experiments. Deleting a project removes its experiments (`ON DELETE CASCADE`). A BEFORE UPDATE trigger (`experiments_updated_at`) re-stamps `updated_at`. NOT AUDITED — AND BY MEANING IT SHOULD BE. A row is what a person chose, like `scenarios` and `disruption_scenarios` beside it, and those are tier 4 and audited at statement grain. This one has no audit triggers in any migration, so claiming tier 4 would fail `dataPlaneAudit.test.ts` on the day the contract regenerates. It is held at tier 5 with `audited: false` as the truthful description of the database; moving it to tier 4 means a migration adding the three `audit_tier_write('4')` triggers in the same commit as the tier change — owed by whichever package mounts the designer, because until a page writes it there is no write to attribute.

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key. Nothing makes an experiment's name unique.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The owning project. ON DELETE CASCADE.

columns.name: name
columns.meaning: The experiment's display name, typed by the user or defaulted to "Experiment <n>". Also the prefix of every scenario it clones.

columns.name: design_type
columns.meaning: How the design rows were generated from the factors — DEFAULT 'factorial' (every combination of levels); the designer also writes 'lhs' (a Latin hypercube sample of a chosen size). No CHECK constraint, so the vocabulary is the designer's `DesignType`, not a rule the database enforces.

columns.name: factors
columns.meaning: The factors the experiment varies, as an array of `{key, label, levels}`: a recovery-playbook factor whose levels are playbook ids, and numeric run settings (replications, horizon, warm-up) whose levels are values. The design rows themselves are not stored — they are materialized into the cloned scenarios.
columns.note: Reaches the engine only through the scenarios it was materialized into; the engine never reads this column.

columns.name: scenario_ids
columns.meaning: The `scenarios` the experiment cloned from its base scenario, one per design row, in design order. The results panel reads the latest run of each. An array with no foreign key, so a deleted scenario leaves a dangling element.

columns.name: status
columns.meaning: DEFAULT 'draft'. The designer inserts 'running' and never updates it, so in practice the column says the runs were queued, not that they finished. No CHECK constraint.

columns.name: created_by
columns.meaning: Meant to name the author. `REFERENCES auth.users ON DELETE SET NULL`, and the hook fills it from `supabase.auth.getUser()` — but this application authenticates against `approved_users`, not Supabase Auth, so for a real user the value can only be NULL.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the experiment was created.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When the experiment was last changed — re-stamped by `experiments_updated_at`.

experiments.note: A TABLE WITH A HOOK AND NO PAGE. `src/hooks/useExperiments.tsx` selects, inserts, updates and deletes it and subscribes to its changes; its only caller is `ExperimentDesigner.tsx`, which nothing imports (§4 D115). So there is code that reads and writes this table and no surface a user reaches — which is why this sidecar has no `surfaces` block. Mounting the designer would also meet three defects at once: the policy above admits only `authenticated` while the product runs as `anon` (D28), so the designer's writes would be refused; `created_by` points at `auth.users`, which this application never populates; and an experiment binds its scenarios but not the dataset, policy or engine version they ran against, so it does not satisfy `result-binding`. The runs it queues are ordinary `simulation_runs` rows; the `experiment_id` the designer sends with each is not persisted anywhere, so a run cannot be traced back to its experiment except through `scenario_ids`.

external_evidence.grain: One retrieved external claim about a supply chain, as a subject–predicate–object triple with the source it came from, the confidence attached to it and the hash of the content it was read from. The network cartographer's evidence store: what an agent FOUND, kept apart from what a person entered.

governance.note: Tier 4 — the DECISION plane: what a person or an agent CHOSE, as against the dataset they chose it over and the result it produced. `result-binding` (I8) needs all three, which is why WP 6.3 keeps the results and this package takes the decisions. Audited from WP 6.4: the three statement-grain triggers land beside this sidecar, because `dataPlaneAudit.test.ts` scopes its rule to tables IN the contract and a deferred table's writes are unaudited with nothing to notice (D54). **Its writers are edge functions, not the browser** — `project-ai- chat`'s cartographer and sentinel tools — so the audit trigger names whoever the function's transaction has set, and an agent write with no actor is the D28 question this table inherits rather than answers. The dedupe index is what makes a re-read of the same page a no-op instead of a second claim.

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key. The dedupe key is the four-column unique index below.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project the claim is about.

columns.name: source_id
columns.meaning: Which source produced it — a registry, a filing, a page. CHECK-constrained, so a claim cannot arrive from a source the system does not name.

columns.name: url_or_ref
columns.meaning: Where a person can go and look. NULL where the source has no addressable reference, which is a real state for a registry lookup and not a missing value.

columns.name: content_hash
columns.meaning: The hash of the content the claim was read from. Part of the dedupe key, so the same bytes re-read produce no second row — and a CHANGED page produces a new claim rather than overwriting the old one.

columns.name: retrieved_at
columns.meaning: When it was fetched. The claim is about the world at that moment, and nothing refreshes it.

columns.name: confidence
columns.meaning: How much weight the extractor put on this claim, CHECK-constrained to its range. It is the EXTRACTOR's number, not a person's, and no surface today turns it into a decision.

columns.name: triple
columns.meaning: THE CLAIM — subject, predicate, object as JSON. Hashed into the dedupe key through `md5(triple::text)`, which is why an expression index appears in the natural key above.

columns.name: lei
columns.meaning: The Legal Entity Identifier the claim is about, where one resolved. CHECK-constrained to the LEI shape, and NULL where the subject is not a registered entity — a great many suppliers are not.

graph_level_versions.tier_name: derived — a pure function of tier 2
graph_level_versions.grain: One row per (project, level, content): the FIRST time a project's product, process, firm or simulation level had that hash. Numbered per project PER LEVEL, so "Product graph v3" and "Firm graph v5" are both sentences the system can say, and a change to one level moves that level's number and no other. A snapshot (`dataset_versions`) names its level versions — its tuple.

governance.note: No page and no API role writes it — `anon`, `authenticated` and `service_role` hold SELECT only. ONE writer: `_graph_level_register`, called by a row trigger on `dataset_versions` (insert, and the level-hash backfill `snapshot_dataset` takes on a row frozen before WP 10.1), so every capture point registers its levels and no second capture path exists. It runs inside the statement that froze the snapshot and names that statement's actor, or the snapshot's author when the statement named nobody. Immutable by trigger: the one change a row takes is the cascade that forgets its first snapshot when that snapshot is deleted. Read through `has_project_access`.

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: The level version's identity. A snapshot names it in `product_version_id`, `process_version_id` or `firm_version_id`.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project whose level this is. Cascades with the project.

columns.name: level
columns.meaning: Which level: `product` (item masters, customers, single-level BOM, lanes), `process` (the flow structure the lane graphs are rebuilt from), `firm` (the deep-tier topology and tier 2/3), or `simulation` (the tables the engine reads — the snapshot's `inputs` domain, registered since WP 11.2). The level rules are WP 10.1's; see `dataset_versions.hash_product` and its siblings.

columns.name: level_hash
columns.meaning: The level's content hash, exactly as its snapshot stores it. Unique per project and level: a reverted edit finds the earlier row (deduplicated against ANY earlier version of the level, not the latest).

columns.name: version_no
columns.meaning: "Product graph v3" — one number per content per project per LEVEL, in order of first appearance, assigned by a BEFORE INSERT trigger under a per-(project, level) lock. History was backfilled in each project's `created_at` order, so v1 is the first content the project ever froze at that level.

columns.name: level_spec
columns.meaning: The level rule the hash was computed under (1 since WP 10.1). It is inside each level digest, so a later rule makes new hashes and never collides with these. NULL for `simulation`, whose hash is the `inputs` domain digest and carries no level rule.

columns.name: first_dataset_version_id
columns.meaning: The snapshot that first carried this content — the frozen world a person can open to see it. NULL once that snapshot is deleted; the level version stays, because its content and number remain true of the project.

columns.name: author_user_id
columns.meaning: Who froze the first snapshot — copied from it, not the session, so the backfill names the same person the live path would have.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the project's level first had this content — the first snapshot's `created_at`, so a backfilled row is dated by its history, not by the migration.

columns.name: version_code
columns.meaning: "Data 20260915" for the `simulation` level — the code a person says. The UTC day this level first had this content (`YYYYMMDD`), and `-n` for the n-th content of the level first seen that day. Assigned by the numbering trigger, unique per project and level, and immutable once stored (a row that predates it learns it once, from the backfill).

inbound_logistics.tier_name: canonical — the only tier humans edit
inbound_logistics.grain: One supply arc as the user uploaded it: this supplier can deliver this material to this plant, at this price and lead time, in this volume. UNIQUE on `natural_key_intended` since WP 3.3 (`20260916000018`): a second upload of the same arc UPDATES it rather than adding a row, and the promotion is the upsert that does so (D5 closed).

governance.note: `write` names the capability that exists today. WP 2.2 splits `data_editing` into `data_edit_inputs` (tier 2) and `data_edit_policies` (tier 4); this row becomes `data_edit_inputs` then, and all twelve sidecars change together.

policies.name: Inbound: modifiers only
policies.using: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = inbound_logistics.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) AND (p.modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR ( SELECT user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1 ) = 'admin') )
policies.with_check: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = inbound_logistics.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) AND (p.modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR ( SELECT user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1 ) = 'admin') )

policies.name: Inbound: organization access
policies.using: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = inbound_logistics.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) )
policies.with_check: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = inbound_logistics.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) )

constraints.name: inbound_logistics_lead_time_unit_known
constraints.definition: CHECK (lead_time_unit IS NULL OR public.unit_days(lead_time_unit) IS NOT NULL)

constraints.name: inbound_logistics_source_row_fk
constraints.definition: FOREIGN KEY (source_row_id) REFERENCES public.ingest_staged_rows(id) ON DELETE SET NULL DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED

constraints.name: inbound_logistics_lead_time_spread_check
constraints.definition: CHECK ( (lead_time_dist IS NULL OR lead_time_dist IN ('deterministic', 'normal', 'lognormal', 'gamma', 'triangular', 'uniform')) AND (lead_time_cv IS NULL OR (lead_time_cv >= 0 AND lead_time_cv <= 1)) AND (lead_time_min IS NULL OR lead_time_min >= 0) AND (lead_time_mode IS NULL OR lead_time_mode >= 0) AND (lead_time_max IS NULL OR lead_time_max >= 0) AND (lead_time_min IS NULL OR lead_time_mode IS NULL OR lead_time_min <= lead_time_mode) AND (lead_time_mode IS NULL OR lead_time_max IS NULL OR lead_time_mode <= lead_time_max) AND (lead_time_min IS NULL OR lead_time_max IS NULL OR lead_time_min <= lead_time_max) )

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate row identifier. Carries no meaning and joins to nothing.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this arc belongs to. Every read is scoped by it.

engine.transform: filter, never read as a value

ingest.validate: set from the selected project, never from the CSV

columns.name: plant_name
columns.meaning: The focal plant receiving the material, by NAME. A displayable string used as a join key — the thing invariant G1 forbids; WP 2.1/3.3 replace it with a uuid.

ingest.validate: must equal the project's plant_name — a trigger raises otherwise

columns.name: supplier_id
columns.meaning: The supplier's code as the user's own systems spell it.

engine.transform: str(); no trimming (D8)

ingest.validate: non-empty after trim — NOT enforced today (D8)

columns.name: material_id
columns.meaning: The material's code as the user's own systems spell it. Joins to materials and the BOM.

engine.transform: str(); arcs whose material is not in the BOM are dropped

ingest.validate: non-empty after trim — NOT enforced today (D8)

columns.name: volume
columns.meaning: How much of this material the user buys from this supplier over one `time_unit`. A RATE, not a quantity — two rows are only comparable after both are converted to the same period.

engine.transform: rateToWeekly(volume, time_unit) — normalized to weeks

substitutions.when: the CSV cell is blank (the column lands NULL — optional since 2026-10-09)
substitutions.value: 0 — the arc carries no supply share
substitutions.visible_as: the upload's per-row "defaulted" count on the review screen

ingest.validate: numeric >= 0; a blank cell lands NULL, never 0 (D7) — the arc carries no supply share

resolution.note: Volume is what the user's own systems recorded. It is not estimated; it is the thing other quantities are estimated FROM — demand_mean names it in estimable_from.

columns.name: time_unit
columns.meaning: The period `volume` is quoted over — day, week, month, quarter, year. It describes the VOLUME only. It says nothing about `lead_time`.

engine.transform: looked up in the one unit table

ingest.validate: one of day/week/month/quarter/year and their -ly spellings

resolution.note: A unit is never estimated. Unrecognised or blank is read on a 7-day basis, i.e. as already weekly (grading.ts::rateToWeekly).

columns.name: lead_time
columns.meaning: How long this supplier takes to deliver this material. The contract fixes the unit at WEEKS; `time_unit` does not apply to it and never has.

engine.transform: _duration_to_weeks(lead_time, lead_time_unit), then round and clamp to [1, 51]

substitutions.when: the column is NULL or zero
substitutions.visible_as: MappingWarning on the run's mapping report

resolution.note: The engine already supports this split and has since scsim was written: SupplierLink carries lead_time_weeks (the CENTRE) separately from lead_time_dist and lead_time_cv (the SPREAD), and core/engine.py samples only when the distribution is not DETERMINISTIC and the CV is above zero. So deterministic is not a degenerate case bolted on — it is the default path, and it skips sampling entirely. default_mode is `asserted` for the same reason: the user states the lead time, and the spread is opt-in. estimable_from names the observations tier that does not exist yet (tier 2-O, reserved in WP 1.2) rather than leaving the door open to estimating this from whatever happens to be lying around.

columns.note: Was `unit_source: fixed` until WP 1.3, and fixed by OMISSION rather than by contract: the engine read a `lead_time_unit` that no column supplied, so every lead time was taken as weeks whatever the user meant. The column now exists and `unit` stays `weeks` because that is what NULL still means.

engine_requirement.reason: Supplier lead time per sourcing arc — missing values default to 2 weeks.

columns.name: unit_price
columns.meaning: What one unit of this material costs from this supplier, delivered.

engine.transform: float(); a value <= 0 is replaced, not rejected

substitutions.visible_as: MappingWarning on the run's mapping report

substitutions.value: this arc's price contributes to the material's cost, weighted by this arc's volume share (its cheapest arc when no arc carries a volume)
substitutions.visible_as: the effective-economics badge in /policies

ingest.validate: numeric >= 0; zero lands WITH A WARNING (the engine reads a zero price as 1.0, with a MappingWarning); a blank cell lands NULL and the same 1.0 default stands in

resolution.note: hybrid is NULL because scsim has nowhere to put a spread: cost and unit_price are bare floats on Material and Product, with no distribution, no CV and no sampling path anywhere in the engine. Recording `hybrid: null` here is a statement about the ENGINE, not about the world — prices obviously vary. Giving them a spread is an engine change on the scsim track; see the RFC in PLAN.md §14. Do not invent one in this contract: a contract that describes a capability the engine does not have is how a fallback ends up in code with no contract entry, which is what I6 forbids in the other direction.

columns.note: The user types `unit_price` and the engine calls it `cost`. Both names are recorded because the manual must lead with the one the user typed (D21).

engine_requirement.reason: Purchase cost per sourcing arc — a missing price defaults to 1.0 and distorts procurement spend.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was inserted. Server-set.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When the row last changed. Server-set.

columns.name: lead_time_unit
columns.meaning: The period `lead_time` is quoted in — day, week, month, quarter or year. Blank means WEEKS, which is what the engine assumed before this column existed. Distinct from `time_unit`, which is the period `volume` is quoted over and has never applied to the lead time.

engine.transform: looked up in the one unit table; an unknown value falls to a 7-day basis

ingest.validate: one of the units public.unit_days() knows — enforced by the column's CHECK constraint

resolution.note: A unit is never estimated. NULL means weeks, matching project_map.py::_duration_to_weeks, and the column's CHECK constraint only admits units public.unit_days() knows.

columns.note: Added by WP 1.3 (D9). The engine had read this field since the scsim bridge was written; no column supplied it, so `r.get("lead_time_unit")` returned None on every row and a lead time entered in days was read as weeks — seven times too long, with no warning, because nothing in the chain knew a unit was expected. This is also the first use of the `contract` provenance state reserved in WP 1.2: the weeks default is supplied by this document, not guessed by code.

columns.name: ingest_run_id
columns.meaning: The ingestion run that last wrote this row (WP 3.3), and through it the project, the source kind and who approved the promotion. NULL for every row that predates the CSV landing path, and for rows whose run has since been deleted — a null here means the provenance is UNKNOWN, never that there was none. Set by `ingest_apply_run` and by nothing else.

columns.name: source_row_id
columns.meaning: The tier-1 staged row this was promoted from (WP 3.3). Its `source_row_number` is the physical line of the uploaded file, header = line 1, so a person can be shown the line rather than told a file name — which is what extends A4 down to the source. `ON DELETE SET NULL` and DEFERRABLE: staging is deleted with its run, and a canonical row belongs to the project rather than to the run that last wrote it.

columns.name: lead_time_dist
columns.meaning: The SHAPE of this lane's lead time — deterministic, normal, lognormal, gamma, triangular or uniform (PLAN.md §26 WP 16.2, blueprint P-S.6). For deterministic, normal, lognormal and gamma, `lead_time` is the mean; a triangular or uniform lane IS its bounds, and its planning lead time is their mean. Blank: the material's shape (`materials.lead_time_dist`), else deterministic — how every lane ran before Phase 16.

engine.transform: lower-cased; an unknown value, or a shape missing a parameter it needs, is warned and the lane runs deterministic

substitutions.value: materials.lead_time_dist + lead_time_cv of the lane's material, else deterministic
substitutions.visible_as: the Supplier table's lead-time distribution cell on /policies

substitutions.when: a shape whose parameters are missing or unusable
substitutions.visible_as: MappingWarning on the run's mapping report

ingest.validate: one of deterministic, normal, lognormal, gamma, triangular, uniform — enforced by the column's CHECK constraint; blank lands nothing

columns.name: lead_time_cv
columns.meaning: How much this lane's lead time varies, as a coefficient of variation — read by normal, lognormal and gamma only (PLAN.md §26 WP 16.2). Bounded 0–1, as the engine bounds it.

engine.transform: float(); the row's CV on /policies wins

ingest.validate: numeric 0–1 — enforced by the column's CHECK constraint; blank lands nothing

columns.name: lead_time_min
columns.meaning: A triangular or uniform lane's shortest lead time — a duration in the lane's `lead_time_unit` (blank = weeks), the unit `lead_time` is quoted in; weeks after promotion. Read by triangular and uniform only (PLAN.md §26 WP 16.2).

engine.transform: _duration_to_weeks(lead_time_min, lead_time_unit); the row's bound on /policies wins

ingest.validate: numeric >= 0; triangular and uniform only; min <= mode <= max — enforced by the column's CHECK constraint; blank lands nothing

columns.name: lead_time_mode
columns.meaning: A triangular lane's most likely lead time — a duration in the lane's `lead_time_unit` (blank = weeks), the unit `lead_time` is quoted in; weeks after promotion. Read by triangular only (PLAN.md §26 WP 16.2).

engine.transform: _duration_to_weeks(lead_time_mode, lead_time_unit); the row's bound on /policies wins

ingest.validate: numeric >= 0; triangular only; min <= mode <= max — enforced by the column's CHECK constraint; blank lands nothing

columns.name: lead_time_max
columns.meaning: A triangular or uniform lane's longest lead time — a duration in the lane's `lead_time_unit` (blank = weeks), the unit `lead_time` is quoted in; weeks after promotion. Read by triangular and uniform only (PLAN.md §26 WP 16.2).

engine.transform: _duration_to_weeks(lead_time_max, lead_time_unit); the row's bound on /policies wins

ingest.validate: numeric >= 0; triangular and uniform only; min <= mode <= max — enforced by the column's CHECK constraint; blank lands nothing

ingest_files.grain: One file as received, in one run: the manifest for bytes held in storage — where they are, how many there were, and the SHA-256 of exactly the sequence received. Write-once: the row records an event that has already happened and cannot be edited into a different one.

governance.note: RLS reaches the project through the run, the same predicate the staging tables use. The grant is narrower than theirs on purpose — `authenticated` holds SELECT and INSERT and nothing else — because tier 0 is write-once and a grant that permits UPDATE would be a promise the trigger then breaks. The trigger is the backstop the grant cannot be: the service role holds every privilege by definition, and `ingest_files_write_once()` refuses its updates too. `audited: true` SINCE WP 3.2, and by the RPC route rather than by a trigger: `audit_tier_write` is a tier 2/3/4 instrument and a tier-0 table has none. `ingest_land_file` writes exactly one `plane='data'` audit row per landing — action `ingest_file_landed`, target `ingest_files`, the file id as target_id, and the hash, the byte count and the staged/rejected counts in `after`. It NAMES the uploader, and it can, because the actor is a PARAMETER of that function rather than a session GUC read at the far end of a pooled connection (D36's failure mode, avoided rather than inherited). The row is written in the same transaction as the landing, so a landed file without its audit row is not a state this table can reach. `supabase/rehearsal/070` asserts all of that against a real database, and is mutation-tested on it. The previous note said this was WP 3.2's to add; it did.

policies.name: ingest_files: project access
policies.using: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM public.ingest_runs r WHERE r.id = ingest_files.ingest_run_id AND public.has_project_access(r.project_id))
policies.with_check: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM public.ingest_runs r WHERE r.id = ingest_files.ingest_run_id AND public.has_project_access(r.project_id))

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key for one landed file.

columns.name: ingest_run_id
columns.meaning: The run this file was landed for. NOT NULL: a file with no run is a byte-stream nobody asked for, and making the run the owner is what keeps a landing attached to a project, a source kind and an approval.
columns.note: ON DELETE CASCADE, and the direction matters: deleting a project deletes its runs and therefore its file manifests. Tier 0 is immutable, not immortal — a RESTRICT here would have made a project undeletable, which is a defect dressed as rigour.

columns.name: source_kind
columns.meaning: csv, orbit-mrp or api — what kind of source produced these bytes. The same closed vocabulary as the run's.
columns.note: No default here either, and unlike the other two tables this column never needed a backfill: the table is new and has no rows to be wrong about.

columns.name: original_filename
columns.meaning: The file's name as the user's machine gave it, verbatim. For display and for the person's own recognition — never a key, and never parsed for meaning: two projects upload `inbound.csv` on the same afternoon (G1's rule, applied to filenames).

columns.name: storage_bucket
columns.meaning: The storage bucket the bytes live in. Recorded rather than assumed, so that moving a bucket is a data change and not a code change.

columns.name: storage_path
columns.meaning: Where the bytes are inside the bucket. Generated by the writer, never supplied by the user, and UNIQUE with the bucket because it addresses exactly one stored object.

columns.name: content_type
columns.meaning: The MIME type as reported at upload. NULLABLE and not trusted: browsers report `application/vnd.ms-excel` for CSVs often enough that a parser keying on it would reject real files. WP 3.2's parser decides from the bytes.

columns.name: byte_size
columns.meaning: How many bytes were received. The cheapest possible check that a file is the file somebody meant to send, and the number a quota will eventually be about.

columns.name: content_sha256
columns.meaning: SHA-256 of the bytes AS RECEIVED, lowercase hex, computed before any parse. The anchor: with it, 'the file you uploaded on Tuesday' is a checkable claim rather than a memory.
columns.note: CHECK-constrained on SHAPE (`^[0-9a-f]{64}$`) rather than on content, because a truncated or upper-cased hash compares unequal to itself and would break every lineage claim built on it — quietly, and much later. It is also the dedup signal: 'you have uploaded these bytes before' is a question asked by hash, not by filename, and the index exists for it.

columns.name: uploaded_by
columns.meaning: The person who uploaded the file, in `approved_users`. NULL when the landing had no human — an API push or a scheduled pull — which is stated rather than filled with a service account — or when the uploader's account has since been DELETED: `ON DELETE SET NULL`, and the one change the write-once guard admits (WP 7.2 (a), §4 D161). The file itself is not touched.

columns.name: received_at
columns.meaning: When the bytes were received. Server-stamped, never the client's clock.

ingest_files.note: TIER 0, CREATED IN PHASE 3 / WP 3.1, AND NOTHING WRITES IT YET. PLAN.md §2 lists six tiers and this repository had five: there has never been a record of what a user actually uploaded. `UploadWizard` parses the file in the browser and throws it away, which is why every parse defect — D6's quoted comma, D7's blank numerics, D8's untrimmed identifiers, D46's integer `time_unit` — is unreproducible after the fact. You cannot re-read a file that was never kept. WP 3.2 is the writer: upload lands the bytes here, opens a run, and parses SERVER-SIDE. Landing the table one package ahead means that package does not have to invent a schema and a parser in the same session. WRITE-ONCE IS ENFORCED, NOT ASSERTED. `ingest_files_write_once()` refuses every UPDATE, and `supabase/rehearsal/060` proves it against a real database — both halves, because the rule is 'immutable' and not 'undeletable'. ONE EXCEPTION, SINCE `20260930000007` (WP 7.2 (a), §4 D161): `uploaded_by` may go from a value to NULL, with every other column unchanged, once that account no longer exists — the SET NULL of deleting the uploader. Content is immutable; the actor may be anonymised. `rehearsal/480` §2 proves the guard still refuses it while the account exists. §2's tier laws have been sentences in a plan for three phases; a sentence nothing enforces drifts within two months, which is the lesson of the two orphan tables.

ingest_runs.grain: One ingestion attempt, from any source — a connector sync, a CSV upload or an API push — with the counts and the mapping report it produced. The unit a person reviews and approves: staged rows belong to a run, and promotion is a decision about a run rather than about a row.

governance.note: RLS keys on the run's own `project_id` — `has_project_access(project_id)` — which is WP 3.1's change. The original policy reached the project through `project_erp_links`, and a run with no link (`source_kind` csv or api) could not be reached that way at all: it would have been ungoverned rather than merely unsupported. `audited: true` SINCE WP 3.2, by the RPC route: `ingest_land_file` writes one `plane='data'` row naming the uploader and carrying this run's id when the run is OPENED, and `ingest_apply_run` sets `app.current_user_id` LOCAL to its own transaction before the tier-2 INSERT, so the statement-level `audit_tier_write` trigger names the promoter too. That is the half D36 said was expensive: it is cheap here because both functions take their actor as a parameter and neither depends on a GUC surviving PostgREST pooling. WHAT IS STILL NOT AUDITED: the CONNECTOR's runs. `erp-sync-orbit-mrp` writes this table as the service role with no actor to name, which is D36 proper and is WP 3.3's, unchanged by this package. `min_project_role: editor` states the intent — a viewer has no business opening an ingestion run — and nothing enforces the role yet; the policy is the modeler-or-admin predicate the connector shipped with.

constraints.name: ingest_runs_triggered_by_user_fkey
constraints.definition: FOREIGN KEY (triggered_by_user_id) REFERENCES public.approved_users(id) ON DELETE SET NULL

constraints.name: ingest_runs_applied_by_user_fkey
constraints.definition: FOREIGN KEY (applied_by_user_id) REFERENCES public.approved_users(id) ON DELETE SET NULL

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key. Not the grain: a run is identified by what it did, and nothing joins to this except the staging rows and the landed files.

columns.name: link_id
columns.meaning: The ERP link this run used, or NULL for a source that has none. NULL means 'this source needs no link', never 'the link was lost' — a CSV upload and an API push have no credential to point at.
columns.note: Was NOT NULL until WP 3.1. Nullable is the widening: with it, a run belongs to a project rather than to a connector.

columns.name: triggered_by
columns.meaning: manual or scheduled. A manual run was asked for by a person; a scheduled one was started by the cron sweep against the link's `sync_schedule_cron`.
columns.note: Not an engine input. It is the field that decides whether `triggered_by_user_id` is allowed to be NULL — a scheduled run has no person, and saying so is `audit-actor` (G4) being honest rather than inventing an actor.

columns.name: triggered_by_user_id
columns.meaning: The person who asked for a manual run, in `auth.users`. NULL for a scheduled run, where there is no person — stated rather than back-filled to a service account, because 'nobody asked, the schedule did' is the true answer (G4).

columns.name: status
columns.meaning: running, staged, applied, failed or skipped. `staged` is the state that matters: rows are in tier 1 and a human has not approved them. Nothing reaches tier 2 before `applied`.
columns.note: Not read by the engine and never will be: tier 1 is invisible below it (I2). The readers are the review UI and the connector's own auto-apply gate, which refuses to promote a run with any `fields_failed`.

columns.name: rows_fetched
columns.meaning: Row counts pulled from the source, per entity — {"products": 1007, "bom_versions": 25}. What the source OFFERED, which is not what was staged and not what was promoted.

columns.name: rows_new
columns.meaning: Staged rows the diff classified as new: no live row carries this source identifier yet. For a file run this is `ingest_diff_run`'s count of rows whose natural key is absent from the tier-2 table, and it excludes the rows a later line of the same file superseded.
columns.note: WP 3.3 SET THIS TO INSERTS PLUS UPDATES. `ingest_apply_run` wrote `rows_new = v_total`, the total number of rows the upsert touched, and never wrote `rows_changed` or `rows_unchanged` at all — so the column named for one half of the split held the whole of it and the other two held zeroes that were not measurements. PLAN.md §4 D63; closed in WP 3.4 by computing the diff BEFORE the upsert and persisting what it found.

columns.name: rows_changed
columns.meaning: Staged rows whose live counterpart exists and differs.

columns.name: rows_unchanged
columns.meaning: Staged rows identical to their live counterpart. Counted rather than dropped: 'nothing changed' is a result, and a report that omits it cannot be distinguished from one that failed.

columns.name: rows_removed
columns.meaning: Rows present in the live table under this source and absent from the pull — `diff_state = removed_upstream`. Never promoted by the connector: a source dropping a row is not authority to delete the project's row. ALWAYS 0 FOR A FILE RUN, and that zero is a statement rather than a measurement: a connector pull speaks for the whole source, a CSV speaks only for the rows it contains, so an upload can never mark anything removed. The review screen says so in those words rather than rendering the zero (§5 T1).
columns.note: WP 3.3's `ingest_apply_run` wrote the count of rows HELD BACK by an error finding into this column — two unrelated facts in one place, and the one that was there was not the one the column is documented to hold. PLAN.md §4 D64. WP 3.4 gave the held-back count its own column, `rows_held`.

columns.name: mapping_warnings
columns.meaning: The per-field mapping report: [{level, entity, field, reason}], the same shape as `simulation_runs.mapping_warnings` and scsim's MappingWarning, so MappingWarningsCard renders it unmodified.

columns.name: fields_mapped
columns.meaning: Source fields that landed in a staged column with a value.

columns.name: fields_defaulted
columns.meaning: Source fields the source did not provide, left null for the project's defaults to fill at promotion. This is the count that drives the amber badge — a defaulted field is a substitution and §5 T2 says it is visible at the point of display.

columns.name: fields_failed
columns.meaning: Source fields that could not be mapped at all. A run with any failure never auto-applies, whatever the link's threshold says.

columns.name: diff_summary
columns.meaning: The rendered diff the review UI reads, kept until the run is applied or rejected. WP 3.4 builds that screen; the column is the connector's own and predates it.

columns.name: applied_at
columns.meaning: When the staged rows were promoted to tier 2. NULL for every run that has not been approved — which is most of them, by design.

columns.name: applied_by_user_id
columns.meaning: Who approved the promotion, in `auth.users`. NULL when the link's auto-apply threshold promoted it, and that NULL is the one D36 is about: an automatic promotion has no actor and says so rather than borrowing one.

columns.name: error_detail
columns.meaning: Why a failed run failed, in the source's own words. Kept verbatim: a paraphrased error is a second source for a fact that already had one.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the run opened. Server-stamped.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this run ingests into. Added in WP 3.1 and NOT NULL: it is what the RLS policy reads, so a run is governed by the project it writes to rather than by the credential it happened to use.
columns.note: Backfilled from `project_erp_links.project_id` for every row that existed. The backfill was total by construction — `link_id` was NOT NULL with a foreign key — which is why the migration sets NOT NULL without the guard `customers` needed.

columns.name: source_kind
columns.meaning: Where this run's rows came from: csv, orbit-mrp or api. CHECK-constrained, so a fourth source cannot appear without a migration that decides what it is.
columns.note: NO DEFAULT, deliberately. The column is backfilled to 'orbit-mrp' for the runs that existed and the default is then dropped, so the next writer must state its source. A default here would record a CSV upload as a connector sync and nobody would be told, which is the §5 T1 failure — a value with no provenance — inside the table that exists to record provenance.

columns.name: rows_held
columns.meaning: Staged rows carrying an `error` finding. They are never promoted and they stay in tier 1 with their reason attached, which is what makes a partial upload reviewable instead of a failure.

columns.name: rows_superseded

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key for one staged row.

columns.name: ingest_run_id
columns.meaning: The run these rows were staged in. NOT NULL, ON DELETE CASCADE: the run is the owner and the only route to a project, exactly as for `ingest_files` and the three connector staging tables.

columns.name: source_kind
columns.meaning: csv, orbit-mrp or api — the same closed vocabulary as the run's and the file's, CHECK-constrained with no DEFAULT.
columns.note: NOT AN ENGINE INPUT and never will be: tier 1 is invisible below it (I2). It is provenance, read by the review screen and by anyone asking where a tier-2 row came from.

columns.name: fact_class
columns.meaning: master or transactional — what KIND of fact one row is. Structure (a BOM) is master; a quantity over a period (a lane) is transactional. The value comes from the target table's own `ingest_dataset.fact_class`, so the contract decides it rather than the uploader.
columns.note: NOT AN ENGINE INPUT, for the same reason `source_kind` is not. It exists so that a later package can treat master data and transactional data differently at promotion without re-deriving which is which from the target table's name.

columns.name: target_table
columns.meaning: The tier-2 table these rows are destined for, by name. Not a foreign key — there is no table of tables — so `ingest_target_is_promotable()` is the closed set, and the landing refuses anything outside it before a row is written.

columns.name: source_row_number
columns.meaning: The physical line in the file, 1-based, counting the header as line 1 — so the first data row is 2, and the number matches what a spreadsheet shows the person who made the file. CHECK > 1 for that reason: line 1 is the header and can never be a staged row.
columns.note: This is the anchor WP 3.4's review screen clicks through to and WP 3.3's tier-2 `source_row_id` points at. It is also why a rejected row is KEPT rather than dropped: "row 42 is why" needs row 42 to exist somewhere.

columns.name: raw
columns.meaning: The cells exactly as the file gave them, keyed by the header the file carried — untrimmed, untyped, verbatim, including columns the contract does not know. The left-hand side of every parse claim.
columns.note: Keeping it is what makes D8 and D46 diagnosable rather than arguable: `" MAT-1 "` and `"MAT-1"` resolve to one id in `parsed` and remain two different strings here, and a `time_unit` of `21` is visible as the token it was rather than as the weekly it used to become.

columns.name: parsed
columns.meaning: What validation made of the cells, keyed by TIER-2 COLUMN NAME rather than by CSV header — the two differ, and the mapping is the contract's `ingest.csv_header`.
columns.note: A field that failed validation is ABSENT here rather than present as null. The distinction is the whole of D7: absent says "no value was established", null says "the file said empty", and a validator that spells them the same way puts 376 null volumes into tier 2 without telling anyone.

columns.name: findings
columns.meaning: [{level, field, code, message}] — the same four-key shape as `ingest_runs.mapping_warnings` and scsim's MappingWarning, so WP 3.4 renders it with `MappingWarningsCard` unmodified.
columns.note: A row carrying any `error` finding is never promoted — that is what "rejected with a row-level finding" means, and it is enforced in `ingest_apply_run`'s WHERE clause rather than hoped for. `warn` and `info` rows ARE promoted and shown, which is §5 T2: a substitution is visible at the point of display, not withheld by rejecting the row it is about.

columns.name: diff_state
columns.meaning: What this row is relative to the CURRENT tier-2 table — new, changed or unchanged — computed by `ingest_diff_run` at landing, again when the review screen is opened and again inside `ingest_apply_run` immediately before the upsert. NULL means the diff has not been computed for this row: a row held back by an `error` finding may have failed on a key field and so has nothing to compare. The CHECK also admits `removed_upstream`, which is the same vocabulary the three connector staging tables use so that one review component serves both sources; nothing writing THIS table ever sets it.

ingest.validate: one of new, changed, unchanged, removed_upstream

columns.note: NULL IS "NOT COMPUTED", AND IT REPLACED A DEFAULT THAT WAS AN ANSWER. Until WP 3.4 this column was `NOT NULL DEFAULT 'new'` and no code path wrote it — `20260916000019` does not mention it once — so every staged row claimed `new`, including the rows the upsert UPDATED, and a review screen reading it would have rendered "340 new" for 340 unchanged rows with a number and no hedge. PLAN.md §4 D62. A file run never writes `removed_upstream`: a connector PULL is a statement about the whole source and a FILE is not — nothing about one upload says it is the complete set of a project's rows, so an absent row means the file does not mention it, and `ingest_runs.rows_removed` is 0 for every file run.

columns.name: staged_at
columns.meaning: When the row was staged. Server-stamped, never the client's clock.

ingest_staged_rows.note: TIER 1, CREATED IN PHASE 3 / WP 3.2 — the fourth staging table and the last one of its kind. The three `ingest_staged_*` tables WP 3.1 renamed are TYPED against one source's entities (`external_id`, `sku`, `cycle_time_seconds`) because the connector knows what an orbit-mrp product is. A CSV of `inbound_logistics` is none of those things, and widening those three to hold it would have made each of them a table about two unrelated grains. So this one is generic where they are specific, and the generality is `ingestion-contract` (I7) working as intended: a new source lands here and never touches a tier-2 schema. WHAT IT CLOSES: the CSV path is the first in this repository for which `no-tier-skip` (I2) is true rather than aspirational. Before WP 3.2 a browser parsed the file and inserted straight into `inbound_logistics`.

materials.tier_name: canonical — the only tier humans edit
materials.grain: One material in one project: the economics the simulation reads for it. The precision path — the CSV lanes carry prices too, and where this row is silent the engine derives the value from them rather than treating it as missing.

governance.note: `write` names the capability that exists today. WP 2.2 splits `data_editing` into `data_edit_inputs` (tier 2) and `data_edit_policies` (tier 4); this row becomes `data_edit_inputs` then, and all thirteen sidecars change together. SEPARATELY — AND THIS REPLACES WHAT WP 1.2 WROTE HERE, WHICH WAS WRONG: this sidecar used to assert `rls_enabled: false` and say "no migration ever runs ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on them". One does. `20260614000001_item_master.sql:57-66` enables RLS and creates two policies (`%s_auth_all`, `%s_anon_read`) on each of the three masters — but through `EXECUTE format(...)` inside a `FOREACH` over an array of table names, which a static replay of the migrations cannot evaluate. The introspector recorded the absence as `enabled: false`, WP 1.2 read that as fact, and the contract was one generated page away from telling a user their item masters were unprotected. WP 1.4 fixed the mechanism, not the guess: the introspector now records dynamic DDL (`dynamic_ddl`) and marks the tables it touches `rls.determinate: false`, the validator refuses to let a sidecar assert an RLS state the migrations do not settle, and the generated page says the state is indeterminate and names the migration. The ONLY way to know is to read the live database — PLAN.md §15, still unrun. WP 2.4's security review owns it.

constraints.name: materials_source_row_fk
constraints.definition: FOREIGN KEY (source_row_id) REFERENCES public.ingest_staged_rows(id) ON DELETE SET NULL DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this material belongs to. Half of the primary key.

engine.transform: filter, never read as a value

ingest.validate: set from the selected project, never from the CSV

columns.name: material_id
columns.meaning: The material's code as the user's own systems spell it. Joins to the BOM and to every inbound arc that supplies it.

engine.transform: str()

columns.name: name
columns.meaning: A human-readable name for the material. Display only.

engine.transform: str(name or material_id)

resolution.note: A label. Recorded for completeness: every engine-consumed field carries a resolution block, including the ones where the answer is trivial.

columns.name: cost
columns.meaning: What one unit of this material costs to buy. The master value; where it is unset the engine values the material at the volume-weighted average price of its inbound arcs — what the project actually pays, which is usually what the user wants and is why leaving it blank is not an error.

engine.transform: float() when > 0
engine.missing_default: the volume-weighted average inbound unit_price for this material, or its cheapest quote when no arc carries a volume; arc prices floored at 1.0

substitutions.when: NULL or <= 0, with at least one inbound arc carrying a volume
substitutions.value: the volume-weighted average of the material's inbound unit_price values, each weighted by that arc's weekly volume (grading.ts::volumeWeightedInboundCost floors a <= 0 price to 1.0 first)
substitutions.visible_as: the effective-economics badge in /policies

substitutions.when: NULL or <= 0, and no inbound arc of the material carries a volume
substitutions.value: the cheapest inbound arc's unit_price (grading.ts::cheapestInboundCost floors a <= 0 price to 1.0 first)
substitutions.visible_as: the effective-economics badge in /policies

resolution.note: hybrid is NULL because scsim has nowhere to put a spread: cost and unit_price are bare floats on Material and Product, with no distribution, no CV and no sampling path anywhere in the engine. Recording `hybrid: null` here is a statement about the ENGINE, not about the world — prices obviously vary. Giving them a spread is an engine change on the scsim track; see the RFC in PLAN.md §14. Do not invent one in this contract: a contract that describes a capability the engine does not have is how a fallback ends up in code with no contract entry, which is what I6 forbids in the other direction. estimable_from is empty for a second reason: the value already has a derivation — the volume-weighted inbound price — and that is a substitution the user can see and trace, not an estimate.

engine_requirement.reason: Inventory valuation and holding cost — the terminal default of 1.0 makes every cost KPI meaningless.
engine_requirement.fallback: volume-weighted average inbound unit_price across the material's supply lanes; the cheapest quoted price when no lane carries a volume

columns.name: holding_cost_pct
columns.unit: fraction of unit value per year
columns.meaning: The annual cost of holding one unit in stock, as a fraction of its value. 0.2 means holding a unit for a year costs a fifth of what the unit is worth.

engine.transform: falls back to the inventory policy bundle's holding_cost_pct when NULL
engine.missing_default: the project's inventory policy bundle value (0.2 in the shipped default)

substitutions.visible_as: the policy grid's provenance dot

resolution.note: A financial policy parameter, not an observation: it is what the business decides holding stock costs it. Falls back to the project's inventory bundle, which is a policy default and is visible as one.

columns.name: moq
columns.meaning: Minimum order quantity: the smallest amount this material can be ordered in. A commercial fact the supplier states, not something to be inferred from order history.

engine.transform: float(moq) when truthy, else 0.0 — applied per (supplier, material) link

resolution.note: estimable_from is EMPTY and that is a positive statement, not an omission. This is an engineering or commercial fact that someone knows exactly — it is written on a drawing, in a contract, or on a machine's nameplate. Fitting a distribution to it would produce a number with error bars around something that has no error, and the error bars would be believed. A future estimator reading this contract must refuse this field. A minimum order quantity is a term the supplier states. Inferring it from observed order sizes learns the ordering policy, not the constraint — and then the simulation optimises against its own past behaviour.

columns.name: initial_on_hand
columns.meaning: How much of this material is in stock when the simulation starts.

engine.transform: float() when not None; None is passed through as None, not as zero

resolution.note: Opening stock is a measurement — someone counted it — so it is the one master economic field where an observations tier could legitimately supply it. Nothing does today.

columns.name: lead_time_dist
columns.meaning: The SHAPE of this material's delivery lead time — deterministic, or a named distribution around the arc's lead time. `deterministic` means the lead time is exactly what the arc says, every time.

engine.transform: LeadTimeDist(value) when set, else LeadTimeDist.DETERMINISTIC. A lane's own shape (inbound_logistics.lead_time_dist) or the Supplier row's wins over it (PLAN.md §26 WP 16.2)

ingest.validate: one of the LeadTimeDist enum values; `empirical` is reserved for the data-import path (M7) and is not selectable yet

resolution.note: The SPREAD half of lead_time's hybrid; the centre is inbound_logistics.lead_time. LeadTimeDist.EMPIRICAL exists in the enum and is RESERVED for the data-import path (M7) — it is the value an estimator would write, which is why it is not offered in the UI today. `deterministic` is the default and means the lead time is exactly what the arc says.

columns.name: lead_time_cv
columns.meaning: How much the lead time varies, as a coefficient of variation. Read only when `lead_time_dist` is not deterministic: the engine skips sampling entirely when the distribution is deterministic or the CV is zero.

engine.transform: float() when truthy, else 0.0; above 1 → 1, warned (§4 D302). A lane's own CV (inbound_logistics.lead_time_cv) or the Supplier row's wins over it (PLAN.md §26 WP 16.2)

substitutions.when: above 1 (a value stored before the upload rule bounded it — §4 D302)
substitutions.visible_as: MappingWarning on the run's mapping report

ingest.validate: numeric 0–1 — the engine's bound (§4 D302: a CV above 1 used to fail the run)

resolution.note: The magnitude of lead_time's spread. Read only when lead_time_dist is not deterministic: core/engine.py tests both, so a CV on a deterministic link is silently inert. Zero and NULL are the same thing here.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When the row last changed. Server-set.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was inserted. Server-set.

columns.name: source_system
columns.meaning: Which external system this row came from, when it was synced rather than uploaded. NULL for a hand-uploaded or hand-edited row.
columns.note: NOT TRACED into the engine, and correctly so: it is provenance, not a parameter. Read by the ERP connector (blueprint G18), which is the only writer. Kept, not a deletion candidate.

columns.name: source_external_id
columns.meaning: This row's identifier in the external system, so a re-sync can match it.
columns.note: NOT TRACED into the engine; ERP-connector provenance, as source_system.

columns.name: source_synced_at
columns.meaning: When the external system last confirmed this row.
columns.note: NOT TRACED into the engine; ERP-connector provenance, as source_system.

columns.name: ingest_run_id
columns.meaning: The ingestion run that last wrote this row (WP 3.3, D55), and through it the project, the source kind and who approved the promotion. NULL for every row that predates the CSV landing path — which, on the day this column lands, is every row — and for rows whose run has since been deleted.

columns.name: source_row_id
columns.meaning: The tier-1 staged row this was promoted from (WP 3.3, D55). Its `source_row_number` is the physical line of the uploaded file, header = line 1. `ON DELETE SET NULL` and DEFERRABLE, because staging dies with its run and an item master belongs to the project rather than to the run.

model_validation_evidence.grain: The evidence one Validated Model rests on, kept beside it rather than summarised into it: per-KPI warm-up series and detector outputs, the replication analysis, the per-KPI tests, the face-validation statement and the evidence runs. One row per model, written with it, never edited (WP 10.3, §4 D243).

governance.note: Written only by `_insert_validated_model`, inside the same transaction as its model; a BEFORE UPDATE trigger refuses every edit. Read through `has_project_access`, and by the browser through `get_validated_model_evidence`, which is no wider than the model row it belongs to (readable by every API role). Audited at statement grain.

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key.

columns.name: validation_id
columns.meaning: The model this is the evidence of. One row per model.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The model's project.

columns.name: warmup
columns.meaning: The warm-up evidence: the method, each selected KPI's detected week (and the series it was detected on where one exists), and the adopted week — the MAXIMUM over them.

columns.name: replication_analysis
columns.meaning: The replication analysis: confidence, target precision, per-KPI mean ± Student-t half-width and n*, the recommendation.

columns.name: kpi_tests
columns.meaning: The KS / Welch tests per selected KPI with their samples' provenance.

columns.name: face_validation
columns.meaning: The face-validation statement, who made it and when; NULL for a statistical model.

columns.name: evidence_run_ids
columns.meaning: The runs whose replications are the evidence.

columns.name: author_user_id
columns.meaning: Who saved the model.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When it was written.

model_validations.grain: One VALIDATED MODEL: a decision about how a project's model may be used, bound to the exact policy content, graph version and scenario world it was established on and stating the run protocol every decision-grade run must follow — how many seeds, the week steady state begins, horizon, analysis window, CI level and stopping rule — with who validated it and when. Immutable: only its lifecycle (status, supersession, revocation) changes. Matched by CONTENT, never by id (WP 10.2).

governance.note: Tier 4 — a DECISION. Readable by every API role (`model_validations_read_all`, D28's pinned list); written only through SECURITY DEFINER functions: `record_validated_model` (Save Validated Model — authenticates the actor through the shared preamble and enforces the adoption rule: every selected KPI passed, or a recorded face-validation statement), the legacy `record_model_validation` (its agent caller), and `revoke_model_validation`; all three reach one insert path. Audited at statement grain since WP 10.3. A BEFORE UPDATE trigger refuses every change but the lifecycle — and three fill-once completions: the engine id, the simulation hash (WP 11.2), and the planning period with its code, set by `set_model_planning_period` (same writer gate as saving the model) on a model saved without one (WP 10.5 follow-up).

constraints.name: model_validations_model_code_check
constraints.definition: CHECK ((planning_period IS NULL) = (model_code IS NULL) AND (model_code IS NULL OR model_code ~ ('^' || planning_period || '(-[0-9]+)?$')))

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: The model. Runs stamp it (`simulation_runs.model_validation_id`); a person sees `name` and `version_no`.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project it validates.

columns.name: policy_version_id
columns.meaning: The policy version row it was recorded under — for display and the foreign key only. Matching is by `policy_hash` (WP 10.2, §4 D242).

columns.name: policy_hash
columns.meaning: The policy CONTENT it was validated on — the policy half of its identity.

columns.name: dataset_version_id
columns.meaning: The graph version ("Graph vN") it was validated on. Required on every model written since WP 10.3 (a BEFORE INSERT trigger); NULL only on cards older than that.

columns.name: graph_hash
columns.meaning: The composite graph it was validated on — the whole snapshot, kept beside `hash_simulation`. Since WP 11.2 it is the data half of a model's identity only for a card with no simulation hash (one no snapshot could teach); every other card is matched on its simulation inputs, so a deep-tier upload the engine never reads does not make it a different model (§4 D259).

columns.name: scenario_hash
columns.meaning: The baseline scenario fingerprint's hash (horizon, time step, demand model). NOT widened with the protocol: a new stress scenario is matched on it BEFORE it inherits the protocol, so widening it would end inheritance (§16 · WP 10.3). The protocol is in `model_hash` instead.

columns.name: scenario_fingerprint
columns.meaning: The fingerprint itself, so the world a model was validated in can be read without a hash.

columns.name: engine_fingerprint
columns.meaning: The evidence run's engine `code_version`, when it had one. Advisory until the engine registry lands (WP 10.4).

columns.name: adopted_warmup_days
columns.meaning: The adopted warm-up in days — `protocol.warmup_week × 7` for a model written since WP 10.3. Kept because Lab scenarios inherit it (`apply_validation_to_scenario`).

columns.name: warmup_method
columns.meaning: Which detector the adopted warm-up came from: engine, welch or mser5.

columns.name: recommended_replications
columns.meaning: The replications a run should use — `protocol.replications` for a model written since WP 10.3; inherited by Lab scenarios.

columns.name: replication_basis
columns.meaning: The replication analysis summary (confidence, target precision, per-KPI mean, half-width, n*).

columns.name: validation_tests
columns.meaning: The per-KPI KS / Welch results the verdict rests on; empty for a face-validated model.

columns.name: findings_snapshot
columns.meaning: The verification findings at the moment of adoption.

columns.name: verdict
columns.meaning: validated or rejected.

columns.name: basis
columns.meaning: statistical (every selected KPI passed) or face (a recorded statement).

columns.name: evidence_run_id
columns.meaning: The run whose replications are the evidence; its series never expire (WP 10.6).

columns.name: status
columns.meaning: active, superseded or revoked — the lifecycle, the one part a model may change.

columns.name: superseded_by
columns.meaning: The model that replaced this one on the same content triple.

columns.name: validated_at
columns.meaning: When it was validated.

columns.name: author_user_id
columns.meaning: Who validated it.

columns.name: author_email
columns.meaning: Their email at the time, kept because a model outlives an account.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was written.

columns.name: name
columns.meaning: What the person who validated it called it.

columns.name: version_no
columns.meaning: "Model v3" — one number per model per project, assigned on insert.

columns.name: protocol
columns.meaning: THE RUN PROTOCOL — `replications`, `root_seed`, `crn`, `warmup_week`, `horizon_weeks`, `analysis_window_weeks`, `ci_level`, `ci_halfwidth_target`, `stopping_rule` (`fixed_horizon` | `ci_halfwidth`). `validated_model_protocol_problems` is its one statement and a CHECK holds it. Cards older than WP 10.3 carry a BACKFILLED protocol (`"backfilled": true`) whose `unknown` list names what no column recorded — CRN and the stopping rule always, the seed where no evidence run stamped one.

columns.name: protocol_hash
columns.meaning: SHA-256 of `protocol`.

columns.name: model_hash
columns.meaning: The Validated Model's identity: policy content, the SIMULATION'S inputs (`hash_simulation`, since WP 11.2 — the composite before), scenario world, protocol hash and engine — what makes two models that would instruct different experiments two models. Recomputed once for existing cards from their own snapshot, through the immutability trigger's completion rule; a card with no snapshot keeps the hash it had.

columns.name: engine_id
columns.meaning: The engine it was validated on; its foreign key lands with the engine registry (WP 10.4).

columns.name: face_validation
columns.meaning: The statement a face-validated model rests on; required for basis `face` since WP 10.3.

columns.name: revoked_at
columns.meaning: When it was revoked.

columns.name: revoked_by
columns.meaning: Who revoked it.

columns.name: revoke_reason
columns.meaning: Why, in their words.

columns.name: hash_simulation
columns.meaning: The hash of what the ENGINE reads — the simulation scope, the `inputs` domain of the snapshot it was validated on (WP 11.2, §4 D259). The model is stale when THIS moves, not when the composite does; the supersede, the active-model unique key, dispatch stamping and inheritance all compare it. NULL on a card whose snapshot cannot be read (no `dataset_version_id`), which keeps the composite rule — said, not defaulted.

columns.name: simulation_version_id
columns.meaning: The simulation scope's level version ("simulation inputs v4") — `graph_level_versions`, from the same snapshot. NULL exactly where `hash_simulation` is.

columns.name: planning_period
columns.meaning: The planning period the model is FOR (`2026Q3`), chosen by the modeller when the model is saved and never derived from a date — a model validated in October may be the Q3 model. CHECK `^[0-9]{4}Q[1-4]$`. Not part of `model_hash`: it names the model, it is not what the model is. NULL on a model saved before it existed, until it is set ONCE through `set_model_planning_period` (the immutability trigger's fill-once completion).

columns.name: model_code
columns.meaning: "2026Q3", or "2026Q3-2" for the second model of that period in the project — the code a person says. Assigned by trigger whenever the period is set, unique per project, and never re-issued: the suffix is one past the highest stored for that period.

multi_tier_supply_chain.tier_name: canonical — the only tier humans edit
multi_tier_supply_chain.grain: One directed firm-to-firm relationship in a project's multi-tier network: who supplies whom, at what depth, and in what capacity. An EDGE between two firm identifiers — not a party, and not a material flow: nothing here says what moves along it or how much.

governance.note: Two policies through the project's organization, the same pair `tier2_suppliers` carries: `org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization)` for SELECT, and the same predicate plus modeler-or-admin for writes. `audited: true` SINCE WP 3.2. No trigger existed before it, because WP 2.3 instrumented the tables the contract DESCRIBED and this was not one of them — the qualifier in `dataPlaneAudit.test.ts` is exactly the hole, and writing this sidecar is what made it visible. `20260916000016` adds the three triggers. On a table nothing writes they will never fire, which is the point: the rule is about every tier-2 table, not about the ones that happen to be busy.

policies.name: Multi-tier: modifiers only
policies.using: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = multi_tier_supply_chain.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) AND (p.modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR ( SELECT user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1 ) = 'admin') )
policies.with_check: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = multi_tier_supply_chain.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) AND (p.modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR ( SELECT user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1 ) = 'admin') )

policies.name: Multi-tier: organization access
policies.using: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = multi_tier_supply_chain.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) )
policies.with_check: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = multi_tier_supply_chain.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) )

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key. Not the grain: the row that means something is the from/to pair within a project.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this edge belongs to, by uuid (G1).

ingest.validate: set by the writer from the project, never from a file

columns.name: plant_name
columns.meaning: The project's plant, copied onto every row and enforced by `ensure_dataset_plant_matches_project`.

ingest.validate: must equal the project's plant_name — a trigger raises otherwise

columns.name: from_firm_id
columns.meaning: The firm the edge points FROM, as the user's own systems spell it. A text identifier with no referential integrity to anything — there is no firm table for it to point at.

ingest.validate: non-empty; NOT NULL at the column

columns.name: to_firm_id
columns.meaning: The firm the edge points TO. Direction is the whole content of the row and nothing in the schema defends it: swapping the two columns produces a valid row that says the opposite thing.

ingest.validate: non-empty; NOT NULL at the column

columns.name: to_firm_tier
columns.meaning: How many hops from the project's own plant the TO firm sits — 1 for a direct supplier, 2 for its supplier, and so on. NULLABLE, and a NULL says the depth was never established rather than that it is zero.
columns.note: NOT TRACED into the simulation engine, and nothing else reads it either — see the table note. `scsim` models one tier of supply; a depth number has nowhere to go.

columns.name: to_firm_relationship
columns.meaning: What the TO firm is to the FROM firm, in the user's own words. No CHECK, no closed vocabulary, no code that branches on it.

columns.name: created_at

columns.name: updated_at
