multi_tier_supply_chain.note:
DESCRIBED IN PHASE 3 / WP 3.2, AND THE DESCRIPTION IS MOSTLY A LIST OF ABSENCES. The deferral that pointed here called these "the other inbound datasets, each with its own bespoke upload path". `tier2_suppliers` and `tier3_suppliers` are that; this table is not. NO APPLICATION PATH PUTS A ROW IN IT: `UploadWizard` offers no template, no screen and no edge function writes it, and no CSV names a column of it — which is why every `ingest.csv_header` above is null. THE DATABASE HAS A WRITE PATH ANYWAY, and the third correction WP 6.2 made is this one. `bulk_insert_multi_tier_supply_chain` exists, it is already on `dataPlaneAudit.test.ts`'s list of tier-2 writers, and it works — `rehearsal/240` §6c calls it and reads the row back. What is true is that NOTHING CALLS IT: no file in `src/` or `supabase/functions/` names it, which is why the reader below is answered with an empty array on every real project. But an RPC with no caller is not an absent write path. This application runs as `anon` against permissive grants (D28), so anyone holding a PostgREST client is one call away from writing this table — the same sentence WP 4.1 wrote about the three legacy `ingest-*` functions before `ingest_legacy_upsert_lane` turned their target list into a whitelist in a migration. The claim is APPLICATION-level; the grant surface is WP 7.1's. AND "NO READER AND NO WRITER" WAS FALSE IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, WHICH THIS FILE HAD ALREADY RECORDED AND ITS OWN PROSE DENIED. The `surfaces` block above lists THREE confirmed entries, and WP 6.2 verified all of them against a real database: · `get_project_datasets` SELECTs this table and returns its rows, and
  `projectLanes.ts` calls it from `/policies` and `/simulation-lab` — so it HAS a
  live reader, feeding two pages.
· `delete_project_dataset` has a `multi_tier` branch AND deletes from this table
  in its `'all'` branch, which is what the "Delete ALL data" button on the project
  manager invokes — so it has a live path that EMPTIES it.
Two statements of one fact, in ONE FILE, disagreeing, with nothing comparing them: §4 D101's shape one scope tighter, and the generated page renders the PROSE half, so the contradiction was published to users. `supabase/rehearsal/240` §6 inserts a row, reads it back through the reader and watches the button's RPC remove it. `contract:check` R15 now refuses a note that denies a surface the same file confirms. What is true, stated once: nothing WRITES it, two pages READ it, and one button CLEARS it. Every occurrence is in migrations — created 2025-08-20, carried through RLS rewrites since, most recently by `20260915000004`'s organization dual read, which rewrote policies governing access to a table nobody can reach. EVERY `ingest.csv_header` ABOVE IS NULL FOR THAT REASON: there is no CSV to name a column of. It is described here rather than deferred again because a deferral is a promise that someone will look, and five packages of looking have now established what there is to see. DROPPING IT WAS NOT WP 3.2'S CALL — a table is not removed by the package that happened to notice. Its gap check added the count to §15 so that the package which does decide is deciding against a number, AND THE NUMBER IS ZERO: run `35143830532`, 2026-09-16, reports 0 rows across 0 projects, and run `35399391429`, 2026-09-19, agrees. WP 6.2 IS THE DECIDING PACKAGE AND ITS DECISION IS TO KEEP THE TABLE. The number says the benefit of dropping it is removing an empty relation. The cost, measured: rewriting `delete_project_dataset` — a live RPC behind a user-facing button — rewriting both dataset-snapshot builders, bumping `hash_network`'s `schema_version` 3 -> 4, which invalidates every stored network digest, deleting a published manual page and its registry entry, and updating four test files and a rehearsal — AND, found by the gate above, rewriting `get_project_datasets`, which two pages call on every load. That is a large and IRREVERSIBLE production change whose only gain is tidiness, taken against a row count measured days earlier. The table contributes an empty array to every project's `hash_network` today and costs nothing measurable. THE DECISION RESTS ON THE CORRECTED FACTS AND NOT THE ROW'S. §4 D58 argued from "no reader and no writer", and had the drop been taken on that premise it would have broken a reader two pages use. The number was right and the sentence beside it was not, which is the whole reason a decision waits for a measurement. What WAS wrong is the published claim, and that is corrected above rather than left standing: a page telling users nothing touches this table, while a button does, is the same defect as D103.

columns.name: echelon
columns.meaning: THE node's role in the supply chain, authored once and read rather than re-inferred. CHECK-constrained to `customer`, `product`, `subassembly`, `material`, `supplier`, `plant`, `unknown`. D127 is what it replaces: eight independent classifiers, across SQL, four pages, the map component and the engine, each inferring a type at render time from a different signal because there is no type column on either edge table — and `supply_chain_data.from_location`'s own sidecar says the id alone cannot answer it ("a supplier, a material, or the plant, depending on which lane produced it"). TWO KINDS OF NOT-KNOWING, deliberately kept apart: NULL means never derived, and `unknown` means derived and unplaceable. Collapsing them is how "we have not looked" becomes "we looked and found nothing", which is the substitution T1 forbids. `subassembly` is the value the old vocabulary had no word for — §15 run 35433474185 found 65 nodes that are both a BOM target and a BOM source on one project, every one of which the old rule called a `product`. Since §4 D314 the priority ladder is `node_echelon_from_flags`, reached from two collectors that gather the same seven facts — `classify_node_echelon` for one node and `node_list_attributes` for a whole project, which the refresh uses — so the rule is still written once and the refresh is one pass, not one per node.
columns.note: The engine reads the tier-2 dataset through `datamap.py` and never the deep-tier graph, so no column of this table reaches it. The two centrality ANALYZERS do read some of them — `meaning` says which.

columns.name: bom_depth
columns.meaning: Depth in the BOM tree, read from `bom_multi_level.level` — the table that OWNS the measurement — and NULL for a node that is in no BOM. This is what `supply_chain_data_multi_tier.level` actually holds on the bom lane, under a name that says so. The rule is MIN, not MAX: a material used by two assemblies at different depths has more than one true depth, and the shallowest is the one that says how close to a finished product it sits; a node that is only ever a PARENT at level 1 is the finished product, depth 0. It is NOT read from the lane's own `level` column, because two live writers disagree about what that column means and one of them discards this very value for a literal 2 (D140).
columns.note: The engine reads the tier-2 dataset through `datamap.py` and never the deep-tier graph, so no column of this table reaches it. The two centrality ANALYZERS do read some of them — `meaning` says which.

columns.name: supply_tier
columns.meaning: Tiers upstream of the focal plant: 0 the plant itself, 1 a direct supplier, 2 and 3 from `tier2_suppliers` / `tier3_suppliers`. NULL when unknown, which includes every material, product and customer — they are not upstream suppliers, and reporting 0 for them would be D134's substitution wearing a different column name. This is what `supply_chain_data_multi_tier.level`'s contract CLAIMED to be, and keeping it apart from `bom_depth` is the whole point: a BOM three levels deep does not mean three tiers of suppliers, and a tier-2 supplier is not "a material at level 2". The rule is MIN across the sources, because "tiers upstream" means the shortest such path. See the table's `grain` for why 2 and 3 are rarely reachable today.

org_capabilities.grain: One grant or denial, for one org_id and one capability. The org layer: a tenant-wide override of the role default.

governance.note: One of the four layers `capabilities_for_user()` resolves, in the order role -> org -> project -> user, most specific winning. `audited: false` and it matters here more than on most tables: these rows ARE the permissions, and a change to one currently leaves no record of who made it (§2.1 `audit-actor`, WP 2.3).

policies.name: org_caps: members read own
policies.using: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.organization_members m WHERE m.org_id = org_capabilities.org_id AND m.user_id = public.get_current_user_id() )
policies.with_check: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.organization_members m WHERE m.org_id = org_capabilities.org_id AND m.user_id = public.get_current_user_id() )

columns.name: org_id
columns.meaning: the organization the row grants for.

columns.name: capability_key
columns.meaning: The capability, naming a row in `capabilities`.

columns.name: allowed
columns.meaning: Whether this layer grants the capability. TRI-STATE in effect: a missing row means "inherit from the next layer out", `false` means "deny here". They are different answers and the resolver's COALESCE depends on the difference.

substitutions.when: no row exists at this layer
substitutions.value: the next layer out decides; the chain ends in false
substitutions.visible_as: capabilities_for_user returns the resolved boolean; which layer decided is not reported

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was created. Server-stamped.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When it was last changed. Server-stamped.

org_capabilities.note: WP 2.2 seeded `data_edit_inputs` and `data_edit_policies` into this table from whatever `data_editing` already said, so effective access on the day of deploy was identical to the day before. `data_editing` is deliberately still here: it is removed when the last call site has moved to one of the new keys, not before.

organization_members.grain: One user's membership of one organization, and the role they hold IN that organization. An account may hold several — one per organization it belongs to (§4 D210). Org-level only: it says nothing about which projects inside the organization the user may touch, which is what WP 2.2's `project_members` is for.

governance.note: A member may read only their OWN membership row (`user_id = get_current_user_id()`); there is no policy letting a member enumerate who else is in their organization, and the admin pages that do so run through super-admin RPCs. `audited: false` is the honest record — `admin_add_org_member` and friends log through `log_admin_action`, but membership rows are also written by the `20260709000002` backfill and by nothing else that audits, so the general claim fails. WP 2.3 is where it becomes true. Since D211 an account's `org_role` in each of its organizations is also set by `admin_set_user_org_role` (active super admin, /admin/users/:userId), logged to `admin_audit_logs`. Since D278 `admin_set_user_role` moves the ACTIVE organization's row between `member` and `admin` when the account role enters or leaves `admin` (never `owner`, never another organization's row), logged the same way.

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate row identifier. The membership's identity is (org_id, user_id).

columns.name: org_id
columns.meaning: The organization joined, by uuid. ON DELETE CASCADE — deleting a tenant removes its memberships rather than orphaning them.

columns.name: user_id
columns.meaning: The approved user who is a member, by uuid. ON DELETE CASCADE.

columns.name: org_role
columns.meaning: The member's standing in the organization — `owner`, `admin` or `member`, CHECK-constrained. This is an ORG vocabulary and it is not the project vocabulary: `min_project_role` throughout this contract speaks of viewer / analyst / editor / owner, which WP 2.2 creates on `project_members`. The two share the word "owner" and mean different things by it. Since D303 an `owner` or `admin` row of the account's ACTIVE organization lets a `user` account create projects there (`project_creation_right`, read by `capabilities_for_user`), and since D304 delete that organization's projects and their data (`project_org_admin`, read by `delete_project` and `delete_project_dataset`).

substitutions.when: a member row is inserted without a role
substitutions.visible_as: the column default, and the admin member list renders the resulting role verbatim

columns.note: NOT READ BY THE CAPABILITY RESOLVER. `capabilities_for_user()` resolves role -> org -> user through `approved_users.role` and the capability tables, so for pages and features an organization `admin` holds no more than a `member` does. ONE reader decides with it: `_api_key_management_org` lets an organization `owner` or `admin` manage that organization's API keys (and use every scope on a personal key, `_api_key_caller.can_manage`) whatever the account role — which is why D278 lowers an `admin` row when the account role leaves `admin`: before it, a demoted account kept that right. Since D278 the row follows the account role on the ACTIVE organization (`admin_set_user_role`); `admin_list_account_role_gaps` lists account admins whose row still says `member`. Recorded rather than implied, per §5 T1.

columns.name: joined_at
columns.meaning: When the membership was created. Server-stamped.

columns.name: is_default
columns.meaning: This membership is the account's DEFAULT organization (§4 D216) — where every sign-in lands (`authenticate_approved_user` makes it the active organization when it is not, and its access period has not ended), and where the account re-points when its active organization goes away. At most one per account, by the partial unique index `organization_members_one_default_per_user`; always one of the account's organizations because it IS a membership row, so removing the membership removes the default with it. Set only by a super admin (`admin_set_default_org`, /admin/users); the account switches freely between sign-ins and cannot change it. `false` on every row of an account with no default, which signs in where it last worked (D210's behaviour). Shown to the account's fellow members by NAME on /profile's My organization tab (§4 D217): `get_my_organization_access` and `project_access_read` return it per person.

substitutions.when: a membership is inserted without saying whether it is the default
substitutions.value: false — no membership becomes the default implicitly
substitutions.visible_as: the column default; /admin/users shows no default for the account until one is set

organization_members.note: THE AUTHORITY FOR WHICH ORGANIZATIONS AN ACCOUNT BELONGS TO since `20260930000004` (§4 D210) — an account may belong to several, and `approved_users.organization_id` names the ACTIVE one (what RLS reads). Between `20260929000002` (D205) and D210 this table was derived from that column and held at most one row per account. The rule now, kept by triggers and asserted by `rehearsal/450`: `organization_id` is NULL exactly when the account has no row here, and otherwise names one of its rows. Setting `organization_id` ADDS its row (`trg_approved_users_sync_org_membership`, the `20260709000002` role mapping — app `admin` → `org_role = 'admin'`, everyone else `member`) and removes none; a first row makes its organization active (`trg_organization_members_activate_first`); deleting the active organization's row re-points the account to its earliest remaining one, or none (`trg_organization_members_repoint_active`) — to its DEFAULT one when it has one (`is_default`, D216), which is also where every sign-in lands. A row's organization and account are fixed — an UPDATE of either is refused. Each row is a SEAT: an organization's `user_limit` counts these rows (`trg_tenant_allowance`, BEFORE INSERT; a re-add of an existing member takes no seat). Written by `admin_add_org_member` / `admin_remove_org_member`, `admin_set_default_org`, `admin_set_user_org_role` and, for the active organization's member/admin role, `admin_set_user_role` (D278) (all logged through `log_admin_action`), by the sync trigger, and by the CASCADEs; read by the account through `list_my_organizations`.

organizations.grain: One tenant. Every project, every dataset and every simulation result in the product belongs to exactly one of these rows, and the boundary between two of them is the boundary the whole access layer is built to hold.

governance.note: `write: super_admin` is enforced, not aspirational: every mutation goes through `admin_create_organization` / `admin_update_organization` / `admin_set_org_status` / `admin_set_org_access_period` / `admin_set_org_limits` / `admin_set_org_capacity` (WP 10.7) / `admin_delete_organization`, each of which opens with `_assert_super_admin` and closes with `log_admin_action`. The last is §4 D208: a PERMANENT delete that takes the organization's projects and accounts with it, and is a different verb from suspension — since §4 D210 only the accounts that belong to NO other organization; an account that also belongs elsewhere loses this membership and keeps the rest. This is one of the few tables where `audited: true` is literally true today — WP 2.3 is what makes the claim general. Read is open to any member of the org via the self-bridge policy below, which WP 2.1 rewrote: it matched the caller's TEXT org against `name` or `slug`, so renaming an organization revoked its own members' read on the row that had just been renamed. It now bridges on `id` first.

constraints.name: organizations_capacity_check
constraints.definition: CHECK ( (storage_quota_bytes IS NULL OR storage_quota_bytes > 0) AND (compute_quota_rep_weeks_month IS NULL OR compute_quota_rep_weeks_month > 0) AND (max_replications_per_run IS NULL OR max_replications_per_run BETWEEN 1 AND 200) AND (max_concurrent_runs IS NULL OR max_concurrent_runs > 0) AND (series_retention_days IS NULL OR series_retention_days > 0))

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: The organization's identity. This is the value that must travel — it is what `projects.organization_id`, `approved_users.organization_id` and the public /v1 API's `p_org_id` all mean. Not displayable, and that is the property that makes it safe as a join key (§2.1 `uuid-identity`).

columns.name: name
columns.meaning: The organization's display name, as an administrator typed it. EDITABLE and NOT UNIQUE — two organizations may legitimately share one. It is a label for humans and it is never an identity.
columns.note: D13's join key. `admin_update_organization` updates this column and nothing else: no trigger, no cascade, and no second UPDATE reaching `approved_users.organization` or `projects.organization`. So a rename leaves those two text copies holding the OLD string, and the next user approved into the organization carries the NEW one — at which point a text comparison between them can never match again. WP 2.1 routes every such comparison through `org_is_current_user_org(uuid, text)`.

columns.name: slug
columns.meaning: A URL-safe form of the name, `lower(regexp_replace(name, '[^a-zA-Z0-9]+', '-', 'g'))` at the moment the row was seeded. UNIQUE, and deliberately NOT recomputed on rename — so after a rename it is a record of what the organization used to be called, which is what makes it usable to match rows written before it.

columns.name: owner_user_id
columns.meaning: The approved user who owns the tenant. Advisory today — nothing in RLS or any RPC reads it; ownership is expressed through `organization_members.org_role = 'owner'`. Two places holding the same fact is an I1 violation waiting to diverge; WP 2.2 owns the resolution.

columns.name: status
columns.meaning: Whether the tenant is live — `active` or `suspended`, CHECK-constrained to those two. Set through `admin_set_org_status`. Suspension is the REVERSIBLE verb; removing a tenant is `admin_delete_organization` (§4 D208), which deletes the row rather than setting a status.
columns.note: SUSPENSION IS NOT ENFORCED IN THE DATA LAYER. No policy and no RPC consults this column before granting access — a suspended organization's members read and write exactly as before. It is a label the admin pages render. Recorded here rather than left to be discovered, per §5 T1; the enforcement belongs with WP 2.2's resolver, which is where a capability decision is made once instead of inevery policy.

columns.name: settings
columns.meaning: Per-tenant configuration, free-form. No key of it is read by any migration, edge function or page today; it is a forward-declared extension point.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the organization was created. Server-stamped.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When the row was last modified. Server-stamped by DEFAULT only — no trigger maintains it, and `admin_update_organization` does not set it, so a renamed organization still shows its creation time here.

columns.name: access_period
columns.meaning: How long the organization may be used, counted from `access_valid_from`: `week`, `month`, `quarter` or `year`, CHECK-constrained to those four; NULL means it does not expire, which every organization that existed before D207 keeps. Set by `admin_set_org_access_period` (choosing a period again renews it from now) or `admin_create_organization`. The lengths are written once, in `org_access_period_interval()`.

ingest.validate: one of week / month / quarter / year, or NULL

columns.name: access_valid_from
columns.meaning: When the current access period started — the database clock at the moment an administrator set it, never the browser's. NULL exactly when `access_period` is NULL (a CHECK).

columns.name: access_valid_until
columns.meaning: When the access period ends. DERIVED by `trg_organizations_access_valid_until` from the two columns above; a write that names it is overwritten. At or after this instant `authenticate_approved_user` refuses every member except a super admin, `get_my_profile` reports `access_expired`, and no project can be added to the organization (D207).

columns.name: project_limit
columns.meaning: The most projects the organization may hold, counted by `projects.organization_id` — 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50 or 100 (D207; the last four added by §4 D218), CHECK-constrained; NULL is unlimited. Enforced on every writer by `trg_tenant_allowance` on `projects`. Lowering it deletes nothing; no project can be added until under it.

columns.name: user_limit
columns.meaning: The most accounts the organization may have, counted as its `organization_members` rows — an account may belong to several organizations and takes a seat in each (§4 D210; between D207 and D210 it counted `approved_users.organization_id`) — 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50 or 100 (D207; the last four added by §4 D218), CHECK-constrained; NULL is unlimited. Enforced on every writer by `trg_tenant_allowance` on `organization_members`, which every path that adds an account to an organization goes through; switching to an organization the account already belongs to takes no seat. Lowering it removes nobody; no account can be added until under it.

columns.name: storage_quota_bytes
columns.meaning: The simulation-result storage the organization's plan grants, in bytes: the `series_bytes` of its runs whose series are still kept (expired runs free theirs). NULL is unlimited. Enforced at dispatch by `create_simulation_run` (WP 10.7 · §4 D247), which refuses a run whose expected bytes overflow it with SQLSTATE P0402 and the numbers; a role's share of it is `plan_role_allowances.storage_share_pct`.

columns.name: compute_quota_rep_weeks_month
columns.meaning: The simulation compute the plan grants per calendar month, in replication-weeks (replications × ceil(horizon days / 7)): counted from `run_usage`, each run at its settled actual if it finished, else at its reservation. NULL is unlimited. A run that would exceed it, or the member's `compute_share_pct` of it, is refused at dispatch (P0402).

columns.name: max_replications_per_run
columns.meaning: The most replications one run may ask for, under the global clamp of 200. NULL is unlimited. /v1's key-scoped `max_replications` folds into it inside `create_simulation_run` — the stricter wins — and a run over it is refused with SQLSTATE P0403 (HTTP 403).

columns.name: max_concurrent_runs
columns.meaning: The most runs the organization may have queued or running at once. NULL is unlimited, and then a role's `max_concurrent` does not bind either — the role's allowance is a share of this one. /v1's key-scoped cap folds in; a run over it is refused with SQLSTATE P0429 (HTTP 429).

columns.name: series_retention_days
columns.meaning: How long a standard run keeps its weekly series after it completes, read by `run_series_retention` when the run completes. Every organization starts at 90 (the column default — WP 10.6's period); NULL keeps series without limit. A change re-dates the organization's standard runs (`admin_set_org_capacity`); a pinned run or a Validated Model's evidence run has no expiry whatever the plan says.

organizations.note: Created by `20260709000002_super_admin_phase1.sql`, which seeded one row per DISTINCT `approved_users.organization` string. That seeding is why the uuid plane and the text plane started out agreeing, and why nothing has kept them agreeing since: the seed ran once, `set_project_defaults()` never stamped the uuid (D27), and `admin_update_organization` renames without propagating. WP 2.1 fixed the trigger, backfilled what it could match unambiguously, and routed every live comparison through one predicate. It deliberately did NOT re-seed this table from distinct strings: after a rename, a user carrying the new name slugifies to a slug no row holds, and seeding would split one organization into two.

outbound_logistics.tier_name: canonical — the only tier humans edit
outbound_logistics.grain: One demand arc as the user uploaded it: this customer buys this product from this plant, at this price and lead time, in this volume. UNIQUE on `natural_key_intended` since WP 3.3 (`20260916000018`): a second upload of the same arc UPDATES it rather than adding a row (D5 closed).

governance.note: `write` names the capability that exists today. WP 2.2 splits `data_editing` into `data_edit_inputs` (tier 2) and `data_edit_policies` (tier 4); this row becomes `data_edit_inputs` then, and all twelve sidecars change together.

policies.name: Outbound: modifiers only
policies.using: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = outbound_logistics.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) AND (p.modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR ( SELECT user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1 ) = 'admin') )
policies.with_check: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = outbound_logistics.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) AND (p.modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR ( SELECT user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1 ) = 'admin') )

policies.name: Outbound: organization access
policies.using: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = outbound_logistics.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) )
policies.with_check: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = outbound_logistics.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) )

constraints.name: outbound_logistics_source_row_fk
constraints.definition: FOREIGN KEY (source_row_id) REFERENCES public.ingest_staged_rows(id) ON DELETE SET NULL DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED

constraints.name: outbound_logistics_demand_spec_check
constraints.definition: CHECK ( (demand_distribution IS NULL OR demand_distribution IN ('deterministic', 'normal', 'triangular', 'triangular_av', 'poisson')) AND (demand_mean IS NULL OR demand_mean >= 0) AND (demand_variation IS NULL OR demand_variation >= 0) AND (demand_min IS NULL OR demand_min >= 0) AND (demand_max IS NULL OR demand_max >= 0) )

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate row identifier. Carries no meaning and joins to nothing.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this row belongs to. Every read is scoped by it.

engine.transform: filter, never read as a value

ingest.validate: set from the selected project, never from the CSV

columns.name: plant_name
columns.meaning: The focal plant this row belongs to, by NAME. A displayable string used as a join key — the thing invariant G1 forbids; WP 2.1/3.3 replace it with a uuid.

ingest.validate: must equal the project's plant_name — a trigger raises otherwise

columns.name: customer_id
columns.meaning: The customer's code as the user's own systems spell it.

engine.transform: str(); no trimming (D8)

ingest.validate: non-empty after trim — NOT enforced today (D8)

columns.name: product_id
columns.meaning: The finished product's code as the user's own systems spell it. Joins to products and the BOM.

engine.transform: str()

ingest.validate: non-empty after trim — NOT enforced today (D8)

columns.name: volume
columns.meaning: How much of this product the customer takes over one `time_unit`. A RATE, not a quantity — two rows are only comparable after both are converted to the same period.

engine.consumed_by: project_map.py::_map_demand -> demand mode when `products.demand_mean` is unset
engine.transform: rateToWeekly(volume, time_unit) — normalized to weeks

resolution.note: Volume is what the user's own systems recorded. It is not estimated; it is the thing other quantities are estimated FROM — demand_mean names it in estimable_from.

columns.name: time_unit
columns.meaning: The period `volume` is quoted over — day, week, month, quarter, year — and, since WP 14.2, the period of the row's `demand_mean`, `demand_min` and `demand_max` too. It says nothing about `expected_lead_time`.

engine.transform: looked up in the one unit table

ingest.validate: one of day/week/month/quarter/year and their -ly spellings

resolution.note: A unit is never estimated. Unrecognised or blank is read on a 7-day basis, i.e. as already weekly (grading.ts::rateToWeekly).

columns.name: expected_lead_time
columns.meaning: How long the customer expects to wait for this product. The contract fixes the unit at WEEKS; `time_unit` does not apply to it.
columns.note: NOT TRACED. `expected_lead_time` appears in no read in project_map.py or datamap.py — datamap's outbound projection selects product_id, customer_id, unit_price, volume, time_unit and nothing else, so the column never leaves the database. Recorded as null rather than guessed. It is a deletion candidate for this WP's gap check; do not delete it here.

columns.name: unit_price
columns.meaning: What the customer pays for one unit of this product.

engine.consumed_by: project_map.py::_map_demand -> ProductRow.sell_price when the master is unset; and (WP 14.3) CustomerLink.unit_price, the row's own price under `revenue_max` and in its fill rates
engine.transform: demand-weighted mean across this product's outbound arcs (the product's price); as is for the row's price, which a Customer-row `price` override beats

substitutions.value: the demand-weighted mean of this product's outbound unit_price
substitutions.visible_as: the effective-economics badge in /policies

resolution.note: hybrid is NULL because scsim has nowhere to put a spread: cost and unit_price are bare floats on Material and Product, with no distribution, no CV and no sampling path anywhere in the engine. Recording `hybrid: null` here is a statement about the ENGINE, not about the world — prices obviously vary. Giving them a spread is an engine change on the scsim track; see the RFC in PLAN.md §14. Do not invent one in this contract: a contract that describes a capability the engine does not have is how a fallback ends up in code with no contract entry, which is what I6 forbids in the other direction.

columns.note: The user types `unit_price`; the engine field it feeds is `sell_price` on the product, and inside scsim it is `unit_price` again on the product model. The manual leads with the CSV header (D21).

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was inserted. Server-set.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When the row last changed. Server-set.

columns.name: ingest_run_id
columns.meaning: The ingestion run that last wrote this row (WP 3.3), and through it the project, the source kind and who approved the promotion. NULL for every row that predates the CSV landing path, and for rows whose run has since been deleted — a null here means the provenance is UNKNOWN, never that there was none. Set by `ingest_apply_run` and by nothing else.

columns.name: source_row_id
columns.meaning: The tier-1 staged row this was promoted from (WP 3.3). Its `source_row_number` is the physical line of the uploaded file, header = line 1, so a person can be shown the line rather than told a file name — which is what extends A4 down to the source. `ON DELETE SET NULL` and DEFERRABLE: staging is deleted with its run, and a canonical row belongs to the project rather than to the run that last wrote it.

columns.name: demand_distribution
columns.meaning: The SHAPE of this customer × product row's weekly demand — deterministic, normal, triangular, triangular_av or poisson (PLAN.md §24 WP 14.2, ADR 0002 decision 2). Blank: the row takes its product's distribution, scaled by its share of the product's volume, which is how every project ran before Phase 14.

engine.transform: lower-cased; `triangularAV` spellings → triangular_av; an unknown value is warned and the row keeps its product's distribution
engine.missing_default: the product's distribution × the row's volume share

substitutions.value: the product's own distribution, scaled by the row's share of the product's outbound volume
substitutions.visible_as: the Customer table's distribution cell on /policies

ingest.validate: one of deterministic, normal, triangular, triangular_av, poisson; blank lands nothing

columns.name: demand_mean
columns.meaning: This row's mean demand — the MODE for a triangular row, as `products.demand_mean` is a product's. A RATE in the row's `time_unit`, weekly after promotion. With a forecast series it is the value the plan uses past the series' end.

engine.transform: rateToWeekly(demand_mean, time_unit) — normalized to weeks at promotion

columns.name: demand_variation
columns.meaning: How much the row's weekly demand varies, READ BY ITS DISTRIBUTION: for `normal` it is the coefficient of variation (σ = variation × centre); for `triangular_av` it is the ± fraction of the centre (0.3 → 70…130 around 100). Deterministic, poisson and triangular (whose bounds are explicit) ignore it.

ingest.validate: numeric >= 0; triangular_av needs <= 1; blank lands nothing

columns.name: demand_min
columns.meaning: A triangular row's lower bound — a rate in the row's `time_unit`, weekly after promotion. Read by `triangular` only.

engine.transform: rateToWeekly(demand_min, time_unit)

ingest.validate: numeric >= 0; triangular only; blank lands nothing

columns.name: demand_max
columns.meaning: A triangular row's upper bound — a rate in the row's `time_unit`, weekly after promotion. Read by `triangular` only.

engine.transform: rateToWeekly(demand_max, time_unit)

ingest.validate: numeric >= 0; triangular only; blank lands nothing

password_reset_requests.grain: One "Forgot password?" request for one account, from the moment the person asks until a super admin resets the password or dismisses the request (PLAN.md §4 D251).

governance.note: RLS on, NO policy and no table grant: which accounts asked for a reset is not one PostgREST query away. The one writer for a NEW row is `request_password_reset(p_email)`, callable by anyone signed out — it records a row only for an ACTIVE account, at most one open per account, and answers identically in every case so it cannot be used to discover which emails exist; it writes an access-plane `auth.password_reset_requested` audit row naming the account as TARGET and no actor, because whoever typed the email is not proven to be its holder. A request changes nothing about the account. Super admins list open requests through `admin_list_password_reset_requests`, close one as `dismissed` through `admin_dismiss_password_reset_request`, and `admin_reset_user_password` closes the account's open request as `resolved`; both write an `admin_audit_logs` row. The super admin's identity is client-asserted (§4 D28).

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate id, `gen_random_uuid()`.

columns.name: user_id
columns.meaning: The account the request is for — the active `approved_users` row whose email was typed. Deleting the account deletes its requests (`ON DELETE CASCADE`).

columns.name: status
columns.meaning: `open` until a super admin acts; then `resolved` (the password was reset) or `dismissed` (the request was not genuine, or was handled another way). CHECK-constrained, and `closed_at` is set exactly when the status is not `open`.

columns.name: requested_at
columns.meaning: When the person asked. Server-stamped.

columns.name: closed_at
columns.meaning: When a super admin resolved or dismissed the request; NULL while it is open.

columns.name: closed_by
columns.meaning: The super admin who closed it; NULL while open, or once that account is deleted (`ON DELETE SET NULL`).

plan_role_allowances.grain: One project role's share of an organization's capacity pool: the percentage of the month's compute and of the series storage a member holding that role may use, and how many runs that member may have in flight. A row with no organization is the platform default; a row naming one overrides it for that organization alone.

surfaces.via: hook useMyCapacity → rpc get_my_capacity (the Run card's remaining line, WP 10.7)

governance.note: The plan, not tenant data: readable by everyone (`plan_role_allowances_read`, `USING (true)`, select only) and written by no API role except through `admin_set_role_allowance`, which opens with `_assert_super_admin`, names the admin to the audit trigger (`app.current_user_id`) and closes with `log_admin_action`. The four defaults (owner 100 %, editor 60 %, analyst 25 %, viewer 0 % of compute and storage; 3 and 1 runs in flight for editor and analyst) are seeded by the migration. Read by `_capacity_state`, which both the admission check inside `create_simulation_run` and the Lab's `get_my_capacity` call, so the Run card and the dispatcher read one answer. The actor the share is resolved for is the app's asserted user (D28).

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: The row's surrogate id.

columns.name: org_id
columns.meaning: The organization this share overrides the default for; NULL is the platform default every organization without an override reads.

columns.name: project_role
columns.meaning: The project role the share applies to — owner, editor, analyst or viewer, as `effective_project_role` resolves it (membership or a live delegation; a super admin is an owner everywhere).

columns.name: compute_share_pct
columns.meaning: The percentage of the organization's monthly compute pool (`organizations.compute_quota_rep_weeks_month`) one member holding this role may use, floored to whole replication-weeks. Binds only where the pool has a quota.
columns.note: Not an engine input: read by the dispatcher's admission check (`_capacity_admit`) before a run exists, never by the simulation.

columns.name: storage_share_pct
columns.meaning: The percentage of the organization's series storage (`organizations.storage_quota_bytes`) one member holding this role may keep. Binds only where the pool has a quota.
columns.note: Not an engine input: read by the dispatcher's admission check (`_capacity_admit`) before a run exists, never by the simulation.

columns.name: max_concurrent
columns.meaning: How many runs one member holding this role may have queued or running. NULL is no role limit. A share of the organization's `max_concurrent_runs`: it binds only where the plan caps concurrency, so an organization with no plan keeps no limits (D207's rule) — whether a role may run at all is the project role's to say.
columns.note: Not an engine input: read by the dispatcher's admission check (`_capacity_admit`) before a run exists, never by the simulation.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was created.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When `admin_set_role_allowance` last changed it.

policy_defaults.grain: One row per project: the policy each family runs with unless a specific node overrides it. The bundle, in other words — and the thing a policy_override is a patch against.

governance.note: `write` names the capability that exists today. WP 2.2 splits `data_editing` into `data_edit_inputs` (tier 2) and `data_edit_policies` (tier 4); this row becomes `data_edit_policies` then.

policies.name: Authenticated users can read policy defaults
Authenticated users can upsert policy defaults
Authenticated users can update policy defaults

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project these defaults belong to. It is the PRIMARY KEY — one bundle per project, enforced.

engine.transform: filter, never read as a value

columns.name: production

engine.consumed_by: project_map.py::_map_policies -> no plugin — stored, not read

governance.note: `write` names the capability that exists today. WP 2.2 splits `data_editing` into `data_edit_inputs` (tier 2) and `data_edit_policies` (tier 4); this row becomes `data_edit_policies` then.

policies.name: Authenticated users can read policy overrides
Authenticated users can insert policy overrides
Authenticated users can update policy overrides
Authenticated users can delete policy overrides

constraints.name: policy_overrides_project_fk
constraints.definition: FOREIGN KEY (project_id) REFERENCES public.projects(id) ON DELETE CASCADE

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate row identifier. The natural key is the UNIQUE constraint, not this.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this override belongs to.

engine.transform: filter, never read as a value

columns.name: scope
columns.meaning: What KIND of thing the override targets — a supplier, a material, a plant, a customer/product pair. Decides how `target_key` is read.

engine.transform: matched against the stage the grid wrote it from

ingest.validate: one of the stage scopes the policy grid emits

columns.name: target_key
columns.meaning: WHICH thing, in the scope's own spelling — a supplier_id, a material_id, or a composite like `customer::product`.

engine.consumed_by: project_map.py::_map_policies -> the node the patch applies to
engine.transform: parsed per scope

ingest.validate: must name a row that exists; an override for a deleted entity is silently inert

columns.name: family
columns.meaning: Which policy family this patch belongs to — the same vocabulary as policy_defaults' jsonb columns.

engine.consumed_by: project_map.py::_map_policies -> which bundle key to patch
engine.transform: matched against the bundle's family keys

ingest.validate: one of sourcing / inventory / transport / fulfillment / production / recovery / demand

columns.name: patch
columns.meaning: The fields this target overrides, and only those. A field absent from the patch keeps the bundle's value — which is exactly why D1 mattered: writing a field the user never supplied turned a default into a decision.

engine.consumed_by: project_map.py::_map_policies -> merged over the family bundle
engine.transform: shallow-merged over the project bundle's family object

columns.note: What may be written here is one rule, `isPrefillPersistable`: an unsaved edit or a value the project data actually said. Never a default. Not every override the engine would honour is reachable from the grid — most per-node fields fall back to project defaults in the mapping (blueprint G1).

columns.name: updated_by
columns.meaning: Who last wrote this patch.
columns.note: Governance, not a parameter. WP 2.3 turns it into an audit row naming the actor.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When the patch last changed. Server-set.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the patch was created. Server-set.

columns.name: seeded_from_hash
columns.meaning: WP 4.4 · the `current_graph_hash` of the moment this override was SEEDED from project data. NULL means a person TYPED it, and the NULL is meaningful rather than missing: a seeded override is a COPY of a number the dataset held, and a typed one is a DECISION. A copy goes stale when the dataset moves; a decision does not, and marking it stale would tell the engine to distrust the one number somebody actually chose. Written by `bulk_upsert_policy_overrides`, which reads the hash from the project ITSELF rather than taking one from the caller — a caller that can supply provenance can supply the wrong provenance. ON CONFLICT it is overwritten, so typing over a seeded override clears it. Freshness is COMPUTED from it by `freshness_of` and never written back (§4 D70). **THE ENGINE READS OVERRIDES, NOT THE GRID**, so a stale value here is a simulation-correctness problem rather than a display one.
columns.note: Provenance, not an engine input: it records where the patch beside it came from. The PATCH is what the engine reads.

policy_presets.grain: One named policy bundle a user can apply to a project — the DECISION plane's catalog of starting points. A system preset (`is_system`) ships with the product; a user preset belongs to its `owner_id`.

governance.note: Tier 4 — the DECISION plane: a preset is a choice a person can make, not a fact about their supply chain. Audited from WP 6.4, with the three statement-grain triggers landing beside this sidecar, because `dataPlaneAudit.test.ts` scopes its rule to tables IN the contract and a deferred table's writes are unaudited with nothing to notice (D54). **`write` is null because NO USER-FACING WRITE PATH EXISTS — and neither does a read path (§4 D126).** The table is granted `SELECT` to `anon` under a permissive policy and nothing in `src/`, in an RPC or in an edge function reads it; the presets a user actually sees come from TypeScript modules under `src/lib/policies/presets/`. So this row's governance describes a table that is reachable and unread, which is a different statement from "restricted", and saying it plainly is the point of the block.

policies.name: Anyone signed in can read system presets
Users can create their own presets
Users can update their own presets
Users can delete their own presets

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key. The natural key is (slug, owner_id) below.

columns.name: slug
columns.meaning: The preset's stable name — `lean_jit`, `make_to_order`. Half the natural key, so one owner may not hold two presets under one slug while two owners may each hold their own.

columns.name: name
columns.meaning: What a person reads — "Lean / JIT". The slug is the key; this is the label.

columns.name: description
columns.meaning: One sentence on what the preset does to a project. NULL where nobody wrote one; there is no default sentence, because an invented description of a decision is worse than none.

columns.name: is_system
columns.meaning: TRUE for a preset that ships with the product and FALSE for one a user saved. It is the only thing separating a catalog entry from somebody's own work, and `owner_id` is NULL on the system rows.

columns.name: owner_id
columns.meaning: The user whose preset this is, or NULL for a system preset. Half the natural key — and the NULL half, which is why the pair behaves the way `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` indexes elsewhere in this contract had to be made to behave (§4 D5): without that, two system presets could share a slug.

columns.name: bundle
columns.meaning: THE DECISION ITSELF — a partial policy bundle, keyed by family, merged over a project's defaults when the preset is applied. Partial on purpose: a preset that carried every field would overwrite choices it has no opinion about.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was written. Server-stamped, never the client's clock.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When it was last changed. Maintained by a trigger where one exists; with no writer at all today (D126) it equals `created_at` on every row.

policy_versions.grain: One saved snapshot of a project's whole policy bundle, with the bundle it replaced and the hash of both. The audit trail of the /policies grid: what the policies WERE at a moment somebody chose to record, which is what makes a simulation result reproducible from the policy side.

governance.note: Tier 4 — the DECISION plane: what a person or an agent CHOSE, as against the dataset they chose it over and the result it produced. `result-binding` (I8) needs all three, which is why WP 6.3 keeps the results and this package takes the decisions. Audited from WP 6.4: the three statement-grain triggers land beside this sidecar, because `dataPlaneAudit.test.ts` scopes its rule to tables IN the contract and a deferred table's writes are unaudited with nothing to notice (D54). **This is the one decision table `result-binding` (I8) already reaches**: a run stores `policy_version_id` and the verifiable export reads the row back, so the policy half of a reproducibility record is bound where the dataset half has to be reconstructed. The row carries THREE author columns beside `created_by`, which is a denormalised copy of a person rather than a second identity (G1) — kept because a version outlives an account and a deleted user should not erase who made a decision.

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key. A run binds to this, so it is the id that makes a result reproducible from the policy side.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project whose policies these are.

columns.name: label
columns.meaning: What a person called this version. NULL where it was saved automatically; there is no generated label, because an invented name for somebody's decision is worse than none.

columns.name: snapshot
columns.meaning: THE DECISION ITSELF — the full policy bundle as it stood. Whole rather than a diff, so reading one row reconstructs the state without replaying a chain.

columns.name: created_by
columns.meaning: The user who saved it, by uuid. The three `author_*` columns beside it are the denormalised copy that survives the account.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When it was saved. Server-stamped, never the client's clock.

columns.name: author_user_id
columns.meaning: The author's uuid, recorded a second time. It duplicates `created_by` by design — one of the two came first and neither was removed, and a version row is append-only, so they cannot drift after the write.

columns.name: author_email
columns.meaning: The author's email AT THE MOMENT OF SAVING. A denormalised copy, not a join key (G1): the account may be renamed or deleted and the decision still has to say who made it.

columns.name: author_name
columns.meaning: The author's display name at the moment of saving, for the same reason as `author_email`.

columns.name: parent_version_id
columns.meaning: The version this one followed, so the chain can be walked. NULL on the first version of a project — and NULL is also what a version saved before this column existed carries, so an absent parent is `unknown`, not `first`.

columns.name: previous_snapshot
columns.meaning: The bundle this version REPLACED, stored beside the new one. It makes a diff readable from one row rather than two, and it is what lets a restore know what it is undoing.

columns.name: policy_hash
columns.meaning: The hash of `snapshot`. What a reproducibility record carries so a reader can check that a bundle they hold is the one a run used, without trusting the id. SINCE WP 10.2 IT IS THE VERSION'S IDENTITY: `snapshot_policy` returns the existing row when the project already has this hash (§4 D241), and a model card is matched by it, never by `id` (D242).

columns.name: notes
columns.meaning: Free text a person wrote about why. The only column here that carries a REASON rather than a state, and nothing reads it today.

columns.name: version_no
columns.meaning: "Policy v4" — one number per CONTENT per project, in order of first appearance, assigned by a BEFORE INSERT trigger (so a direct insert numbers too). Rows saved before WP 10.2 that share a `policy_hash` share the number, because they are one model saved twice (§4 D241).

columns.name: version_code
columns.meaning: "Policy 20261004" — the code a person says. The UTC day this CONTENT was first saved (`YYYYMMDD`), and `-n` for the n-th distinct content first saved that day. Rows of one content share it, as they share `version_no`. Assigned by the numbering trigger and STORED, so deleting an older same-day version never moves a surviving code; the suffix is one past the highest ever stored that day (WP 10.5 follow-up, `20261004000002`).

products.tier_name: canonical — the only tier humans edit
products.grain: One finished product in one project: the economics and the demand shape the simulation reads for it. Where this row is silent the engine derives price and demand from the outbound arcs.

governance.note: `write` names the capability that exists today. WP 2.2 splits `data_editing` into `data_edit_inputs` (tier 2) and `data_edit_policies` (tier 4); this row becomes `data_edit_inputs` then, and all thirteen sidecars change together. SEPARATELY — AND THIS REPLACES WHAT WP 1.2 WROTE HERE, WHICH WAS WRONG: this sidecar used to assert `rls_enabled: false` and say "no migration ever runs ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on them". One does. `20260614000001_item_master.sql:57-66` enables RLS and creates two policies (`%s_auth_all`, `%s_anon_read`) on each of the three masters — but through `EXECUTE format(...)` inside a `FOREACH` over an array of table names, which a static replay of the migrations cannot evaluate. The introspector recorded the absence as `enabled: false`, WP 1.2 read that as fact, and the contract was one generated page away from telling a user their item masters were unprotected. WP 1.4 fixed the mechanism, not the guess: the introspector now records dynamic DDL (`dynamic_ddl`) and marks the tables it touches `rls.determinate: false`, the validator refuses to let a sidecar assert an RLS state the migrations do not settle, and the generated page says the state is indeterminate and names the migration. The ONLY way to know is to read the live database — PLAN.md §15, still unrun. WP 2.4's security review owns it.

constraints.name: products_source_row_fk
constraints.definition: FOREIGN KEY (source_row_id) REFERENCES public.ingest_staged_rows(id) ON DELETE SET NULL DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED

constraints.name: products_fg_policy_check
constraints.definition: CHECK (fg_policy IS NULL OR fg_policy IN ('base_stock', 'min_max', 'days_of_cover'))

constraints.name: products_fg_levels_nonnegative
constraints.definition: CHECK (coalesce(fg_base_stock, 0) >= 0 AND coalesce(fg_reorder_point, 0) >= 0 AND coalesce(fg_cover_days, 0) >= 0 AND coalesce(fg_initial_on_hand, 0) >= 0)

constraints.name: products_production_lead_time_check
constraints.definition: CHECK ( (production_lead_time_unit IS NULL OR public.unit_days(production_lead_time_unit) IS NOT NULL) AND (production_lead_time_dist IS NULL OR production_lead_time_dist IN ('deterministic', 'normal', 'lognormal', 'gamma', 'triangular', 'uniform')) AND (production_lead_time_cv IS NULL OR (production_lead_time_cv >= 0 AND production_lead_time_cv <= 1)) AND coalesce(production_lead_time, 0) >= 0 AND coalesce(production_lead_time_min, 0) >= 0 AND coalesce(production_lead_time_mode, 0) >= 0 AND coalesce(production_lead_time_max, 0) >= 0 AND (production_lead_time_min IS NULL OR production_lead_time_mode IS NULL OR production_lead_time_min <= production_lead_time_mode) AND (production_lead_time_mode IS NULL OR production_lead_time_max IS NULL OR production_lead_time_mode <= production_lead_time_max) AND (production_lead_time_min IS NULL OR production_lead_time_max IS NULL OR production_lead_time_min <= production_lead_time_max) )

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this product belongs to. Half of the primary key.

engine.transform: filter, never read as a value

ingest.validate: set from the selected project, never from the CSV

columns.name: product_id
columns.meaning: The product's code as the user's own systems spell it. Joins to the BOM and to every outbound arc that sells it.

engine.transform: str()

columns.name: name
columns.meaning: A human-readable name for the product. Display only.

engine.transform: str(name or product_id)

resolution.note: A label. See materials.name.

columns.name: sell_price
columns.meaning: What one unit of this product sells for. Where it is unset the engine uses the demand-weighted mean of the outbound arcs' prices, which is usually what the user means and is why leaving it blank is not an error.

engine.transform: float() when > 0
engine.missing_default: the demand-weighted mean outbound unit_price, else ENGINE_DEFAULT_PRICE

substitutions.value: demandWeightedSellPrice over this product's outbound arcs
substitutions.visible_as: the effective-economics badge in /policies

resolution.note: hybrid is NULL because scsim has nowhere to put a spread: cost and unit_price are bare floats on Material and Product, with no distribution, no CV and no sampling path anywhere in the engine. Recording `hybrid: null` here is a statement about the ENGINE, not about the world — prices obviously vary. Giving them a spread is an engine change on the scsim track; see the RFC in PLAN.md §14. Do not invent one in this contract: a contract that describes a capability the engine does not have is how a fallback ends up in code with no contract entry, which is what I6 forbids in the other direction. As with materials.cost, the demand-weighted outbound mean is a visible substitution, not an estimate.

columns.note: D21 in one line: the user types `sell_price`, the database column is `sell_price`, and the engine's field is `unit_price`. The legacy docs led with the engine's name, so a reader searching their own CSV for `unit_price` found nothing. The manual leads with `sell_price`.

engine_requirement.reason: Revenue and lost-sales valuation — the terminal default of 1.0 makes revenue KPIs meaningless.

columns.name: production_capacity
columns.meaning: How much of this product the plant can make per week. The canonical G4 example: when it is unset the engine invents a capacity generous enough that capacity never binds, so an unset value silently turns off the constraint the user thinks they are simulating.

engine.transform: float() when > 0
engine.missing_default: max(2 x demand, 1000) — a value chosen so the constraint never binds

substitutions.visible_as: MappingWarning on the run's mapping report

resolution.note: estimable_from is EMPTY and that is a positive statement, not an omission. This is an engineering or commercial fact that someone knows exactly — it is written on a drawing, in a contract, or on a machine's nameplate. Fitting a distribution to it would produce a number with error bars around something that has no error, and the error bars would be believed. A future estimator reading this contract must refuse this field. This is the canonical G4 field: unset, the engine invents max(2 x demand, 1000), which is chosen so the constraint never binds. Estimating it from output would do the same thing with more ceremony — output is bounded by demand, so the fitted capacity can never explain a shortage.

engine_requirement.reason: With no capacity source the engine defaults to max(2·demand, 1000), so plant capacity never binds.

columns.name: fulfillment_mode
columns.meaning: Whether this product is made to order or made to stock. Decides whether the simulation holds finished goods for it.

engine.transform: resolved against the project's supply_chain_model; an unknown value warns rather than raising

substitutions.visible_as: MappingWarning on the run's mapping report

ingest.validate: mto or mts; ato is a reserved enum that hard-errors, eto/cto are UI labels only

resolution.note: Make-to-order or make-to-stock is a decision about how the business runs, not a quantity. Falls back to the project's fulfillment_strategy.

columns.name: demand_distribution
columns.meaning: The SHAPE of weekly demand for this product — constant, normal, triangular and so on. What the user types here is `demand_distribution`; the engine calls the resolved value `demand_model`. `normal` IS A REAL NORMAL since engine 0.3.0 (PLAN.md §24 WP 14.1, ADR 0002 decision 8): N(mean, σ = demand_cv × mean), negative draws set to 0 and counted on the run — before it, `normal` ran as triangularAV with a mapping warning. A customer × product row may state its own distribution on `outbound_logistics` (WP 14.2); this product-level one is what a row that states none runs on, scaled by its volume share.

engine.transform: resolved against the scenario's demand_model; unknown values fall back

resolution.note: The SHAPE of demand is a modelling choice, not something to fit: which distribution to believe is exactly the judgement the user is making. Falls back to the scenario's demand_model.

columns.note: D21: CSV header `demand_distribution`, engine field `demand_model`. Recorded both ways; the manual leads with the header.

columns.name: demand_mean
columns.meaning: Typical weekly demand for this product. The engine treats it as the MODE of the demand distribution, not its arithmetic mean — a distinction that matters the moment the distribution is skewed.

engine.transform: float() when > 0; otherwise derived from the outbound arcs
engine.missing_default: the weekly-normalized outbound volume for this product

substitutions.value: sum of this product's outbound volumes, normalized to weeks
substitutions.visible_as: the effective-economics badge in /policies

resolution.note: default_mode is `hybrid` and this is the only field in the twelve where that is true. Demand is the one quantity here that is genuinely observed rather than specified: the user may state a figure, and the outbound arcs independently say what was actually taken. The engine already resolves it that way — the master value wins, the weekly-normalized outbound volume stands in when it is unset. on_conflict is assertion_wins: a stated forecast beats history, because a forecast is a decision about the future and history is not.

columns.note: D21: CSV header `demand_mean`, engine field `demand_mode`. The rename is not cosmetic — calling a mode a mean is a modelling claim. Both recorded.

engine_requirement.reason: Demand generation — with neither source the product is never ordered (zero demand).

columns.name: demand_cv
columns.meaning: How much weekly demand varies — READ BY THE DISTRIBUTION (PLAN.md §24 WP 14.1): for `normal` it is the coefficient of variation (σ = cv × mean); for `triangular` / `triangularAV` it is the ± fraction of the triangularAV form, triangular(mean·(1−cv), mean, mean·(1+cv)), unless explicit `demand_min` / `demand_max` are given; Poisson and deterministic ignore it. The two readings are not interchangeable: 0.3 is σ = 30 % of the mean under normal and a ±30 % range under triangular.

engine.transform: float() when not None, else the scenario's demand_cv

resolution.note: The SPREAD half of demand's hybrid. Falls back to the scenario-level demand_cv rather than to zero, so an unset CV does not silently make demand deterministic.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When the row last changed. Server-set.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was inserted. Server-set.

columns.name: demand_min
columns.meaning: The lowest weekly demand the distribution allows. Used by the triangular demand shape; a value above the mode is clamped to the mode rather than rejected.

engine.transform: float(); clamped to the mode with a warn when it exceeds it

substitutions.visible_as: MappingWarning on the run's mapping report

resolution.note: The lowest value the triangular shape allows. Derived from the mode and CV when unset, and clamped to the mode with a warning when it contradicts it — the engine never rejects the row, so the clamp is a substitution the mapping report must show.

columns.name: demand_max
columns.meaning: The highest weekly demand the distribution allows. Used by the triangular demand shape; a value below the mode is clamped to the mode rather than rejected.

engine.transform: float(); clamped to the mode with a warn when it falls below it

substitutions.visible_as: MappingWarning on the run's mapping report

resolution.note: The highest value the triangular shape allows. Derived from the mode and CV when unset, and clamped to the mode with a warning when it contradicts it — the engine never rejects the row, so the clamp is a substitution the mapping report must show.

columns.name: source_system
columns.meaning: Which external system this row came from, when it was synced rather than uploaded. NULL for a hand-uploaded or hand-edited row.
columns.note: NOT TRACED into the engine, and correctly so: it is provenance, not a parameter. Read by the ERP connector (blueprint G18), which is the only writer. Kept, not a deletion candidate.

columns.name: source_external_id
columns.meaning: This row's identifier in the external system, so a re-sync can match it.
columns.note: NOT TRACED into the engine; ERP-connector provenance, as source_system.

columns.name: source_synced_at
columns.meaning: When the external system last confirmed this row.
columns.note: NOT TRACED into the engine; ERP-connector provenance, as source_system.

columns.name: ingest_run_id
columns.meaning: The ingestion run that last wrote this row (WP 3.3, D55), and through it the project, the source kind and who approved the promotion. NULL for every row that predates the CSV landing path — which, on the day this column lands, is every row — and for rows whose run has since been deleted.

columns.name: source_row_id
columns.meaning: The tier-1 staged row this was promoted from (WP 3.3, D55). Its `source_row_number` is the physical line of the uploaded file, header = line 1. `ON DELETE SET NULL` and DEFERRABLE, because staging dies with its run and an item master belongs to the project rather than to the run.

columns.name: fg_policy
columns.meaning: The finished-goods inventory policy of an MTS product (PLAN.md §24 WP 14.4, ADR 0002 decision 3): `base_stock` fills to S, `min_max` fills to S only when the stock left after the week's demand is below s, `days_of_cover` fills to D/7 × the projected weekly demand, so its target moves with the forecast. NULL is base-stock with today's derived target. An MTO product holds no FG stock and does not read it.

engine.transform: the Plant-stage override, else this; an incomplete min_max or days_of_cover runs as base_stock, warned

substitutions.visible_as: the Plant cell's empty note

ingest.validate: base_stock | min_max | days_of_cover; blank lands nothing

columns.name: fg_base_stock
columns.meaning: S — the end-of-week finished-goods target in units, for `base_stock` and `min_max` (WP 14.4). A STATED S is the target: P-P.4's safety stock is never added on top of it (one source per number). Empty under base-stock is the derived target: one week of forecast, plus P-P.4's buffer when it is on.

engine.transform: the Plant-stage override, else this
engine.missing_default: derived: one week of forecast (+ P-P.4)

columns.name: fg_reorder_point
columns.meaning: s — `min_max` only: the plant builds up to S when the stock left after the week's demand falls below s, and builds nothing otherwise (WP 14.4). Must be below S.

engine.transform: the Plant-stage override, else this

columns.name: fg_cover_days
columns.meaning: D — `days_of_cover` only: how many days of FUTURE demand the stock should cover. The target is D/7 × the projected weekly demand, so it moves with the forecast (WP 14.4). Days, not converted: the engine divides by 7 itself.

engine.transform: the Plant-stage override, else this; target = D/7 x projected weekly demand

columns.name: fg_initial_on_hand
columns.meaning: The finished-goods stock an MTS product starts the run with — engine RFC 4, closed by WP 14.4 (the capability first, then this column, in RFC 4's own order). Empty starts the run at the policy target, which is today's behaviour.

engine.transform: the Plant-stage override, else this

substitutions.visible_as: the Plant cell's empty note

columns.name: production_lead_time
columns.meaning: How long this product takes to make at the focal plant: output started in a week is finished stock L weeks later (P-P.13, PLAN.md §26 WP 16.5). A duration in `production_lead_time_unit` (blank = weeks); weeks after promotion. Empty is 0 — the product completes in the week it starts, which is how every product ran before Phase 16. For deterministic, normal, lognormal and gamma it is the mean; a triangular or uniform product plans on the mean of its bounds instead.

engine.transform: the Plant-stage override, else _duration_to_weeks(this, production_lead_time_unit); rounded half to even, clamped 0–26
engine.missing_default: 0 weeks — completes in the week it starts

substitutions.visible_as: the Plant cell's empty default

columns.name: production_lead_time_unit
columns.meaning: The period `production_lead_time` and its bounds are quoted in — day, week, month, … (PLAN.md §26 WP 16.5). Blank means WEEKS, the convention `inbound_logistics.lead_time_unit` set. After promotion it reads `week`.

engine.transform: looked up in the one unit table; an unknown value falls to a 7-day basis

ingest.validate: one of the units public.unit_days() knows — enforced by the column's CHECK constraint

columns.name: production_lead_time_dist
columns.meaning: The SHAPE of this product's production lead time — deterministic, normal, lognormal, gamma, triangular or uniform, chosen like a lane's lead time (PLAN.md §26 WP 16.5). Blank is deterministic.

engine.transform: lower-cased; an unknown value, or a shape missing a parameter it needs, is warned and the product runs deterministic

substitutions.visible_as: the Plant table's production lead-time distribution cell

substitutions.when: a shape whose parameters are missing or unusable
substitutions.visible_as: MappingWarning on the run's mapping report

ingest.validate: one of deterministic, normal, lognormal, gamma, triangular, uniform — enforced by the column's CHECK constraint; blank lands nothing

columns.name: production_lead_time_cv
columns.meaning: How much the production lead time varies — read by normal, lognormal and gamma only (PLAN.md §26 WP 16.5). Bounded 0–1, as the engine bounds it.

engine.transform: float(); the Plant row's CV on /policies wins

ingest.validate: numeric 0–1 — enforced by the column's CHECK constraint; blank lands nothing

columns.name: production_lead_time_min
columns.meaning: A triangular or uniform product's shortest production lead time — a duration in `production_lead_time_unit` (blank = weeks); weeks after promotion. Read by triangular and uniform only (PLAN.md §26 WP 16.5, P-P.13).

engine.transform: _duration_to_weeks(production_lead_time_min, production_lead_time_unit); the Plant row's bound on /policies wins

ingest.validate: numeric >= 0; triangular and uniform only; min <= mode <= max — enforced by the column's CHECK constraint; blank lands nothing

columns.name: production_lead_time_mode
columns.meaning: A triangular product's most likely production lead time — a duration in `production_lead_time_unit` (blank = weeks); weeks after promotion. Read by triangular only (PLAN.md §26 WP 16.5, P-P.13).

engine.transform: _duration_to_weeks(production_lead_time_mode, production_lead_time_unit); the Plant row's bound on /policies wins

ingest.validate: numeric >= 0; triangular only; min <= mode <= max — enforced by the column's CHECK constraint; blank lands nothing

columns.name: production_lead_time_max
columns.meaning: A triangular or uniform product's longest production lead time — a duration in `production_lead_time_unit` (blank = weeks); weeks after promotion. Read by triangular and uniform only (PLAN.md §26 WP 16.5, P-P.13).

engine.transform: _duration_to_weeks(production_lead_time_max, production_lead_time_unit); the Plant row's bound on /policies wins

ingest.validate: numeric >= 0; triangular and uniform only; min <= mode <= max — enforced by the column's CHECK constraint; blank lands nothing

project_erp_links.grain: One authorized link between one project and one company in one external system: project ownership proved on this side, company membership proved on that side by the linking user's own OAuth consent. One link is one credential and one project — never shared, so revoking one project's link cannot be bypassed by a sibling.

governance.note: One FOR ALL policy — `has_project_access(project_id)` — so reading and writing a link are the same permission: whoever can administer the project can connect it to a source and disconnect it. That is deliberate and it is also the loosest thing on this page, because `min_project_role: owner` is the intent and nothing enforces a project role yet (WP 2.2 landed the resolver; no policy here calls it). `audited: false` is the one that should be uncomfortable: creating a link grants an external system standing access to a project's data and revoking one takes it away, and neither writes an audit row. It is not a tier transition, so G4 does not formally cover it; it is a governance event by any reading of §5, and it is recorded here as a named gap rather than left to be noticed. The table's own honesty is elsewhere and it is real: `status`, `status_detail`, `last_verified_at` and `revoked_at` mean a revoked link says when and why. NO `rls_enabled` FIELD, and its absence is the point. The connector migration enables RLS on this table in a plain statement and creates its policy in another — but the same file also builds the staging policies inside a `DO $$ EXECUTE format(...) $$` loop whose SQL mentions this table, so the introspector marks its RLS indeterminate: "the migrations do not say", which is a different claim from "off" and may not be rendered as one. Only the live database can answer (§15), and a sidecar may not assert what the schema does not settle.

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key. The link's identity for every run that used it.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The SuReSuite project this link feeds. One side of the two-sided grant.

columns.name: external_system
columns.meaning: Which external system — `orbit-mrp` is the only value any code writes. Free text, not CHECK-constrained, and that is the one place this table still assumes a single vendor: `ingest_runs.source_kind` is the closed vocabulary WP 3.1 added, and it is the one a reader should trust.
columns.note: A second connector would add a value here AND a `source_kind`, and the two would have to agree. Whoever adds it: make this column a CHECK, or derive it. Two vocabularies for one fact is what I1 exists to prevent, and this is the half WP 3.1 did not close.

columns.name: external_company_id
columns.meaning: The company/tenant identifier IN THE EXTERNAL SYSTEM. Part of the natural key with the project and the system: one project may link one company of one system exactly once.

columns.name: external_company_name
columns.meaning: The company's display name, cached for the picker and refreshed on each sync. A LABEL and never a key (G1) — the id above is what the grant is about.

columns.name: linked_by_user_id
columns.meaning: The person whose own OAuth consent proved membership of that company, in `auth.users`. NOT NULL because the link IS that proof: there is no way to create one from a hand-typed company id, and an unattributed link would be a credential with no owner.

columns.name: external_oauth_token_ref
columns.meaning: The NAME of a secret in Supabase Vault, never a token. `get_erp_oauth_token(p_ref)` resolves it and is granted to `service_role` only, so a browser session cannot read the credential even though it can read this row.
columns.note: The pointer is readable by any project member and the value is not. That is the design: a per-link, per-user delegated token, so revoking one project's link cannot be bypassed by a sibling project.

columns.name: status
columns.meaning: active, needs_attention or revoked. A sync re-verifies both sides before touching data and revokes the link on failure rather than continuing on the old assumption.
columns.note: Not an engine input. It is the field the sync path reads first, and `revoked` is terminal: the connector never resurrects a link, a person re-links.

columns.name: status_detail
columns.meaning: Why the status is what it is, in words a user can act on — "Access revoked in orbit-mrp — reconnect". The reason a revoked link is not a mystery.

columns.name: last_verified_at
columns.meaning: When both sides were last proved live. The age of the claim that this link still works.

columns.name: auto_apply_threshold_pct
columns.meaning: The percentage of changed rows below which a sync may promote itself without a human. 0 — the default — means every sync waits for approval.
columns.note: A number with teeth: above it, staged rows reach tier 2 with no person in the loop, and the resulting audit row names no actor (D36). It is bounded 0..100 by CHECK, and the connector additionally refuses to auto-apply any run with `fields_failed > 0`.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the link was created. Server-stamped.

columns.name: revoked_at
columns.meaning: When the link was revoked, or NULL. With `status_detail`, the revocation is a record rather than a disappearance.

columns.name: sync_schedule_cron
columns.meaning: A cron expression for scheduled syncs, or NULL for manual-only. Read by the pg_cron sweep and by any external scheduler driving the same RPC.

columns.name: sync_enabled
columns.meaning: Whether the schedule is live. Two fields rather than one because a paused schedule must not lose its expression — turning sync off and on again should not require retyping the cron.
columns.note: Not an engine input. `due_erp_sync_links()` reads it with `status = 'active'` and a non-null cron; its own comment records that it is a placeholder that does not evaluate the expression, so today the sweep offers every enabled link and the Edge Function decides.

project_erp_links.note: NOT RENAMED BY WP 3.1, AND THAT IS A DECISION. The four tables around it became `ingest_*` because they hold rows from ANY source; this one holds the credential and the consent for ONE source, and calling it `ingest_links` would promise a generality it does not have — a CSV upload has nothing to link. When a second connector arrives, the question to ask is whether it shares this shape (a per-user delegated token proving membership of an external tenant) or needs its own; `ingest_runs.source_kind` already carries the distinction that matters to everything downstream. ITS SIDECAR IS HERE BECAUSE WP 3.1 IS WHERE IT WAS DUE. The table was deferred under this package in `coverage.yaml` since WP 1.4, and a deferral is a commitment: carrying it forward to the next open package would have been the same move that produced D41 — an owner who has gone home, indistinguishable from an owner.

project_graph_state.tier_name: derived — a pure function of tier 2
project_graph_state.grain: One row per project: every hash of the project's LIVE data — the composite `graph_hash`, its two domains and the three levels — stored, so a page that asks "has this project's graph changed?" reads a row instead of rebuilding a snapshot of thirteen tables.
