A CACHE of a pure function of tier 2, safe to drop: the next read rebuilds it.

governance.note: No page and no API role writes it. Two writers, both SECURITY DEFINER and both inside somebody else's statement: the statement triggers on the thirteen hashed tables (`_graph_state_touch_*`) raise `dirty`, and `project_graph_hashes` stores a recomputed set — only when `generation` has not moved since it read the row, so a reader that started before a write cannot store the pre-write hash over the flag the write raised. Read through `has_project_access`. Audited at statement grain like every tier-3 table; its audit rows name whoever made the edit that dirtied it.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project these hashes describe. Cascades with the project.

columns.name: schema_version
columns.meaning: The snapshot rule the stored hashes were computed under (3 since WP 5.3; WP 10.1 did not bump it — the levels are projections, not new facts).

columns.name: level_spec
columns.meaning: The level rule the three level hashes were computed under (1 since WP 10.1). A stored row on another spec is recomputed on read rather than trusted.

columns.name: graph_hash
columns.meaning: The composite — identical to `current_graph_hash` and to a `dataset_versions` row of the same content.

columns.name: hash_inputs
columns.meaning: The `inputs` domain hash (WP 4.1).

columns.name: hash_network
columns.meaning: The `network` domain hash (WP 4.1, deep tier since WP 5.3).

columns.name: hash_product
columns.meaning: The PRODUCT level — see `dataset_versions.hash_product`.

columns.name: hash_process
columns.meaning: The PROCESS level — see `dataset_versions.hash_process`.

columns.name: hash_firm
columns.meaning: The FIRM level — see `dataset_versions.hash_firm`.

columns.name: dirty
columns.meaning: True when a hashed table changed since the stored hashes were computed. It means "recompute before answering", NEVER "stale": a write of a row's own value back raises it and the recomputed hash is unchanged (`rehearsal/140` §6 holds that line).

columns.name: generation
columns.meaning: Incremented by every touch. The store step updates only if it still matches the value read before computing — the race guard a boolean alone cannot be.

columns.name: computed_at
columns.meaning: When the stored hashes were last computed. NULL while a row has only ever been dirtied.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When the row last changed for any reason.

project_members.grain: One person's standing on one project. This is the level of access the platform did not have until WP 2.2 — between "in the organization" (sees every project) and "not in it" (sees none).

governance.note: `write: null` is LITERAL and load-bearing. The table has a SELECT policy and NO insert/update/delete policy, so RLS denies writes by default and the SECURITY DEFINER RPCs are the only way in. That is not an oversight to be tidied up later: D28 says every policy here is PERMISSIVE and permissive policies OR, so a "deny writes" policy added beside anything else would deny nothing. The ABSENCE of a policy is the enforcement. `audited: false` — a membership change writes no audit row; WP 2.3 is where that becomes true, and this table is one of the reasons it matters. Since D211 the writers are the WP 3.4 owner trigger and `admin_set_project_member` / `admin_remove_project_member` (active super admin, /admin/users/:userId), which log to `admin_audit_logs` and refuse to change the project modeler's own row. Since D212 `admin_transfer_project` writes it too, because ownership is this row as well as `projects.modeler_id`: the owner becomes a standing `owner`, the previous owner's row is removed, and on an organization change so is the row of every account outside the target organization.

policies.name: project_members: read own and co-members
policies.using: user_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM public.project_members m WHERE m.project_id = project_members.project_id AND m.user_id = public.get_current_user_id()) OR public.current_is_super_admin()
policies.with_check: user_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM public.project_members m WHERE m.project_id = project_members.project_id AND m.user_id = public.get_current_user_id()) OR public.current_is_super_admin()

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project the membership is on. CASCADEs when the project is deleted.

columns.name: user_id
columns.meaning: The approved user who holds it. CASCADEs when the account is deleted.

columns.name: project_role
columns.meaning: What they may do here — `owner`, `editor`, `analyst` or `viewer`, CHECK-constrained and totally ordered by `project_role_rank()`. A PROJECT vocabulary, and deliberately not `organization_members.org_role` (owner|admin|member): they share the word "owner" and mean different things by it.

ingest.validate: one of owner / editor / analyst / viewer

columns.name: granted_by
columns.meaning: Who granted the membership. SET NULL rather than CASCADE on purpose — losing the granter's account must not silently delete the grant they made.

columns.name: expires_at
columns.meaning: When the membership lapses. NULL means standing — unlike `delegation_grants`, where an end date is mandatory. `effective_project_role()` applies the comparison so no caller can forget it.

columns.name: rationale
columns.meaning: Why the person is on the project, in the granter's words. Optional here and REQUIRED on a delegation: a standing membership is usually self-evident from the project, a temporary elevation never is.

substitutions.when: a row is backfilled from projects.modeler_id
substitutions.value: 'backfilled from projects.modeler_id by WP 2.2 — the de-facto owner'
substitutions.visible_as: the stored rationale says so verbatim, so a reader can tell a backfilled row from a granted one

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the membership was created. Server-stamped.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When it was last changed. Server-stamped by DEFAULT only; no trigger maintains it.

project_members.note: Backfilled from `projects.modeler_id` — every project's modeler becomes its owner. That records a fact that already held rather than granting anything new: every write policy in the schema already reads `modeler_id` as the project's owner. `modeler_id` is NOT a declared foreign key to `approved_users`, so the backfill filters on the user existing; a project whose modeler row is gone gets no owner and is visible only to the organization, which is the honest outcome and a §15 question worth asking.

project_role_capabilities.grain: What one project role may do — one row per (project_role, capability). The project layer of the four-layer resolver, shaped exactly like `role_capabilities` so all four layers read the same way.

governance.note: Read is open to everyone (`USING (true)`): it is a static policy table with no per-tenant content, and every client needs it to render what a role can do. As with the other capability tables there is no write policy, so writes are service-role only.

columns.name: project_role
columns.meaning: The project role the row grants for — owner, editor, analyst or viewer.

ingest.validate: one of owner / editor / analyst / viewer

columns.name: capability_key
columns.meaning: The capability, FK to `capabilities.key`. CASCADEs, so retiring a capability cannot leave grants pointing at nothing.

columns.name: allowed
columns.meaning: Whether this role gets it. The layer is TRI-STATE in effect: a missing row means "inherit from the org layer", `false` means "deny at the project level". They are different answers and the resolver's COALESCE relies on it.

substitutions.when: no row exists for this (project_role, capability)
substitutions.value: the org layer's answer, then the role layer's, then false
substitutions.visible_as: capabilities_for_user returns the resolved boolean; the layer that decided it is not currently reported

columns.note: WHICH LAYER DECIDED IS NOT RETURNED, and that is a §5 T1 gap worth naming: a user told "you cannot export" cannot learn whether that came from their role, their org, their project role or an explicit user deny. The resolver has the information and discards it. WP 2.4 renders governance and is the place to fix it.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the grant row was created. Server-stamped.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When it was last changed. Server-stamped.

project_role_capabilities.note: Seeded by WP 2.2 with the split that gives `analyst` its meaning: an analyst may edit tier-4 decisions (`data_edit_policies`) and may NOT edit the tier-2 measured inputs those decisions are judged against (`data_edit_inputs`). Before the split one `data_editing` flag governed both, so the role could not exist.

projects.grain: One modelling project: a named supply chain, owned by one modeller, belonging to one organization. It is the scope every other project-scoped table hangs off `project_id`, and it is the row almost every RLS policy in the schema reaches through to decide whether the caller may see anything at all.

governance.note: Tier G rather than a data tier: `projects` holds no measured quantity. It is the SCOPE, and its access rules are the ones every other table inherits by joining to it — which is why WP 2.1 had to redefine 58 policies on 24 other tables to change one comparison. Read is org-wide (any member of the owning organization sees every project in it); write is restricted to the project's own modeller or a global `admin`. There is no project-level role between those two — a member cannot be given read on one project and not another, which is `subtractive-delegation` (§2.1 G3) having nowhere to attach. WP 2.2's `project_members` is where `min_project_role: editor` above stops being a forward declaration. `audited: false`: project creation and deletion write no audit row (WP 2.3).

policies.name: Projects: org create by modeler or admin
policies.using: public.org_is_current_user_org(organization_id, organization) AND ( ( (SELECT user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1) = 'modeler' AND modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() ) OR ( (SELECT user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1) = 'admin' ) )
policies.with_check: public.org_is_current_user_org(organization_id, organization) AND ( ( (SELECT user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1) = 'modeler' AND modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() ) OR ( (SELECT user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1) = 'admin' ) )

policies.name: Projects: org delete by owner or admin
policies.using: public.org_is_current_user_org(organization_id, organization) AND ( modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR ( (SELECT user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1) = 'admin') )
policies.with_check: public.org_is_current_user_org(organization_id, organization) AND ( modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR ( (SELECT user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1) = 'admin') )

policies.name: Projects: org update by owner or admin
policies.using: public.org_is_current_user_org(organization_id, organization) AND ( modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR ( (SELECT user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1) = 'admin') )
policies.with_check: public.org_is_current_user_org(organization_id, organization) AND ( modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR ( (SELECT user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1) = 'admin') )

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: The project's identity, and the `project_id` foreign key of every project-scoped table in the schema.

columns.name: name
columns.meaning: The project's title, as the modeller typed it.

columns.name: modeler_id
columns.meaning: The approved user who owns the project. Stamped by `set_project_defaults()` from the calling user when not supplied, and it is the second half of every write policy: org match AND (modeller is caller OR caller is admin).

substitutions.when: a project is inserted without a modeler_id
substitutions.visible_as: the project lists render the resulting owner

columns.note: NOT a declared foreign key to `approved_users` — it is a bare uuid. WP 2.2 backfills it into `project_members` as the project's `owner`, which is where the reference becomes real.

columns.name: plant_name
columns.meaning: The name of the plant this project models. Part of the `(modeler_id, plant_name, name)` unique constraint, and the join key the lane and BOM tables carry as their own `plant_name`.

columns.name: supply_chain_model
columns.meaning: Whether the chain is modelled as `Make-To-Stock` or `Make-To-Order`, CHECK-constrained to those two.

substitutions.visible_as: the project settings page renders the resulting mode

columns.note: NOT TRACED into `scsim` from this column. The engine's make-to-stock versus make-to-order behaviour comes from the policy set, not from a project flag; this is the label the pages branch on when deciding which forms to show.

columns.name: completed
columns.meaning: Whether the project has the datasets it needs to simulate. Maintained by `update_project_completion_status()`, not set by hand.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the project was created. Server-stamped.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When the project row was last modified. Server-stamped.

columns.name: organization
columns.meaning: The owning organization, as a string, copied from the creating user at insert. NOT NULL with a default, so it always holds something.

substitutions.when: a project is inserted with no user context to copy from
substitutions.visible_as: nowhere. The string authorizes like any other tenant name, so a project that fell to the default is readable by every other account that also fell to it.

columns.note: The other half of D13, and the right-hand side of 73 of the 122 live org comparisons WP 2.1 rewrote. Nothing updates it when the organization is renamed — `admin_update_organization` touches `organizations.name` only — so after a rename this column holds the old name indefinitely.

columns.name: modeler_name
columns.meaning: The owner's name, denormalized at insert. A display convenience, and stale the moment the user renames themselves; `modeler_id` is the fact.

columns.name: bom_level
columns.meaning: Which bill-of-materials shape the project uses — `single` or `multi`. It decides which of `bom_single_level` / `bom_multi_level` is read, and every dataset RPC branches on it.

substitutions.visible_as: the data manager renders the single-level BOM uploader

columns.name: simulation_start
columns.meaning: First day of the horizon the project simulates.
columns.note: NOT TRACED into `scsim` from this column: the engine reads run weeks only, and the worker takes the horizon from the run request. Since WP 18.1 (§4 D318) it is RUN WEEK 0 — the anchor through which a disruption start entered as an ISO week or a date becomes the run week that is stored (`start_day`), with what was entered kept beside it (`scenarios.disruption_schedule[].start_anchor`). Every new run records it (`simulation_runs.calendar_start`), so a later edit here never re-dates a past run. With `simulation_end` it is the project window, the one authored run length: a new scenario with no validated or baseline world takes its horizon from it, and a scenario that runs another length says so. The engine's demand calendar is a second anchor (the earliest `demand_forecasts.period_start`); the Lab says when the two differ. Until WP 18.1 the form stored a picked date through `toISOString()`, a day early east of UTC; `20261101000002` (WP 18.3) moved every window carrying that signature (`YYYY-12-31 → (YYYY+1)-12-30`) to the days picked. Runs backfilled before it keep the 31 December they recorded.

columns.name: simulation_end
columns.meaning: Last day of the horizon the project simulates.
columns.note: As `simulation_start` — the run request is what the engine actually reads. Since WP 18.1 (§4 D318) the start and end are the project window, the one authored run length: project settings state it in weeks, refuse a window outside the engine's 52–520 weeks, and the /policies delivery schedule, a new scenario's horizon and the Lab's mismatch note all read it through `src/lib/sim/projectWindow.ts`.

columns.name: plant_latitude
columns.meaning: The plant's latitude in decimal degrees, WGS 84, for the network map.
columns.note: NOT TRACED into the engine, and correctly so: `scsim` has no geography. Coordinates place a node on the map; they do not affect a simulated quantity. A later package wanting distance to DRIVE anything must add the concept to the engine first.

columns.name: plant_longitude
columns.meaning: The plant's longitude in decimal degrees, WGS 84, for the network map.
columns.note: As `plant_latitude` — rendered, never simulated.

columns.name: plant_location_text
columns.meaning: The plant's location as typed, e.g. "Hanoi, Vietnam". The last comma-separated segment, uppercased and trimmed, is what the map matches against `risk_data.country`.

columns.name: deep_tier_enabled
columns.meaning: Whether the project models tier-2 and tier-3 suppliers as well as its direct ones. Gates the deep-tier tables and the multi-tier network pages.

columns.name: data_type
columns.meaning: Whether the project's data was uploaded and curated by a user (`curated`) or generated for demonstration (`synthetic`).

substitutions.visible_as: nothing distinguishes the two in an export today. A synthetic project whose flag defaulted to 'curated' is indistinguishable from a real one downstream — the §5 T3 blind spot this column exists to prevent, not yet closed.

columns.name: organization_id
columns.meaning: The owning organization by uuid. This is what the public /v1 API authorizes on (`api_can_access_project`: `p.organization_id = p_org_id`), and it is the plane that survives a rename.
columns.note: D27 lived here. `set_project_defaults()` stamped `NEW.organization` and never this column, so the one-time backfill in `20260709000002` was the only thing that had ever set it and every project created afterwards was NULL — visible through RLS, which compared text, and invisible to /v1, which compares this. WP 2.1 fixed the trigger first and then backfilled, because a backfill in front of a trigger that does not stamp rots at the next insert. Still NULLABLE: rows whose text org matches no organization row, or matches two, were deliberately left alone rather than resolved to a guess, and the dual read keeps them reachable. The count is a §15 question.

projects.note: `natural_key_intended` is `(organization_id, name)` and the declared constraint is `(modeler_id, plant_name, name)` — they are different claims, and the declared one is the weaker: two modellers in one organization may each hold a project called the same thing for the same plant. Changing it is not WP 2.1's to do; `natural-key` (§2.1 I4) lands in WP 3.3 and this row is one of its inputs. Recorded here so the gap has an owner rather than being noticed again in a quarter.

recovery_playbooks.grain: One named recovery strategy a scenario can apply after a disruption — the levers, their order and their parameters. A system playbook (`is_system`, `project_id` NULL) ships with the product; a project playbook belongs to one project.

governance.note: Tier 4 — the DECISION plane: what a person or an agent CHOSE, as against the dataset they chose it over and the result it produced. `result-binding` (I8) needs all three, which is why WP 6.3 keeps the results and this package takes the decisions. Audited from WP 6.4: the three statement-grain triggers land beside this sidecar, because `dataPlaneAudit.test.ts` scopes its rule to tables IN the contract and a deferred table's writes are unaudited with nothing to notice (D54). **Two of the six recovery strategies a scenario can name reach no engine plugin (§4 D114)**, so a playbook's `config` can record an intent the run will not act on. The row is stored faithfully either way; what is missing is a reader that says so, and the manual states it meanwhile.

policies.name: playbooks_insert_own
policies.using: is_system = false AND project_id IS NOT NULL AND created_by = auth.uid()
policies.with_check: is_system = false AND project_id IS NOT NULL AND created_by = auth.uid()

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key. There is no natural key: two playbooks may share a name, in one project or across projects, and the product treats that as legitimate rather than as a collision.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this playbook belongs to, or NULL for a system playbook. Nullable on purpose — that NULL is what makes a row part of the shipped catalog, and it is read as such by `useRecoveryPlaybooks`'s `is_system.eq.true,project_id.eq.<id>` filter.

columns.name: name
columns.meaning: What a person reads in the picker. Not a key; see `id`.

columns.name: description
columns.meaning: One sentence on what the playbook does. Defaults to the empty string rather than NULL, so a reader gets a blank rather than the word `null` — and a blank here means nobody wrote one, not that the playbook does nothing.

columns.name: is_system
columns.meaning: TRUE for a playbook that ships with the product. The only thing separating the catalog from a user's own work, and the first sort key in the picker.

columns.name: config
columns.meaning: THE DECISION ITSELF — which levers, in what order, with what parameters. Free-form JSON: the levers are validated where they are USED rather than where they are stored, which is why D114's two unmapped strategies can be saved at all.

columns.name: created_by
columns.meaning: The user who created it, where one is recorded. NULL on system rows and on anything written before the column existed — unknown, not nobody.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was created. Server-stamped, never the client's clock.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When it was last changed, server-stamped.

risk_data.tier_name: project-independent, versioned by vintage rather than by project
risk_data.grain: One country's current risk class, as one named publisher graded it in one named edition. NOT project-scoped: two projects sourcing from the same country see the same row, which is the point — a per-project copy drifts.

governance.note: `write: null` is literal: no page, edge function or upload path writes this table. It is loaded by an operator through the service role, which bypasses RLS — so the ABSENCE of an INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE policy is the write rule, not an omission. Read is open to `authenticated` and `anon` because the risk shading renders on the public network pages.

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate row identifier. Carries no meaning and joins to nothing.

columns.name: country
columns.meaning: The country the risk class applies to, spelled as the network pages spell it — `upper(btrim(...))`, matching the last comma-separated segment of a node's `location_text`. A CHECK enforces the spelling so the unique index and the page lookup cannot disagree about whether 'Vietnam' and 'VIETNAM' are one country.

columns.name: risk_class
columns.meaning: The publisher's risk grade for the country, in the five-value vocabulary the map renders — Very Low, Low, Medium, High, Very High. An ordinal label, not a score: it may be compared for order and never averaged.

substitutions.when: no row exists for the node's country
substitutions.value: the map renders the node grey and labels it "Unknown"
substitutions.visible_as: RiskDataNotice — the page says the dimension is missing rather than shading it away

ingest.validate: one of Very Low / Low / Medium / High / Very High — CHECK risk_data_risk_class_known

columns.note: NOT TRACED into the engine, and that is correct: country risk shades the network map, it is not a simulation input. `scsim` has no country concept — disruption targets are suppliers, plants and lanes (blueprint §2.3 G11). A later package that wants country risk to DRIVE anything must add it to the engine first, not read this column from the mapper. 'Unknown' is deliberately not a storable value: it is what the absence of a row looks like, and storing it would turn "we have no figure" into a figure (§5 T1; the same over-claim as D17).

columns.name: source
columns.meaning: Who published the figure — the named index or provider. NOT NULL because a country-risk grade with no named origin is an assertion the product cannot defend, and its only output is a colour a reader will take for fact.

columns.name: vintage
columns.meaning: The edition the figure is from, as the publisher labels it (e.g. "2025-H1"). This is the table's version axis: reference data is versioned by vintage, not by project (PLAN.md §2).

columns.name: licence
columns.meaning: The licence the row is held under. NOT NULL, and the reason is specific: country-risk indices are mostly commercial, so a row whose licence is unrecorded is a row nobody can tell you may republish — including in an export (§5 T4).

columns.name: refreshed_at
columns.meaning: When this row was last written from the source. Freshness, not row age.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was first inserted. Server-stamped.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When the row was last modified. Server-stamped.

risk_data.note: The second of WP 1.4's three orphans (D4), and the one that turned out not to be an orphan at all. Two network pages read it and no migration created it — but the table EXISTS in the production database, untracked, with the spreadsheet-header columns `COUNTRY` and `"RISK CLASS"`. CI proved it: the first version of the migration was a plain `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`, which no-opped, and the next statement failed on a column that was not there. Same class as `approved_users`: created outside migration tracking, invisible to a static replay, which can only tell you no migration creates a table and not whether one exists. `20260915000003_risk_data.sql` now both builds it on a fresh database and ADOPTS the one already there — renaming the quoted columns, adding the provenance columns, and marking the pre-contract rows `source: 'unrecorded (loaded before the reference-tier contract)'` rather than inventing a publisher for them. The new CHECKs land `NOT VALID` on the adopted table: enforced for every future write, not retroactively asserted about rows nobody has looked at.

role_capabilities.grain: One grant or denial, for one role and one capability. The OUTERMOST layer: what a role gets before any org, project or user says otherwise.

governance.note: One of the four layers `capabilities_for_user()` resolves, in the order role -> org -> project -> user, most specific winning. `audited: false` and it matters here more than on most tables: these rows ARE the permissions, and a change to one currently leaves no record of who made it (§2.1 `audit-actor`, WP 2.3).

columns.name: role
columns.meaning: the global app_role the row grants for — super_admin, admin, modeler or user.

columns.name: capability_key
columns.meaning: The capability, naming a row in `capabilities`.

columns.name: allowed
columns.meaning: Whether this layer grants the capability. TRI-STATE in effect: a missing row means "inherit from the next layer out", `false` means "deny here". They are different answers and the resolver's COALESCE depends on the difference.

substitutions.when: no row exists at this layer
substitutions.value: the next layer out decides; the chain ends in false
substitutions.visible_as: capabilities_for_user returns the resolved boolean; which layer decided is not reported

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was created. Server-stamped.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When it was last changed. Server-stamped.

role_capabilities.note: WP 2.2 seeded `data_edit_inputs` and `data_edit_policies` into this table from whatever `data_editing` already said, so effective access on the day of deploy was identical to the day before. `data_editing` is deliberately still here: it is removed when the last call site has moved to one of the new keys, not before.

run_item_series.tier_name: results — pinned to dataset + policy + engine version
run_item_series.grain: One item's weekly series from one INSPECTION run: a material or a product of the project, and a map of named weekly arrays for it (on-hand, in-transit and orders for a material; demand, production, fulfillment, backlog and lost units for a product). Written ONLY for an inspection run — exactly one replication, user-chosen seed, engine trace raised to full debug — because per-item evidence at multi-replication scale is deliberately not exposed; every other run has no rows here. Tier 5 — a RESULT of one run, input to nothing; a row is superseded by re-running, never edited.

surfaces.via: component ItemSeriesExplorer (mounted by RunValidateStage) → select kind,item_id,series from run_item_series (every item, paged)
surfaces.note: Run & Validate is where an inspection run is STARTED, and the explorer sits under it. It reads every item's row for the run, 100 rows a read, once per run: the inventory explorer's ranked tables need every material and every finished good at once (a few MB for a large project). It used to read an id index and then one item on demand, which could chart an item and could not rank them. The table stays a sibling of `run_replications` so none of this rides the realtime stream.

surfaces.via: component ItemSeriesExplorer (mounted by ResultsDashboard) → select kind,item_id,series from run_item_series (every item, paged)
surfaces.note: Simulation Lab dispatches no inspection run, so this panel shows rows only for a run started from Run & Validate, and says so rather than rendering empty without a reason (§4 D113's shape).

governance.note: `write: simulation_lab` because the table has two PREDICATE-LESS write policies — `run_item_series_auth_all` (authenticated) and `run_item_series_anon_write` (anon and authenticated, widened by WP 7.1 stage 1a in `20260919000010`) — and a policy with no predicate is a user-facing write path whether or not a page uses it, so `governanceEnforcement.test.ts` refuses a `null` claim here exactly as it did for `run_replications`. The capability named is the one that gates the action which writes these rows: running a simulation, here an inspection run from Run & Validate. TWO WRITERS, both upserting on `(run_id, kind, item_id)` in chunks of 100: the Fly worker with the service role (`_write_item_series`, which FAILS the run rather than reporting it green when the rows do not persist), and the browser engine as `anon` (`pyodideEngine.persistEngineResult`, best-effort). The second is why this is one of the eleven tables §4 D154 measured as genuinely writable from the browser's `anon` role — D28's standing decision (document, do not change), WP 7.1's to close. `min_project_role` is `viewer` because nothing here enforces a role today, not because a viewer ought to be able to write results. Deleting the run or the project removes its rows (`ON DELETE CASCADE` on both foreign keys). NOT AUDITED, and that is the tier: `audit-actor` covers tiers 2–4, and a row here is the output of one run and an input to nothing.

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key. The row's identity is `natural_key_intended`; nothing reads or joins on this.

columns.name: run_id
columns.meaning: The `simulation_runs` row this series belongs to. ON DELETE CASCADE — a series of a run that no longer exists is not evidence. A third of the natural key, and what the explorer filters every read on.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The owning project, denormalized from the run so a project's rows can be reached without the join. ON DELETE CASCADE.

columns.name: kind
columns.meaning: Whether `item_id` names a material or a product — 'material' or 'product' (CHECK `run_item_series_kind_check`). It decides which measures `series` carries.

engine.transform: the prefix of the engine's item_series key, before the '.'

columns.name: item_id
columns.meaning: The material or product id, exactly as the engine's compiled model carries it — the ids the run's dataset supplied. Text, not a foreign key: the series is evidence about the run's world, and must survive an edit to the item master that came after it.

engine.transform: str() of the engine's item_ids[kind][row], the row label of each per-item matrix

columns.name: series
columns.meaning: The item's weekly series, one array per measure, each as long as the run's horizon in weeks. The measures are the engine's per-item trace matrices, declared once as the `item_series` dict in scsim/scsim/core/engine.py and keyed `<kind>.<measure>` there; this column carries the part after the dot. Every measure is in units of the item. `unit_source` is `derived` because some measures are stocks (on hand, in transit, backlog) and some are weekly flows (orders, demand, production, fulfillment, lost units), and that follows from the measure, not from one token for the column.

engine.transform: one row per (kind, item) of each item_series matrix; _finite(x, 5) per element, so NaN and ±inf become null

columns.note: The explorer's legend names the measures for display; it is a label map, not a second declaration, and a measure it does not know still renders under its key. The migration's header comment also lists them — written when the table was created and not maintained since, so the engine is the authority. NO `computed_by`, for `run_replications`' reason: the producer is scsim (Python, in the Fly worker or in Pyodide), which `contract:check` R18 cannot resolve; `engine.consumed_by` carries the path instead. DEFAULT `'{}'` — a row whose series is empty is a row the engine produced no measures for, not a row of zeros.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was first inserted. An upsert of the same key does not re-stamp it.

run_replications.tier_name: results — pinned to dataset + policy + engine version
run_replications.grain: One replication of one simulation run: the seed it used, the KPI row the engine computed for it, and its weekly series. A run has as many rows here as it has replications, and `rep_index` orders them. Tier 5 — a RESULT, derived from a tier-2 dataset by a named engine version, never an input to anything. Nothing downstream reads it except the result surfaces; a row is superseded by re-running, never edited.

surfaces.note: Both result surfaces reach this table through the SAME hook, so the evidence is the hook's read rather than either page's render. Run & Validate reads every replication of the newest run: the weekly series charts, the financial statement, the per-seed explorer and the inventory chart all render from these rows.

The run-results workbook. This is the path by which a replication row leaves the system, so it is the one A5's Reproducibility Record has to bind (`result-binding`, still owed — WP 10.4, which absorbed WP 9.2).

governance.note: `write: simulation_lab` is the capability that gates the only user-facing action which writes this table — running a simulation. It is NOT `null`, and the first draft of this sidecar said it was: `analysis_runs` can claim `write: null` because it has no write policy at all and every write goes through a SECURITY DEFINER RPC, but this table is written by the BROWSER, as a PostgREST upsert from `pyodideEngine.persistEngineResult`, behind two predicate-less policies (`rep_auth_all` and `run_replications_anon_write`). `governanceEnforcement.test.ts` refused the `null` claim on exactly that evidence, and it was right: a policy with no predicate permits any holder of the table grant to write, which is a user-facing write path whether or not a page uses it. So the capability is declared and the exposure is stated rather than implied: this is one of the eleven tables §4 D154 measured as genuinely writable from the browser's `anon` role. That is D28's standing decision (document, do not change) and WP 7.1's to close — `min_project_role` is `viewer` because nothing here enforces a role today, not because a viewer ought to be able to write results. NOT AUDITED, and that is the tier rather than an omission: the audit rule (`audit-actor`) covers tiers 2, 3 and 4, where a write changes the world a later run will see. A replication row is the OUTPUT of one run and an input to nothing; re-running writes new rows rather than mutating these, so there is no tier transition here for an audit row to name.

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key. The row's identity is `natural_key_intended`; this exists because the table predates that rule.
columns.note: NOT TRACED to the engine because nothing in the engine reads it — the engine produces these rows and never joins back to them.

columns.name: run_id
columns.meaning: The `simulation_runs` row this replication belongs to. ON DELETE CASCADE: deleting a run takes its replications with it, which is right for a result — a replication of a run that no longer exists is not evidence.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The owning project. Denormalized from `simulation_runs` so RLS and the per-project reads do not need the join.

columns.name: rep_index
columns.meaning: This replication's position in the run, from 0. Half of the natural key, and the order the convergence plot walks.

engine.transform: the enumeration index of ScenarioResult.kpis

columns.name: seed_used
columns.meaning: The run's ROOT seed since WP 10.6 (§4 D246). The engine draws every stream from a keyed SeedSequence tree on (root seed, `model_rep`, `event_rep`), so a replication is reproduced by re-running with this root seed and is identified by `rep_index` and its cell (`kpis.model_rep`, `kpis.event_rep`). Before WP 10.6 the bridge wrote `project_seed * 1000 + model_rep` here — not a seed (typing it in reproduced nothing) and shared by every event draw of one world — and this description called it "the seed this replication actually ran with", which it never was.

engine.transform: project_seed * 1000 + int(rep_cells[i][0])

columns.note: The per-seed explorer addresses replications by this value (`ReplicationSeedExplorer`), but the read that fetches it is the hook's `select *` cited at table grain — there is no column-grain read to point at, and inventing one would be the shape D21 and D22 warn about.

columns.name: status
columns.meaning: Lifecycle of the one replication — 'queued' until the engine returns it, 'done' once its KPI row and series are written. The result surfaces filter on 'done' so a partially-streamed run does not render half-written rows as if they were results.
columns.note: DEFAULT 'queued' and no CHECK constraint, so the vocabulary is a convention rather than a rule the database enforces. Not widened here: constraining it is a migration this package does not need, and the honest record is that the column accepts any text today.

columns.name: kpis
columns.meaning: This replication's KPI row, exactly as `compute_replication_kpis` built it: fill rate, revenue, lost sales, peak backlog, the inventory window averages, capacity utilization and one `cost_<component>` key per entry of scsim's COST_COMPONENTS. Units are per-key and follow the engine's definition of each measure, which is why `unit_source` is `derived` rather than a single token.

engine.transform: _finite(v, 6) per key — NaN and ±inf become null, which is valid JSON

columns.note: The KEYS are a vocabulary this file does not restate — they are the engine's, and `deriveRunKpis` reads them from it so the manual cannot drift from what a run carries. §4 D113 is what restating them costs: a display list built from the LEGACY engine's KPI shape offered eleven rows the canonical engine never writes. NO `computed_by`: its contract is a writer `contract:check` R18 can find in `src/` or `supabase/functions/`, and the producer here is Python (`scsim/scsim/kpi/compute.py::compute_replication_kpis`) running in Pyodide. Naming it there would be a declaration R18 cannot resolve — §4 D118's shape. `engine.consumed_by` carries the path instead.

columns.name: time_series
columns.meaning: This replication's weekly series, one array per key, each as long as the horizon in weeks — OR `{}` when they are kept elsewhere: since WP 10.6 a worker run writes them to ONE Parquet object per run (`simulation_runs.series_object`, private `run-results` bucket) and `runSeries.ts` hydrates the rows from it, and the retention sweep empties them when a standard run's series expire (`series_expired_at`). `{}` and not NULL because the column is NOT NULL DEFAULT `{}`, the value every reader already treats as "no series". The keys are scsim's PUBLISHED weekly series and are declared in ONE place — `WEEKLY_SERIES` in scsim/scsim/core/context.py — which also fixes each series' unit and how it may be aggregated across weeks (`level` = a stock, average it; `flow` = a weekly quantity, sum it; `ratio` = neither). `unit_source` is `derived` because the unit is per-key, from that declaration, not one token for the column. The four inventory series (`on_hand_value`, `fg_value`, `on_hand_units`, `fg_units`) are what WP 9.1 added to a user's view; `fg_value` had been computed on every replication since the trace was written and published by nothing, because the vocabulary was authored six times and it was present in only two of them (§4 D164).

engine.transform: fill_rate from fr_series, every other published series iterated generically out of extra_series; _finite(x, 5) per element

columns.note: Rendered on BOTH result surfaces — `InventoryOverTime` (materials and finished goods, units or value), `WeeklySeriesChart` and `ReplicationSeedExplorer` — all fed by the hook's `select *` cited at table grain, so there is no column-grain read to cite. A run made before a series existed carries a row WITHOUT that key. The inventory panel states that rather than drawing a zero line, because a missing measurement and a measured zero are different facts and T1 does not allow one to stand in for the other. NO `computed_by`, for the reason given on `kpis`: the producer is scsim, which R18 cannot resolve. `engine.consumed_by` carries the path.

columns.name: warmup_at
columns.meaning: The week the run's warm-up was detected to end, copied onto every replication of the run. Nullable because it is known only at run end: the rows streamed live during a run carry null and the final upsert fills it.

engine.transform: ScenarioResult.warmup.adopted_week, or null when no warm-up report
engine.missing_default: null — not measured, which the charts render as no warm-up marker

columns.note: Drawn as the warm-up `ReferenceLine` on every weekly series chart, including the inventory panel, from the hook's `select *`.

columns.name: started_at
columns.meaning: When this replication began executing. Null until it starts.

columns.name: ended_at
columns.meaning: When this replication finished. Null while it is queued or running.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was inserted.

run_series_orphans.tier_name: results — pinned to dataset + policy + engine version
run_series_orphans.grain: One series object in the `run-results` bucket whose run no longer exists, waiting to be removed. A deleted run queues its object here instead of deleting a storage row with SQL — which would orphan the stored file, and which hosted Supabase refuses — and the next series sweep hands the path to the worker, which removes it through the Storage API.

governance.note: No API role reads or writes it: RLS is on with no policy. Written only by the `simulation_runs_drop_series` trigger (SECURITY DEFINER) and drained only by `sweep_expired_run_series`, which is executable by the service role alone. NOT AUDITED: a work queue for one kind of cleanup, each row living from a run's delete to the next sweep; the delete itself is the audited event.

columns.name: path
columns.meaning: The object's path in the `run-results` bucket (`<project_id>/<run_id>/series.parquet`), as the run's `series_object` held it.

columns.name: run_id
columns.meaning: The deleted run's id — a record, not a reference: the run is gone.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The deleted run's project — also a record; the project may be gone too.

columns.name: queued_at
columns.meaning: When the run was deleted; the sweep hands objects over oldest first.

run_usage.tier_name: results — pinned to dataset + policy + engine version
run_usage.grain: One capacity event of one run: its reservation when it was dispatched (`dispatch`), what it actually used when it finished (`complete`), or the release of its series storage when the sweep expired them (`expire`). The ledger a month's compute is read from.

surfaces.via: hook useMyCapacity → rpc get_my_capacity (what this member has used)

governance.note: No API role reads or writes it: RLS is on with no policy. Written only by SECURITY DEFINER code — `create_simulation_run` (the reservation, in the same statement as the run row it reserves for), the `simulation_runs_usage_complete` trigger (the actual, once per run) and `simulation_runs_usage_expire` (the release) — and read only through `get_my_capacity` and the super admin's `admin_org_capacity_usage` (the super admin's usage view, `src/pages/admin/AdminUsage.tsx` — an admin page, outside §5.1's lineage). NOT AUDITED: tier 5 is output, append-only by its `(run_id, kind)` key, and each row names the member and the run itself. Compute used is the ledger's, so deleting runs does not hand a month's compute back; storage used is derived from the live runs, so a deleted run frees its bytes whatever deleted it.

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: The row's surrogate id.

columns.name: org_id
columns.meaning: The organization whose pool the run drew on — its project's `organization_id` when it was dispatched. NULL for an account with no organization, which has no plan.

columns.name: user_id
columns.meaning: The member whose role share the run drew on: the app's asserted user the dispatcher passed in (D28 — client-asserted, `approved_users.id`). NULL when the caller named nobody (/v1, whose principal is an API key); such a run is held to the pool alone.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The run's project.

columns.name: run_id
columns.meaning: The run. Kept as NULL when the run is deleted, so the month's compute it used stays counted.

columns.name: rep_weeks
columns.meaning: Compute, in replication-weeks: at `dispatch` the reservation (replications × ceil(horizon days / 7)); at `complete` what actually ran (replications done × the same weeks — a cancelled or failed run counts what it computed); 0 at `expire`. A month's use counts each run once, at its actual if it completed.
columns.note: Not an engine input: what a run COST, read by the admission check and the usage views, never by the simulation.

columns.name: bytes
columns.meaning: Series storage: 0 at `dispatch`; at `complete` the bytes a finished run keeps (`simulation_runs.series_bytes`); at `expire` the negative of what the sweep released. A record — storage in use is read from the live runs.
columns.note: Not an engine input: what a run COST, read by the admission check and the usage views, never by the simulation.

columns.name: kind
columns.meaning: `dispatch`, `complete` or `expire`, at most one of each per run.

columns.name: at
columns.meaning: When the event happened; the month a reservation counts in.

scenario_templates.grain: One shipped starting point for a scenario: a named disruption shape with its schedule, its suggested playbook and the run settings that go with it. A template is not a scenario — applying one WRITES a scenario, and the two diverge from that moment.

governance.note: Tier 4 — the DECISION plane: what a person or an agent CHOSE, as against the dataset they chose it over and the result it produced. `result-binding` (I8) needs all three, which is why WP 6.3 keeps the results and this package takes the decisions. Audited from WP 6.4: the three statement-grain triggers land beside this sidecar, because `dataPlaneAudit.test.ts` scopes its rule to tables IN the contract and a deferred table's writes are unaudited with nothing to notice (D54). **Every row is a system row (`is_system` defaults true) and there is no user-facing write path**, so `write` is null and the audit triggers guard a table only a migration changes — which is the point: a change to the shipped catalog is exactly the kind of change nobody notices. **Six of the seven presets name a disruption target the mapper cannot resolve (§4 D112)**, so a run from one of them completes with the disruption ABSENT rather than failing, and that is the open question this package carries.

policies.name: Anyone authenticated can read system templates

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key.

columns.name: slug
columns.meaning: The template's stable name, UNIQUE across the catalog. What a preset is cited by.

columns.name: name
columns.meaning: What a person reads.

columns.name: description
columns.meaning: One sentence on the scenario it sets up. Defaults to the empty string rather than NULL.

columns.name: category
columns.meaning: Which family of disruption this is. Free text with no vocabulary table behind it, so a typo creates a category rather than failing — the same shape `disruption_scenario_settings.key` carries (§16 · WP 6.4 slice 13).

columns.name: severity
columns.meaning: How hard the shipped version of this scenario hits. A label on the template, not a parameter the engine reads.

columns.name: icon
columns.meaning: The glyph the picker draws. NULL where none was chosen.

columns.name: disruption_schedule
columns.meaning: THE DECISION SHAPE — the events, their timing and their targets, copied into a scenario when the template is applied. **This is where D112 lives**: six of seven name a target `_map_events` cannot resolve.

columns.name: suggested_playbook_name
columns.meaning: The recovery playbook this scenario is usually paired with, BY NAME rather than by id. A name is not a join key (G1) and this one is resolved at apply time, so a renamed playbook silently stops matching — recorded here rather than fixed, because the fix is a decision about what a suggestion IS.

columns.name: horizon_days
columns.meaning: How long the shipped run covers, in days. The scenario gets its own copy and may be changed after.

columns.name: warmup_days
columns.meaning: How much of that horizon is discarded before measurement.

columns.name: replications
columns.meaning: How many replications the shipped version runs.

columns.name: seed
columns.meaning: The root seed, so two people applying the same template get the same draws.

columns.name: is_system
columns.meaning: TRUE for every row today. The column exists so a user template could be told apart from a shipped one, and nothing writes a user template.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was created. Server-stamped.

scenarios.grain: One what-if a person set up and can run: the horizon, the warm-up, the replications, the seed, the demand model, the disruption schedule and the recovery overrides. The scenario half of `result-binding` (I8) — a run cites one of these rows, and the export reads it back whole.

governance.note: Tier 4 — the DECISION plane: what a person or an agent CHOSE, as against the dataset they chose it over and the result it produced. `result-binding` (I8) needs all three, which is why WP 6.3 keeps the results and this package takes the decisions. Audited from WP 6.4: the three statement-grain triggers land beside this sidecar, because `dataPlaneAudit.test.ts` scopes its rule to tables IN the contract and a deferred table's writes are unaudited with nothing to notice (D54). **This is the widest decision row in the product** — twenty-two columns, seven of them the engine reads directly — and it is the one a reproducibility record quotes rather than summarises, because a scenario summarised is a scenario that cannot be re-run. **Three settings are a name rather than an id** (`primary_kpi`, `time_step`, `warmup_mode`), which is legitimate for an enum and is the reason D113's KPI vocabulary mattered: a `primary_kpi` naming a measure the engine never emits is a scenario whose objective no run can report.

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key. A run binds to this, and so does the reproducibility record.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this what-if belongs to.

columns.name: name
columns.meaning: What a person called it.

columns.name: description
columns.meaning: Their own note about it. Defaults to the empty string rather than NULL.

columns.name: horizon_days
columns.meaning: How long the simulated world runs, in days. The engine's own clock is weekly, so this is divided at the boundary rather than stored twice — `normalize-at-promotion` (I3) applied to a decision.

columns.name: time_step
columns.meaning: A step-size label (`day` by default) that NO run reads: the engine steps in weeks (`run_window.days_per_tick`), and no screen offers the control any more (WP 9.4). Retained because the model card's baseline fingerprint (`_build_scenario_fingerprint`, fingerprint v1) hashes it, so dropping or rewriting it would turn every validated scenario stale. A new scenario copies its baseline's value rather than choosing one (§4 D222).

columns.name: warmup_mode
columns.meaning: Whether the warm-up is detected or fixed. `auto` means the run decides and writes `warmup_detected_at`; `fixed` means `warmup_days` below is used verbatim.

columns.name: warmup_days
columns.meaning: The fixed warm-up, in days. Read only when `warmup_mode` is not `auto` — so a non-default value here with `auto` set is a setting that does nothing, and nothing says so.

columns.name: replications
columns.meaning: How many independent runs. The KPI table's `n` column is the count that ACTUALLY completed, which is a different number whenever a replication fails.

columns.name: seed
columns.meaning: The root seed. With `crn` below, this is what makes two runs of one scenario comparable rather than merely similar.

columns.name: crn
columns.meaning: Common random numbers: whether two scenarios draw the same randomness so their difference is the POLICY and not the dice. Default true, and turning it off makes a comparison a different kind of claim.

columns.name: demand_model
columns.meaning: How demand is generated when the project's own data does not supply it — kind plus parameters, as JSON. A DECLARED substitution (T2) rather than a silent default, and the default is a Poisson.

columns.name: disruption_schedule
columns.meaning: THE WHAT-IF ITSELF — the events, their timing and their targets. Copied from a template when one is applied and diverging from that moment. §4 D112's unresolvable targets arrive here. Timing is `start_day` (days from run week 0) and `duration_days`; an event whose start was entered as an ISO week or a date also carries `start_anchor` {kind: iso_week | date, value, project_start} — what was typed and the project start it was converted against (§4 D318). The engine never reads `start_anchor` (`scsim/tests/test_start_anchor_ignored.py`); Compare ignores it too.

columns.name: recovery_overrides
columns.meaning: Per-lever changes to the chosen playbook, so a scenario can adjust a strategy without forking the playbook.

columns.name: stopping_rule
columns.meaning: When the run stops — a fixed horizon by default, as JSON so a precision-based rule can be expressed without a migration.

columns.name: primary_kpi
columns.meaning: The objective this scenario is judged on. A KEY, not a label, and it must be one the engine emits: `fill_rate` by default (§4 D113).

columns.name: created_by
columns.meaning: The user who set it up, where recorded. NULL is unknown, not nobody.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When it was created. Server-stamped.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When it was last changed, server-stamped. A scenario is mutable, which is why a run binds to a scenario ID AND carries its own copy of what it ran.

columns.name: recovery_playbook_id
columns.meaning: The playbook this scenario applies, by id. The one place a playbook is referenced by key rather than by name, which is what `scenario_templates.suggested_playbook_name` is not.

columns.name: from_network
columns.meaning: TRUE when the scenario was created from a network screen rather than from the simulation lab. It records the door a decision came through, which nothing else does.

columns.name: inherited_validation_id
columns.meaning: The model card (`model_validations.id`) whose adopted warm-up and recommended replication count `apply_validation_to_scenario` wrote into this scenario. NULL where nothing was inherited, or where a person hand-edited either value afterwards — divergence from the validated settings is explicit, never silent. A credibility provenance, not a data-readiness grade, which is what this line said until §4 D222.

columns.name: role
columns.meaning: What the scenario is for — `experiment`, a what-if a person set up in the Lab (the default), or `validation_baseline`, the one scenario per project that Run & Validate on /policies runs its validation into (a partial unique index keeps it to one). The Lab pins the baseline, shows it read-only and reuses its run, and every new scenario is seeded from it. It replaced finding that scenario by its display name, which a rename broke (§4 D227). The door a scenario came through is `from_network`, a different fact.

sim_engine_builds.tier_name: project-independent, versioned by vintage rather than by project
sim_engine_builds.grain: One row per engine build that produced a result or was reported running, keyed by (engine, code_version). Append-only: `last_seen_at` moves forward, a part the row did not know is filled once, and a build found wrong is WITHDRAWN with a reason, never deleted. The CURRENT build is not stored here — it is `sim_engines.code_version`, which the worker's boot report authors.

governance.note: A registry, like `sim_engines`: read by everyone through `sim_engine_builds_read` (`USING (true)`, select only), written by no API role. Its one writer is `_engine_build_record`, internal and service-only (D248), reached three ways: the worker's boot report (`sim_engine_report`), an AFTER trigger on every run row that names its build (the browser writes runs as anon), and the WP 15.2 backfill. The one human act, `sim_engine_build_withdraw`, is super-admin only and records its actor in the row. Not audited: a reference table whose writers name no person, with an append-only trigger instead of an audit trail.

constraints.name: sim_engine_builds_withdrawal_whole
constraints.definition: CHECK ((withdrawn_at IS NULL) = (withdrawn_reason IS NULL) AND (withdrawn_reason IS NULL OR btrim(withdrawn_reason) <> ''))

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: The build's id within the ledger. A run names its build by `(engine_id, code_version)`, the table's key, not by this id.

columns.name: engine_id
columns.meaning: The registered engine (`sim_engines`) the build belongs to.

columns.name: code_version
columns.meaning: The build, spelled exactly as a run's `code_version` is stamped. Since WP 15.1 it is `scsim-<ENGINE_VERSION>+<12 hex>`, a digest of scsim's source and the worker's compute path, so different code is a different build. A row from before WP 15.1 carries the bare label (`scsim-0.2.8`), which several builds shared; what ran under it is unknown, and the row says so by having no digests.

columns.name: scsim_digest
columns.meaning: sha256 over scsim's source files, as the worker reported it. Filled once; NULL for a build no worker reported (a browser run, or history).

columns.name: sim_worker_digest
columns.meaning: sha256 over the worker's compute-path modules (`sim_worker/build.py` `COMPUTE_MODULES`). Filled once; NULL as `scsim_digest`.

columns.name: commit_sha
columns.meaning: The git commit of the first worker deploy that reported this build. Identical source from a later commit is the same build, so the first commit stands. NULL when no deploy stated one.

columns.name: image_digest
columns.meaning: The worker image (Fly) that first reported this build. Filled once.

columns.name: first_seen_by
columns.meaning: How the ledger first learned of the build: `worker_report` (the boot report), `run` (a run row named it — the browser's builds arrive this way), or `backfill` (history, WP 15.2).

columns.name: first_seen_at
columns.meaning: When the build was first recorded (for backfill, its earliest run).

columns.name: last_seen_at
columns.meaning: When a report or a run last named the build. Moves forward only.

columns.name: withdrawn_at
columns.meaning: When a super admin withdrew the build. NULL = not withdrawn. Never cleared.

columns.name: withdrawn_reason
columns.meaning: Why the build was withdrawn, as stated by the super admin. Shown wherever a result of the build is.

columns.name: withdrawn_by
columns.meaning: The super admin who withdrew the build (`approved_users`). Set to NULL if that user is later deleted.

sim_engines.tier_name: project-independent, versioned by vintage rather than by project
sim_engines.grain: One row per simulation engine the platform knows: whether dispatch may use it (`status`) and which build the worker last reported running. scsim is the one active engine; the legacy worker engine is registered RETIRED — it stays frozen (CLAUDE.md's standing law) and is never offered. A run row names its engine (`simulation_runs.engine_id`) and the build is part of its RunKey.

surfaces.via: hook useSimEngines → select active rows from sim_engines (the Engine step, WP 10.5)

governance.note: A registry, not project data: read by everyone through `sim_engines_read` (`USING (true)`, select only), written by no API role. Rows are seeded by the migration; the one runtime writer is `sim_engine_report`, executable by the service role alone (the worker, at boot), which updates the row the worker runs and never creates one. Not audited: a reference table whose rows change by migration, and whose one runtime write is a build report stamped with `reported_at`.

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: The engine's id — what `simulation_runs.engine_id` and `model_validations.engine_id` reference.

columns.name: slug
columns.meaning: The engine's stable name: `scsim`, `legacy-worker`. The worker reports under it; `_engine_for_code_version` maps a recorded code version to it.

columns.name: name
columns.meaning: The display name the Lab's engine selector shows (WP 10.5).

columns.name: version
columns.meaning: The engine's version as the worker last reported it (scsim's `ENGINE_VERSION`). NULL until a worker has reported — the registry does not restate a version the engine's own code authors.

columns.name: code_version
columns.meaning: The build string, spelled exactly as a run's `code_version` is stamped (`scsim-0.2.8`). Part of every RunKey: a new build makes a new key, so a run on another build is never offered as identical (§4 D245).

columns.name: status
columns.meaning: `active` (dispatch may use it) or `retired` (dispatch refuses it).

columns.name: capabilities
columns.meaning: What the engine can do — where it computes (`worker`, `browser`) and its replication limit. Declared at seed; a report may refresh it.

columns.name: reported_at
columns.meaning: When a worker last reported this engine's build. NULL = never reported.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was seeded.

simulation_cache.tier_name: results — pinned to dataset + policy + engine version
simulation_cache.grain: One cached payload of the RETIRED batch pipeline, per project and cache key: baseline data, scenario data, network analysis or risk factors that the legacy `simulation-cache-manager` stored with a time-to-live so the next legacy run could skip recomputing it. Tier 5 — derived, disposable, input to nothing that still runs. DORMANT IN THE REPOSITORY: no code in `src/`, `supabase/functions/`, `sim-worker/` or `scsim/` reads or writes it. The current product's cache is a different mechanism entirely — `analysis_get_or_start` keyed on the graph hash, and the run reuse that `simulation_runs` performs.

governance.note: Two policies through the project's organization (`org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization)`): SELECT for any member of that organization, ALL for the project's modeler or an organization admin. Neither is predicate-less, so `write: null` agrees with `governanceEnforcement.test.ts`, and no user-facing write path exists in the repository. `cleanup_simulation_cache()` (SECURITY DEFINER, deletes expired rows) still exists and has no caller; nothing schedules it, so expired rows are not removed — `expires_at` is a statement of intent, not a guarantee. Deleting a project removes its rows through the inline `REFERENCES projects ON DELETE CASCADE`. NOT IN PRODUCTION'S CASE: §4 D168 found `simulation-cache-manager` and `simulation-availability-checker`, the legacy functions that wrote and read this table, still LIVE in production with no source here. NOT AUDITED: tier 5, and `audit-actor` covers tiers 2–4.

policies.name: Simulation cache: project access modify
policies.using: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = simulation_cache.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) AND (p.modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR (SELECT user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1) = 'admin') )
policies.with_check: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = simulation_cache.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) AND (p.modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR (SELECT user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1) = 'admin') )

policies.name: Simulation cache: project access view
policies.using: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = simulation_cache.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) )
policies.with_check: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = simulation_cache.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) )

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key. The row's identity is (project_id, cache_key).

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The owning project; half of the unique key. `REFERENCES projects ON DELETE CASCADE`, inline.

columns.name: cache_key
columns.meaning: The legacy caller's name for the cached thing, unique within a project. Its composition was the caller's convention and is not recoverable from the schema.

columns.name: cache_type
columns.meaning: What kind of payload `data` is: 'baseline_data' (DEFAULT), 'scenario_data', 'network_analysis' or 'risk_factors' (CHECK `simulation_cache_cache_type_check`).

columns.name: data
columns.meaning: The cached payload itself, shaped by whichever legacy computation produced it. NOT NULL.
columns.note: NOT TRACED to scsim: produced and consumed by the retired pipeline only.

columns.name: data_hash
columns.meaning: A hash of `data` as stored, computed by the writer. It identifies the payload, NOT the inputs the payload was computed from, so it cannot tell a reader whether the cache is stale.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was inserted.

columns.name: expires_at
columns.meaning: When the entry stops being valid — DEFAULT 24 hours after insert; the legacy manager set it from a per-call TTL and read only unexpired rows.

columns.name: access_count
columns.meaning: How many times the legacy manager served this entry; it incremented the count on every hit.
columns.note: NOT TRACED to the engine: an operational counter, read by nothing that still runs.

columns.name: last_accessed_at
columns.meaning: When the entry was last served. The defaults trigger also re-stamps it on every insert and update, so it is a write time as much as a read time.

columns.name: data_version
columns.meaning: A version number for the payload format, DEFAULT 1; the legacy manager always wrote 1.

columns.name: dependencies
columns.meaning: Names of what the entry depended on, for invalidation by the caller. Free text, DEFAULT empty; nothing ever invalidated by it in the schema.

columns.name: organization
columns.meaning: The organization's NAME at write time, DEFAULT 'default_org'. Legacy tenancy text; the policies read the project's organization instead.

simulation_cache.note: A RETIRED PIPELINE'S CACHE, LEFT IN PLACE ON PURPOSE by the 2026-07-02 commit that removed the legacy batch stack. A drop needs a production row count first, which no §15 run has taken. A cache whose writer is gone holds nothing anyone should trust: `data_hash` is a hash of the PAYLOAD, not of the inputs that produced it, so a hit could never say whether the project had changed since — which is the defect the graph-hash-keyed analysis store exists to avoid (`input-hash`, I5).

simulation_job_magnitudes.tier_name: results — pinned to dataset + policy + engine version
simulation_job_magnitudes.grain: One disruption effect as one legacy job actually applied it: the job, the legacy disruption profile, the effect type, and the magnitude and unit used — with whether that magnitude came from the stored profile or from a slider the user had moved. It was the legacy pipeline's record of "what was this run told", written beside each `simulation_jobs` row. Tier 5 — run bookkeeping, input to nothing. DORMANT IN THE REPOSITORY: no code in `src/`, `supabase/functions/`, `sim-worker/` or `scsim/` reads or writes it.

governance.note: Two policies through the project's organization (`org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization)`): SELECT for any member of that organization, ALL for the project's modeler or an organization admin. Neither is predicate-less, so `write: null` agrees with `governanceEnforcement.test.ts`, and no user-facing write path exists in the repository. A BEFORE INSERT trigger (`set_simulation_job_magnitudes_defaults`) still fires on any insert. Deleting a project removes these rows through `simulation_job_magnitudes_project_fk … ON DELETE CASCADE`, which WP 6.2 added (`20260919000005`, §4 D117) — and the before-reading for that migration is the one production measurement this table has: 35 rows whose project had already been deleted, removed so the key could be added. So production HELD rows; how many remain is not measured. NOT IN PRODUCTION'S CASE: §4 D168 found the legacy writer (`simulation-runner`) and readers (`simulation-availability-checker`, `delete-simulation-job`) still LIVE in production with no source here. NOT AUDITED: tier 5, and `audit-actor` covers tiers 2–4.

policies.name: Simulation job magnitudes: project access modify
policies.using: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = simulation_job_magnitudes.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) AND ( p.modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR (SELECT g.user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() g LIMIT 1) = 'admin' ) )
policies.with_check: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = simulation_job_magnitudes.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) AND ( p.modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR (SELECT g.user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() g LIMIT 1) = 'admin' ) )

policies.name: Simulation job magnitudes: project access view
policies.using: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = simulation_job_magnitudes.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) )
policies.with_check: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = simulation_job_magnitudes.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) )

constraints.name: simulation_job_magnitudes_project_fk
constraints.definition: FOREIGN KEY (project_id) REFERENCES public.projects(id) ON DELETE CASCADE

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key. One row per effect per job; nothing enforces that grain.

columns.name: job_id
columns.meaning: The `simulation_jobs.id` this magnitude was recorded for — a UUID, NOT the job's text `simulation_jobs.job_id`, despite the name. No foreign key, so deleting a job did not delete these rows; the legacy job-deletion function removed them by hand.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The owning project. Foreign key with ON DELETE CASCADE since `20260919000005`.

columns.name: scenario_id
columns.meaning: The legacy disruption profile (`disruption_scenario_profiles.id`) the effect belongs to. Not a `scenarios` id. No foreign key.

columns.name: magnitude
columns.meaning: How large the effect was, as the job applied it — a capacity reduction, a delay, a demand change, in whatever unit `unit` names.
columns.note: NOT TRACED to scsim: the consumer was the retired `ml-service`, and the strategic engine reads disruptions from the scenario a run binds, never from here.

columns.name: magnitude_source
columns.meaning: Where `magnitude` came from: 'database' (DEFAULT — the stored profile's effect) or 'ui_current' (a value the user had set on a slider for that run and that the profile did not hold). A legacy provenance flag, and the only record that a run used a number no table stored.

columns.name: effect_type
columns.meaning: The kind of effect, as the legacy profile's effect named it (for example 'capacity_reduction', 'time_delay'). No CHECK constraint.

columns.name: unit
columns.meaning: The unit `magnitude` is stated in, copied from the effect. Free text, not a token `unit_days()` knows — this table predates the one unit table.

columns.name: recorded_at
columns.meaning: When the magnitude was recorded — at job creation. DEFAULT now().

columns.name: organization
columns.meaning: The organization's NAME at write time, DEFAULT 'default_org'. Legacy tenancy text; the policies read the project's organization instead.

columns.name: created_by
columns.meaning: The approved user who queued the job. No foreign key.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was inserted.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When the row was last changed. The legacy writer only inserted; no trigger re-stamps it.

simulation_job_magnitudes.note: A RETIRED PIPELINE'S TABLE, LEFT IN PLACE ON PURPOSE by the 2026-07-02 commit that removed the legacy batch stack. A drop needs a current production row count first. Its intent — record the magnitudes a run actually used — is what the current product does by snapshotting the scenario and policy a run binds (`result-binding`); this table did it for a run identity nothing else carries, so it is not a precedent to revive, only a description of what is there.

simulation_jobs.tier_name: results — pinned to dataset + policy + engine version
simulation_jobs.grain: One queued run of the RETIRED batch pipeline: a project, the legacy disruption profiles it applied, a priority, a status and progress, and a pointer to the `simulation_results` row it produced. It was the queue between `simulation-runner` and `external-simulation-processor` / the Render-hosted `ml-service`. Tier 5 — run bookkeeping for a result, input to nothing. DORMANT IN THE REPOSITORY: no code in `src/`, `supabase/functions/`, `sim-worker/` or `scsim/` reads or writes it. The current product's run queue is `simulation_runs`, driven by `sim-command` and the Fly worker, and it never touches this table.

governance.note: Two policies through the project's organization (`org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization)`): SELECT for any member of that organization, ALL for the project's modeler or an organization admin — recreated in that form by WP 2.1's `20260915000004`, which is why the duplicate-policy question of §4 D30 no longer leaves the end state in doubt. Neither policy is predicate-less, so `write: null` agrees with `governanceEnforcement.test.ts`, and no user-facing write path exists in the repository. Two BEFORE triggers still fire on any write (`simulation_jobs_defaults`, `simulation_job_timing_trigger`); the AFTER trigger that once posted every new job to `external-simulation-processor` was dropped on 2025-09-19, so the database no longer calls out on a write. Deleting a project removes its jobs through the inline `REFERENCES projects ON DELETE CASCADE`. NOT IN PRODUCTION'S CASE: §4 D168 found the legacy functions that wrote this queue (`simulation-runner`, `external-simulation-processor`, `simulation-status`, `delete-simulation-job`) still LIVE in production with no source here. "Dormant" is true of the repository; whether those endpoints are still called is D168's production question (WP 7.1). NOT AUDITED: tier 5, and `audit-actor` covers tiers 2–4.

policies.name: Simulation jobs: project access modify
policies.using: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = simulation_jobs.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) AND (p.modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR (SELECT user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1) = 'admin') )
policies.with_check: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = simulation_jobs.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) AND (p.modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR (SELECT user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1) = 'admin') )

policies.name: Simulation jobs: project access view
policies.using: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = simulation_jobs.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) )
policies.with_check: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = simulation_jobs.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) )

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key, and the job's identity as the Supabase half of the legacy pipeline saw it: `simulation_job_magnitudes.job_id` and `simulation_performance_metrics.simulation_job_id` both point here.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The owning project. `REFERENCES projects ON DELETE CASCADE`, declared inline in `20250913085427`.

columns.name: simulation_result_id
columns.meaning: The `simulation_results` row this job produced, set by the processor when the external run returned. Null for a job that never completed. `REFERENCES simulation_results ON DELETE CASCADE`, inline.

columns.name: job_type
columns.meaning: What the legacy job ran. DEFAULT 'baseline_scenario'; the last runner wrote 'baseline' for an availability check and 'scenarios' otherwise. No CHECK — the one that would have constrained it was in the aborted re-declaration.

columns.name: status
columns.meaning: Queue state: one of 'pending', 'queued', 'running', 'completed', 'failed', 'cancelled' (CHECK `simulation_jobs_status_check`). A change of status fires `update_simulation_job_timing`, which stamps `started_at` on 'running' and `completed_at` on a terminal state.

columns.name: priority
columns.meaning: Queue priority, DEFAULT 1; the queue index orders by it descending. No range CHECK (the 1–10 rule was in the aborted re-declaration).

columns.name: progress
columns.meaning: How far the legacy run had got, 0–100 (CHECK `simulation_jobs_progress_check`), as the external service reported it.
columns.note: NOT TRACED to the engine: it was reported by the retired `ml-service`, not consumed by anything.

columns.name: config
