columns.meaning: The request the runner queued — horizon in days, a convergence threshold and a snapshot of each scenario's effects with any magnitude the UI overrode. The legacy equivalent of a run's parameters, bound to nothing versioned.

columns.name: scenario_ids
columns.meaning: The legacy disruption profiles (`disruption_scenario_profiles` ids) the job applied; copied onto the result row it produced. Not `scenarios` ids.

columns.name: baseline_enabled
columns.meaning: Whether the job also ran an undisrupted baseline. The last runner set it from its availability-check flag.

columns.name: python_job_id
columns.meaning: The external Python service's handle for the job, when it reported one.

columns.name: python_status
columns.meaning: The external Python service's own status string for the job, kept beside `status` rather than mapped onto it.

columns.name: queued_at
columns.meaning: When the job entered the queue. DEFAULT now().

columns.name: started_at
columns.meaning: When the job started running — stamped by the timing trigger on the transition to 'running' if the writer did not set it.

columns.name: completed_at
columns.meaning: When the job reached 'completed', 'failed' or 'cancelled' — stamped by the timing trigger if the writer did not set it.

columns.name: estimated_duration_seconds
columns.meaning: The runner's guess at how long the job would take — the last runner wrote a constant 60. An estimate, never a measurement.
columns.note: NOT TRACED to the engine: written by the retired runner as a constant, read by nothing.

columns.name: error_message
columns.meaning: Why the job failed, in one line, when it did.

columns.name: error_details
columns.meaning: The failure's structured detail — the processor wrote the error and its stack.

columns.name: partial_results
columns.meaning: Progress payload the external service posted while the job ran — in the last version, only `{current_stage}`. Never a result.

columns.name: created_by
columns.meaning: The approved user who queued the job; the defaults trigger fills it from the session's user when the writer leaves it null. No foreign key.

columns.name: organization
columns.meaning: The organization's NAME at write time, DEFAULT 'default_org'. Legacy tenancy text; the policies read the project's organization instead.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was inserted.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When the row was last changed — re-stamped by both BEFORE triggers on every write.

columns.name: job_id
columns.meaning: The external `ml-service`'s text key for the job — the column that service updated rows BY. Added by `20250914113757` (nullable), which backfilled it with `id::text` for every row existing at that moment, then gave it `simulation_jobs_job_id_key UNIQUE`. Rows queued afterwards by `simulation-runner` did not set it, so it is NULL wherever the service never claimed the job — and a plain unique constraint permits any number of NULLs.
columns.note: This is the column the shadowed definition disagreed about: the aborted `20250914113723` declared it `TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL`. The resolution and its evidence are in the table note. NOT the key `simulation_job_magnitudes.job_id` holds — that one is a uuid and points at `id`.

columns.name: current_stage
columns.meaning: A human-readable stage label the external service reported while the job ran ("Initializing", …, "Completed"). Added by `20250914113757`.

simulation_jobs.note: A RETIRED PIPELINE'S QUEUE, LEFT IN PLACE ON PURPOSE by the 2026-07-02 commit that removed the legacy batch stack ("left in place, inert, for a later cleanup migration"). A drop needs a production row count first, which no §15 run has taken, and D168's live legacy functions are a reason to take one. THE SHADOWED DEFINITION IS RESOLVED, AND THE ARTIFACT ALREADY HAD THE ANSWER. `20250913085427` created this table with no `job_id`; `20250914113723` re-declared it with `job_id TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL`, `plant_name`, `current_stage` and three CHECKs (`valid_status`, `valid_job_type`, `valid_priority`). The re-declaration never took effect, by three independent lines of evidence. (1) Its `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` was a no-op against the existing table, and its later `CREATE INDEX … (job_id)` names a column that table did not have, so PostgreSQL raised 42703 and the whole file rolled back — §4 D97, which taught the introspector to record a rejected statement as an abort; `build/schema.introspected.json` lists `20250914113723` under `aborted_migrations` for that reason, so the columns above come from `20250913085427` alone. (2) Production agrees: §4 D30's trigger probe (§15 run `35064364537`) found all four of `20250913085427`'s triggers and NONE of `20250914113723`'s, so the later file never ran to its end there. (3) Its author knew: `20250914113757`, 34 seconds later, is titled "Fix existing simulation_jobs table structure" and ADDs `job_id TEXT` (nullable), backfills it with `id::text`, adds `simulation_jobs_job_id_key UNIQUE (job_id)` and ADDs `current_stage` — the shape recorded here. So: `job_id` is NULLABLE text with a unique constraint, `plant_name` was never a column, and the `job_type`/`priority` CHECKs do not exist (the legacy runner wrote `job_type` values 'baseline' and 'scenarios', which `valid_job_type` would have refused — consistent with it never landing). The one residual risk is a fresh database replayed from empty, where `20250914113723` has nothing to collide with and would run — D30's closing sentence, unchanged.

simulation_performance_metrics.tier_name: results — pinned to dataset + policy + engine version
simulation_performance_metrics.grain: One telemetry record for one legacy job: how long the RETIRED `ml-service` took, what memory and CPU it used, how many iterations it needed and how many service calls and database queries it made. Operational measurements of a run, not results of the simulated supply chain. Tier 5 — input to nothing. DORMANT IN THE REPOSITORY: no code in `src/`, `supabase/functions/`, `sim-worker/` or `scsim/` reads or writes it; its only writer was the `ml-service`, whose source left this repository with the legacy stack.

governance.note: Two policies through the project's organization (`org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization)`): SELECT for any member of that organization, ALL for the project's modeler or an organization admin. Neither is predicate-less, so `write: null` agrees with `governanceEnforcement.test.ts`, and no user-facing write path exists in the repository. Deleting a project, or a legacy job, removes these rows through the inline `REFERENCES … ON DELETE CASCADE` on `project_id` and `simulation_job_id`. The `ml-service` that wrote it ran on Render, outside this repository and outside D168's function list; the 2026-07-02 removal commit asks for that service to be deleted by hand, and the repository does not record whether it was. §4 D168 does list `delete-simulation-job` — which deleted these rows — among the legacy edge functions still LIVE in production with no source here. NOT AUDITED: tier 5, and `audit-actor` covers tiers 2–4.

simulation_performance_metrics.note: A RETIRED PIPELINE'S TELEMETRY, LEFT IN PLACE ON PURPOSE by the 2026-07-02 commit that removed the legacy batch stack. A drop needs a production row count first, which no §15 run has taken. Every measure below was whatever the `ml-service` chose to report — its writer spread a metrics dict straight into the insert — so no column has a definition this repository can still check.

simulation_results.tier_name: results — pinned to dataset + policy + engine version
simulation_results.grain: One result of one run of the RETIRED batch pipeline (the "Legacy Sim" path: `simulation-runner` → `external-simulation-processor` → the Render-hosted `ml-service`), for one project, one plant and a set of legacy disruption profiles: a status and a `metrics` blob. Tier 5 — a result, input to nothing. DORMANT IN THE REPOSITORY: no code in `src/`, `supabase/functions/`, `sim-worker/` or `scsim/` reads or inserts it. The current product's results are `simulation_runs` + `run_replications`, which this table predates and which never write here.

governance.note: Two policies, both routed through the project's organization (`org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization)`, the WP 2.1 dual-read shape): SELECT for any member of the project's organization, and ALL for the project's modeler or an organization admin. Neither is predicate-less, so `write: null` is consistent with `governanceEnforcement.test.ts` — and it is also the plain truth: no user-facing write path exists in the repository. THE ONLY STATEMENTS THAT STILL TOUCH IT ARE DELETES. `_delete_project_rows` (reached from `delete_project` and the organization and user deletions) sweeps it BY NAME, because it has no foreign key to `projects` and the cascade (§4 D117) cannot reach it. `admin_delete_project` does NOT go through that sweep — it deletes the project row alone — so a project a super admin deletes from /admin/projects leaves its rows here behind, unreachable: D117's class, on a table no screen reads. The SECURITY DEFINER readers and writers the legacy path used (`create_simulation_result`, `get_simulation_results`, `get_baseline_simulation_results`, `get_scenario_simulation_results`, `delete_simulation_result`, `delete_simulation_results_batch`, `seed_synthetic_simulation_data`) still exist in the database and have no caller in the repository; the two views over it (`simulation_results_with_settings`, `simulation_result_scenarios`, `security_invoker` since D38) have none either. NOT IN PRODUCTION'S CASE: §4 D168 read production's function list and found the legacy functions that wrote this table — `simulation-runner`, `external-simulation-processor`, `simulation-availability-checker`, `delete-simulation-job` — still LIVE there with no source in this repository. So "dormant" is a statement about the repository; whether anything still calls those endpoints is a production question (D168, WP 7.1). NOT AUDITED, and that is the tier rather than an omission: `audit-actor` covers tiers 2–4, and a result row is an input to nothing.

The retired `ml-service` wrote it on its own direct insert path and 2025-09 seed migrations filled it with synthetic demo data; `external-simulation-processor` did NOT — it folded the service's payload into `metrics` instead, so which of the two columns holds a legacy row's output depends on which path wrote the row.

simulation_results.note: A RETIRED PIPELINE'S RESULT TABLE, LEFT IN PLACE ON PURPOSE. The commit that removed the legacy batch stack (2026-07-02, "Remove legacy simulation stack and ML service") deleted every reader and writer and left this table and its four siblings (`simulation_jobs`, `simulation_job_magnitudes`, `simulation_cache`, `simulation_performance_metrics`) "in place, inert, for a later cleanup migration". Described rather than dropped: a drop needs a production row count first, which no §15 run has taken for this table, and the live legacy functions (D168) are a reason to take it rather than assume zero. It binds none of dataset, policy, scenario or engine version, so it can never satisfy `result-binding` and nothing should begin reading it.

simulation_runs.tier_name: results — pinned to dataset + policy + engine version
simulation_runs.grain: One simulation run: what it was bound to (engine, graph version, policy version, scenario run spec, Validated Model, deviations), its status, and the run-level KPIs. Tier 5 — a RESULT. Its replications are `run_replications`. Since WP 10.4 every binding of a NEW run resolves from this row alone (`run_spec`, `run_key`, `engine_id`, `model_validation_id`, `protocol_overrides`, `exploratory`); runs dispatched earlier carry the three content hashes, the seed and the schedule, and say so in the record.

surfaces.note: The run-results workbook, whose reproducibility sheet binds the run from this row (WP 10.4).

governance.note: `write: simulation_lab` is the capability behind the one user action that creates a run. The row itself is created by the dispatcher through `create_simulation_run` (service role only — §4 D248 keeps it off the API) and moved on by the worker, or by the browser engine for a browser-computed run. BUT the table carries two predicate-less policies (`sim_runs_auth_all`, `sim_runs_anon_all`), so any holder of the table grant can write a row directly, RunKey and class included — one of the tables §4 D154 measured as writable from the browser's `anon` role, D28's standing decision and WP 7.1's to close. `min_project_role` is `viewer` because nothing here enforces a role, not because a viewer ought to write results. NOT AUDITED: tier 5 is output, and a re-run writes a new row rather than mutating this one.

constraints.name: simulation_runs_retention_expiry_check

constraints.name: simulation_runs_calendar_start_source_check
constraints.definition: CHECK ((calendar_start IS NULL) = (calendar_start_source IS NULL) AND (calendar_start_source IS NULL OR calendar_start_source IN ('dispatch', 'backfill')))

indexes.name: simulation_runs_series_due

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: The run's id. Replications, item series and the reproducibility record hang off it.

columns.name: scenario_id
columns.meaning: The scenario the run was dispatched from. Its run spec as it was at dispatch is in `run_spec.scenario` — a later edit to the scenario row moves nothing here.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project. Every read is scoped by it.

columns.name: status
columns.meaning: `queued` → `running` → `done` | `failed` | `cancelled`. Only the dispatcher writes `queued`; the worker (or the browser engine for a browser-computed run) moves it on, through guarded transitions.

columns.name: started_at
columns.meaning: When the engine started the run.

columns.name: ended_at
columns.meaning: When the run reached a terminal status.

columns.name: policy_hash
columns.meaning: The `policy_hash` of the saved policy version the run used — content, not id (WP 10.2). Part of the RunKey.

columns.name: code_version
columns.meaning: The engine build that computed the run, as the WRITER of the results stamped it: `scsim-<ENGINE_VERSION>` from the worker or the browser wheel, `worker-legacy` from the frozen engine. Empty while queued. The dispatch-time build is `run_spec.engine.code_version`; the two differ only when the worker was redeployed between dispatch and run.

columns.name: aggregate_kpis
columns.meaning: The run-level KPI aggregates the engine computed over the replications.

columns.name: ci_half_widths
columns.meaning: Per-KPI confidence-interval half-widths over the replications.

columns.name: warmup_detected_at
columns.meaning: The engine's own detected warm-up, in weeks.

columns.name: rep_count_target
columns.meaning: Replications requested.

columns.name: rep_count_done
columns.meaning: Replications persisted so far — the counter the worker's cancel check writes.

columns.name: error_message
columns.meaning: Why a failed run failed — including a worker refusing a run bound to an engine it does not run (WP 10.4).

columns.name: created_by
columns.meaning: The Supabase Auth user who dispatched it, when there is one (`auth.users`); this application's own accounts are not Supabase Auth users (D28), so it is usually NULL.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the run row was created.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: Last write to the row.

columns.name: policy_version_id
columns.meaning: The saved policy version the run used. The run never reads live policies.

columns.name: mapping_warnings
columns.meaning: What the project-to-engine mapper could not map, as the engine reported it.

columns.name: dataset_version_id
columns.meaning: The graph version the run was bound to (`dataset_versions`), snapshotted at dispatch.

columns.name: graph_hash
columns.meaning: The composite graph hash of that version. It was part of the RunKey until WP 11.2; RunKey v2 hashes `hash_simulation` instead, and the composite stays on the row as the frozen world the run can be re-executed against.

columns.name: gate_skipped
columns.meaning: The pre-run required-data gate could not load its data and dispatch proceeded unchecked.

columns.name: scenario_hash
columns.meaning: The scenario's baseline fingerprint hash (horizon, time step, demand model) at dispatch — what a Validated Model is matched on.

columns.name: model_validation_id
columns.meaning: The Validated Model the run follows: the one the caller chose (WP 10.4 — it must be this project's and not revoked), else the one in force for this policy, graph and scenario by content. NULL = the run followed no model, and is then exploratory. This is the binding the brief called `validated_model_id`; it is not a second column (§16 · WP 10.4).

columns.name: seed
columns.meaning: The root seed that ran, stamped at dispatch (audit WP 8).

columns.name: disruption_schedule
columns.meaning: The disruption schedule that ran, stamped at dispatch (audit WP 8).

columns.name: engine_id
columns.meaning: The registered engine the run was dispatched to (`sim_engines`). Dispatch refuses a retired engine and defaults to the single active one; the worker refuses a run bound to an engine it does not run. Backfilled for history from `code_version`, and derived the same way for a writer that does not state it.

columns.name: run_spec
columns.meaning: Everything the RunKey hashes, as data: the engine (id, slug, version, code_version as registered at dispatch), `policy_hash`, the graph term, the scenario row minus its identity and presentation columns, and `protocol_overrides`. Every binding of the run resolves from here with no live read. NULL for runs dispatched before WP 10.4. `run_key_version` says which graph term: 1 is `graph_hash` (the composite), 2 — every run since WP 11.2 — is `simulation_hash`, the scope the engine reads. A spec is never rewritten, so a v1 key never equals a v2 key.

columns.name: run_key
columns.meaning: sha256 of `run_spec` — the run's identity. Identical submissions share it: `create_simulation_run` offers a completed run with this key for reuse and attaches a second submission to one in flight. NULL before WP 10.4.

columns.name: protocol_overrides
columns.meaning: Deviations from the Validated Model's protocol, as the caller stated them; `{}` = faithful. Part of the RunKey, and shown on results and exports (T2, T4).

columns.name: exploratory
columns.meaning: The run followed no Validated Model, or was dispatched explicitly as exploratory. Never false for a run with no model. Badged everywhere and excluded from surrogate training (WP 10.5, 10.8). Backfilled as `model_validation_id IS NULL`.

columns.name: series_object
columns.meaning: The run's weekly series object in the private `run-results` bucket, `<project_id>/<run_id>/series.parquet` — zstd Parquet, long form (one row per replication and week, one column per series). When set, the replication rows hold `time_series = {}` and `runSeries.ts` hydrates them through a signed URL `sim- command` mints. NULL for a run whose series are in its rows (before WP 10.6, browser-computed runs, or a failed upload — the worker keeps the JSONB rather than lose it) and for a run whose series expired.

columns.name: series_bytes
columns.meaning: What the run's series cost: the object's size when there is one (written by the worker), else the JSONB series in its rows, measured when the run completed.

columns.name: retention
columns.meaning: `standard` (the series expire after `run_series_retention`), `pinned` (an editor or owner keeps them — `set_run_retention`), or `evidence` (the run a Validated Model rests on — set when the model is saved, never released here).

columns.name: series_expires_at
columns.meaning: When a standard run's series expire — set when the run completes. NULL for pinned and evidence runs (a CHECK holds it so).

columns.name: series_expired_at
columns.meaning: When `sweep_expired_run_series` removed the series (object, JSONB, per-item rows). The run row, its aggregates and every replication's KPI row are kept; the screen says the series expired and which RunKey reproduces them.

columns.name: hash_simulation
columns.meaning: The simulation scope's hash — the `inputs` domain of the run's snapshot, what the engine read (WP 11.2, §4 D260). RunKey v2 hashes it, so a deep-tier upload no run reads does not make an identical simulation a new key. Read by `create_simulation_run` off the snapshot row itself; history learnt it from its own snapshot. NULL where the run has no snapshot that carries one.

columns.name: simulation_version_id
columns.meaning: The simulation scope's level version the run computed over ("simulation inputs v4", `graph_level_versions`). NULL exactly where `hash_simulation` names no version.

columns.name: calendar_start
columns.meaning: Run week 0's calendar date — `projects.simulation_start` as it stood when the run was inserted, stamped by the `simulation_runs_calendar_ins` trigger and never changed after (PLAN.md §4 D318). Every date shown for this run's weeks reads it, never the project's current start. NULL when the project had no start. The engine never reads a calendar date, so it is not in `run_spec` and moves no RunKey.

columns.name: calendar_start_source
columns.meaning: How `calendar_start` was recorded: 'dispatch' (stamped at insert) or 'backfill' (filled by `20261101000001` for a run that predates the column, from the project's start as of that day — the run itself recorded none, and the reproducibility record and Compare say so). NULL exactly when `calendar_start` is (CHECK).

suppliers.tier_name: canonical — the only tier humans edit
suppliers.grain: One supplier in one project: what the simulation needs to know about them beyond the arcs that connect them to materials.

governance.note: `write` names the capability that exists today. WP 2.2 splits `data_editing` into `data_edit_inputs` (tier 2) and `data_edit_policies` (tier 4); this row becomes `data_edit_inputs` then, and all thirteen sidecars change together. SEPARATELY — AND THIS REPLACES WHAT WP 1.2 WROTE HERE, WHICH WAS WRONG: this sidecar used to assert `rls_enabled: false` and say "no migration ever runs ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on them". One does. `20260614000001_item_master.sql:57-66` enables RLS and creates two policies (`%s_auth_all`, `%s_anon_read`) on each of the three masters — but through `EXECUTE format(...)` inside a `FOREACH` over an array of table names, which a static replay of the migrations cannot evaluate. The introspector recorded the absence as `enabled: false`, WP 1.2 read that as fact, and the contract was one generated page away from telling a user their item masters were unprotected. WP 1.4 fixed the mechanism, not the guess: the introspector now records dynamic DDL (`dynamic_ddl`) and marks the tables it touches `rls.determinate: false`, the validator refuses to let a sidecar assert an RLS state the migrations do not settle, and the generated page says the state is indeterminate and names the migration. The ONLY way to know is to read the live database — PLAN.md §15, still unrun. WP 2.4's security review owns it.

constraints.name: suppliers_source_row_fk
constraints.definition: FOREIGN KEY (source_row_id) REFERENCES public.ingest_staged_rows(id) ON DELETE SET NULL DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this supplier belongs to. Half of the primary key.

engine.transform: filter, never read as a value

ingest.validate: set from the selected project, never from the CSV

columns.name: supplier_id
columns.meaning: The supplier's code as the user's own systems spell it. Joins to every inbound arc.

engine.transform: str()

columns.name: name
columns.meaning: A human-readable name for the supplier. Display only.

engine.transform: str(name or supplier_id)

resolution.note: A label. See materials.name.

columns.name: capacity_per_week
columns.meaning: How much this supplier can ship per week, across everything they supply. NULL means UNLIMITED — an infinite supplier, which is a deliberate modelling choice and not a missing value.

engine.transform: passed through as None when NULL; None means no capacity constraint

substitutions.visible_as: the grid renders it as 0 with no dot — which is D17, and wrong

resolution.note: estimable_from is EMPTY and that is a positive statement, not an omission. This is an engineering or commercial fact that someone knows exactly — it is written on a drawing, in a contract, or on a machine's nameplate. Fitting a distribution to it would produce a number with error bars around something that has no error, and the error bars would be believed. A future estimator reading this contract must refuse this field. Capacity is what the supplier CAN ship, not what they HAVE shipped. Estimating it from delivery history caps it at observed demand, so a capacity constraint fitted this way can never bind and can never explain a shortage — which is precisely the question it exists to answer. NULL continues to mean unlimited; that is an assertion too.

columns.note: D17 lives here. NULL means unlimited, but the grid's liveDefault is `derivedVal ?? 0`, so an unlimited supplier renders as a capacity of ZERO with provenance `default` — whose colour is null, so there is no dot to question. The grid states the opposite of what the model means. WP 6.2 fixes it.

engine_requirement.reason: Empty means unlimited (a valid modeling choice) — but partial-magnitude supplier disruptions need a finite capacity to throttle, else they degrade to full outages.
engine_requirement.chain: none — the absence is the value

columns.name: reliability_score
columns.unit: fraction of orders delivered as promised
columns.meaning: How often this supplier delivers as promised, as a fraction. 0.98 means two per cent of orders do not arrive as agreed. Defaults to 1.0 — a perfect supplier.

engine.transform: float(value or 1.0)
engine.missing_default: 1.0 (perfect reliability) — and the column is NOT NULL DEFAULT 1.0, so the default is the schema's, not the engine's

substitutions.when: the supplier has no master row at all

resolution.note: Reliability is the second field that an observations tier could honestly supply: on-time delivery is counted, not decided. Defaults to 1.0 — a perfect supplier — which is a strong assumption stated quietly, and the column's own DEFAULT rather than the engine's.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When the row last changed. Server-set.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was inserted. Server-set.

columns.name: source_system
columns.meaning: Which external system this row came from, when it was synced rather than uploaded. NULL for a hand-uploaded or hand-edited row.
columns.note: NOT TRACED into the engine, and correctly so: it is provenance, not a parameter. Read by the ERP connector (blueprint G18), which is the only writer. Kept, not a deletion candidate.

columns.name: source_external_id
columns.meaning: This row's identifier in the external system, so a re-sync can match it.
columns.note: NOT TRACED into the engine; ERP-connector provenance, as source_system.

columns.name: source_synced_at
columns.meaning: When the external system last confirmed this row.
columns.note: NOT TRACED into the engine; ERP-connector provenance, as source_system.

columns.name: ingest_run_id
columns.meaning: The ingestion run that last wrote this row (WP 3.3, D55), and through it the project, the source kind and who approved the promotion. columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate row identifier. Carries no meaning.

columns.name: from_location
columns.meaning: The upstream end of the edge — a supplier, a PURCHASED material, or a finished product, depending on which lane produced it. THIS SENTENCE IS WHY §4 D127 EXISTS: the column carries no role, so every consumer infers one at render time and eight of them disagree. The role is authored once now, on `node_list.echelon`, and read rather than inferred.

engine.consumed_by: network pages and the analyzers; not read by the engine mapping
engine.transform: copied from the lane row's id column

columns.name: to_location
columns.meaning: The downstream end of the edge — a customer, a FINISHED PRODUCT, or a purchased material, by lane. On the bom lane it is always a finished product, never an intermediate assembly: this lane is the collapsed graph.

engine.consumed_by: network pages and the analyzers; not read by the engine mapping
engine.transform: the customer, the root product of the demand walk, or the material

columns.name: plant_name
columns.meaning: The focal plant this edge belongs to, by NAME — the join key G1 forbids. Renamed from `plant` by 20250822025432, which is also when its incorrect UNIQUE constraint stopped meaning one-row-per-plant.

engine.transform: copied from the lane row

columns.name: weighted
columns.meaning: The volume on this edge after unit normalization — always per WEEK, whatever period the uploaded row quoted. This is where D2's fix lands: before it, a supplier quoting 52 000 a year and one quoting 1 000 a week were summed as 52 000 and 1 000.

engine.consumed_by: the analyzers and the policy grid's volume basis; not the engine mapping
engine.transform: `rate_to_weekly(volume, time_unit)` in `rebuild_supply_chain_lanes`, over the one unit table

columns.note: numeric(16,6) since 20250816031317. Normalization SHRINKS every value quoted coarser than a day and multiplies day-quoted rows by 7, so overflow needs a pre-existing value above ~1.43e9 in a day-quoted project. Bounded by analysis, not measurement — the §15 baseline has never been run.

columns.name: material_consumption_rate
columns.unit: units of upstream per unit of downstream
columns.meaning: How much of the upstream item one unit of the downstream item consumes. On a bom edge that is the EFFECTIVE rate through the collapsed tree — the sum over every path of the product of the rates along it, which on a single-level BOM is exactly the uploaded `consumption_rate`. Before WP 8.2 the multi-level path wrote a literal 0 here while the single-level path wrote the real number, so one column meant two things depending on the project's shape (§4 D136).

engine.consumed_by: the analyzers and the network pages; not the engine mapping
engine.transform: weighted / the product's weekly demand — the rates multiplied down every path

columns.name: sourcing_ratio
columns.unit: fraction of the destination's inbound flow
columns.meaning: This edge's share of everything flowing into its destination. A share, so the D2 unit error did not cancel: it decides which supplier the platform calls primary.

engine.consumed_by: the policy grid's primary-source suggestion; the analyzers
engine.transform: volumeShare(weeklyVolume(row), weeklyVolumeTotalsBy(...)) in _shared/laneVolumes.ts

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the edge was first computed. Server-set.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When the edge was last recomputed. Server-set.

columns.name: is_critical_node
columns.meaning: DEPRECATED (§4 D307). Whether the old lane-row scorer flagged this edge's source node as critical. The live answer is `node_list.is_critical_node`, one per node, which a lane rebuild does not delete.
columns.note: NOT an engine input. It is analyzer output written onto a tier-3 entity row with no identity, no version and no input hash (D19). WP 4.2 moves it to `analysis_results`; WP 5.3 drops the column. Recorded here so the move has a starting inventory.

columns.name: critical_node_score
columns.meaning: The score behind `is_critical_node`. DEPRECATED (§4 D307): the live destination is `node_list`, one row per node; nothing in the repository writes this lane-row column, and only the published pre-D307 build of `predict-critical-nodes` does until it redeploys.
columns.note: Analyzer output smeared onto the entity row (D19). See is_critical_node.

columns.name: prediction_timestamp
columns.meaning: When the criticality prediction was made. The closest thing this table has to a version stamp, and it names no model and no input hash. DEPRECATED (§4 D307): the live destination is `node_list`, one row per node; nothing in the repository writes this lane-row column, and only the published pre-D307 build of `predict-critical-nodes` does until it redeploys.
columns.note: Analyzer output smeared onto the entity row (D19). See is_critical_node.

columns.name: uploaded_by
columns.meaning: The user whose upload produced this edge. Referenced by the RLS policies. NULL once that account is deleted (`ON DELETE SET NULL` since `20260930000007`; before it the key had no ON DELETE rule and refused the delete — §4 D213).
columns.note: Governance, not a parameter. Read by this table's RLS policies, which grant on `uploaded_by = get_current_user_id() AND organization = get_current_user_org()`.

columns.name: organization
columns.meaning: The owning organization, as a NAME with a `default_org` default. A displayable string used as an authorization key — the second half of G1, and the identity D13 says is compared by string.
columns.note: Governance, not a parameter. WP 2.1 replaces it with an org uuid.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this edge belongs to. NULLABLE here, unlike every lane table — a row with no project is reachable only through the organization/uploader policies.

engine.transform: filter, never read as a value

columns.name: data_source
columns.meaning: Which lane produced this edge — inbound, outbound or BOM.

engine.consumed_by: the network pages, to colour and filter edges by origin
engine.transform: set by the ETL per lane

columns.name: is_zero_flow_filtered
columns.meaning: Whether this edge was hidden for carrying no flow in either direction.

engine.consumed_by: the network pages, to exclude dead edges from the drawn graph
engine.transform: set by the ETL

columns.name: zero_flow_filter_applied_at
columns.meaning: When the zero-flow filter last ran over this edge.
columns.note: ETL bookkeeping; not an engine input and not analyzer output.

columns.name: zero_flow_filter_reason
columns.meaning: Why the edge was filtered. One value is used today: zero_incoming_outgoing_flow.
columns.note: ETL bookkeeping; not an engine input and not analyzer output.

columns.name: computed_from_hash
columns.meaning: WP 4.3 · the `analysis_runs.input_hash` of the run that last wrote `is_critical_node` and `critical_node_score` on this row. It describes THOSE TWO COLUMNS ONLY — the rest of the row is `combine-project`'s ETL output, whose own run is recorded under `analysis_kind = 'combine_etl'`. NULL means the prediction predates WP 4.3 or was made through the deprecated two-argument `analysis_mark_critical_nodes`, which cannot name its run; NULL is the honest record and not a silent default (`declared-fallback`, I6). This is the column invariant `input-hash` (I5) is about. DEPRECATED (§4 D307): the live destination is `node_list`, one row per node; nothing in the repository writes this lane-row column, and only the published pre-D307 build of `predict-critical-nodes` does until it redeploys.

columns.name: computed_at
columns.meaning: WP 4.3 · when the run that wrote the criticality columns finished. It is provenance, not staleness: staleness is `computed_from_hash <> current_graph_hash()`, WP 4.4's one rule, and a timestamp comparison is precisely what that rule replaces (§4 D12). DEPRECATED (§4 D307): the live destination is `node_list`, one row per node; nothing in the repository writes this lane-row column, and only the published pre-D307 build of `predict-critical-nodes` does until it redeploys.

supply_chain_data_multi_tier.tier_name: derived — a pure function of tier 2
supply_chain_data_multi_tier.grain: One edge of the REAL BOM TREE, at the BOM's own depth — where `supply_chain_data` is the same network with the BOM COLLAPSED to purchased-material → finished-product. A bom edge appears once per root product, so `(from_location, to_location, path_root)` is its grain and not `(from_location, to_location)`. Read by the network pages, and NOT propagated into the simulation: the engine models a single focal plant with three echelons (blueprint §2.4). WP 8.2 REWROTE THIS LINE. It said "tier-2 and tier-3 suppliers behind the direct ones", which is `tier2_suppliers` / `tier3_suppliers` and a different node universe — and it is where `level`'s "tiers upstream" claim came from (§4 D140). Nothing has ever written a tier-2 supplier into this table.

governance.note: Written by `rebuild_supply_chain_lanes` — the ONE ETL since WP 8.2 — and never by a page. It had TWO writers until then, this and the `combine-project` edge function, disagreeing about what `level` meant (§4 D140); the edge function's lane build is deleted and it now calls the RPC. Invariant I2: pages never write tier 3. `write: null` is therefore a statement, not an omission — there is no user-facing write path and there must not be one. For precision, since WP 2.4 checked it: three PROJECT-SCOPED write policies do exist here, serving that ETL path. They are consistent with `write: null`, which names the capability gating a USER-facing write and not the existence of any policy — and unlike `dataset_versions` they carry a real predicate, so they do not admit an arbitrary holder of the table grant.

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate row identifier. Carries no meaning.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this edge belongs to. NOT NULL here, unlike supply_chain_data.

engine.transform: filter, never read as a value

columns.name: plant_name
columns.meaning: The focal plant this edge hangs off, by NAME — the join key G1 forbids.

engine.transform: copied from the lane row

columns.name: data_source
columns.meaning: Which deep-tier upload produced this edge.

engine.transform: set by the ETL

columns.name: from_location
columns.meaning: The upstream end of the edge: the finished product on the outbound lane, the component on a bom edge, the supplier on an inbound one. It said "a tier-2 or tier-3 supplier" until WP 8.2 and no writer has ever put one here (see the table's `grain`).

engine.transform: the child of a BOM row, a product, or a supplier, by lane

columns.name: to_location
columns.meaning: The downstream end of the edge: the customer on the outbound lane, the parent assembly on a bom edge, the material on an inbound one. Where a `bom_multi_level` row names NO parent, this is the FINISHED PRODUCT — never blank and never `ROOT` (§4 D129, D141).

engine.transform: the parent of a BOM row, resolved to the finished product when it names none

columns.name: material_consumption_rate
columns.unit: units of upstream per unit of downstream
columns.meaning: How much of the upstream item one unit of the downstream item consumes — this BOM row's own `consumption_rate`. On the outbound and inbound lanes it is the row's WEEKLY volume instead, which is the convention both writers have always had and is stated here rather than left to be inferred.

engine.transform: `bom_*.consumption_rate`, or `rate_to_weekly(volume, time_unit)` off the BOM lane

columns.name: sourcing_ratio
columns.unit: fraction of the destination's inbound flow
columns.meaning: This edge's share of everything flowing into its destination. Its denominator is the eighth raw-volume read D2 missed — a share computed over unnormalized volumes until WP 0.2 in the edge function and until WP 8.2 in the SQL writer that was actually deployed (§4 D148). 1.0 on a bom edge: a BOM row is the whole of what its parent takes from that component.

engine.transform: volume over the destination's total, both `rate_to_weekly`-normalized

columns.name: weighted
columns.meaning: The weekly flow along this edge: on a bom edge, the parent's demand for this edge's `path_root` times this row's consumption rate — so the edge carries ITS OWN contribution and not the child's whole requirement, which double-counted a material used by two assemblies. Unconstrained `numeric` here, unlike supply_chain_data's numeric(16,6) — so the normalization carries no overflow risk.

engine.transform: the demand walk in `rebuild_supply_chain_lanes`, over `rate_to_weekly` volumes

columns.name: level
columns.unit: levels down the bill of materials
columns.meaning: DEPRECATED since WP 8.2 — a deprecated ALIAS of `bom_depth`, written with the same value (NULLs included) for one release while the network pages move to the honest name. Read `bom_depth`. This column named FOUR different measurements across two live writers (§4 D140) — 0 on outbound, a literal 1 on the single-level bom lane, a literal 2 on the multi-level one whatever the BOM's real depth, and `max_level + 1` on inbound — while this sidecar claimed a fifth ("tiers upstream of the plant; 2 is a supplier's supplier"), which is `supply_tier` and lives on `node_list`.

engine.transform: copied from `bom_depth`

columns.name: path_root
columns.meaning: The node at the DOWNSTREAM end of the path this edge belongs to. On the outbound and bom lanes that is the FINISHED PRODUCT whose demand flows along the edge — a bom edge appears once per root product, so one BOM row feeding two products is two rows with two roots. On the inbound lane it is the material the supplier delivers. NULL on a bom edge that no finished product reaches: the structure is real and no demand flows through it, and that is a thing to say rather than a row to drop. CORRECTED IN WP 8.2. This field previously read "the direct (tier-1) supplier this deep chain hangs off", which NEITHER writer has ever written — the RPC wrote the product, the product, the parent component and the material on its four lanes, and the edge function wrote the root product. A sidecar describing a fifth thing is §5 T1 in the contract itself.

engine.consumed_by: the network pages, to group deep edges under the product they serve
engine.transform: the root of the demand walk, or the material on the inbound lane

columns.name: uploaded_by
columns.meaning: The user whose upload produced this edge. Referenced by RLS.
columns.note: Governance, not a parameter. See supply_chain_data.

columns.name: organization
columns.meaning: The owning organization, as a NAME with a `default_org` default (G1, D13).
columns.note: Governance, not a parameter. WP 2.1 replaces it with an org uuid.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the edge was first computed. Server-set.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When the edge was last recomputed. Server-set.

columns.name: bom_depth
columns.unit: levels down the bill of materials
columns.meaning: How deep in the BILL OF MATERIALS this edge's UPSTREAM end sits — 0 a finished product, 1 a material directly under one, N the Nth level of `bom_multi_level`. A bom edge takes it from `bom_multi_level.level`, the table that OWNS the measurement; an inbound edge takes the depth of the material it feeds PLUS ONE, from `node_bom_depth`, which is the one rule `node_list.bom_depth` also reads. NULL means UNKNOWN — a supplier of a material that is in no BOM has no depth, and reporting 0 for it is §4 D134: the ladder calls 0 a PRODUCT, so an unknown arrives as a confident wrong answer and the page's own `unknown` case can never be reached.

engine.consumed_by: the network pages' depth filter and column position
engine.transform: `bom_multi_level.level` for a bom edge, `node_bom_depth(...) + 1` for a supplier

tier2_suppliers.tier_name: canonical — the only tier humans edit
tier2_suppliers.grain: One tier-2 supply relationship: a direct supplier of this project's plant and the supplier BEHIND it, for one material. The row is an EDGE, not a party — the same supplier appears in as many rows as it has upstream sources.

governance.note: Two policies, both routed through the project's organization — `org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization)` for SELECT and the same predicate plus modeler-or-admin for writes. It is the dual-read shape WP 3.0 made uuid-only at the predicate (D29); the one remaining text branch is `organizations`' own read policy (D47, WP 6.2), not this one. `audited: true` SINCE WP 3.2, and the sequence is worth keeping. WP 2.3 instrumented twelve tier-2/3/4 tables and this was not among them, because nothing in the contract described it: `dataPlaneAudit.test.ts` requires the three triggers on every tier-2/3/4 table IN THE CONTRACT, so a table with no sidecar was outside the rule and nobody could see that its writes were unattributable. Writing this sidecar turned that gate red in the same session, and `20260916000016` is the gate being obeyed rather than a decision taken. It matters here more than most: `ingest_apply_run` promotes a CSV into this table, and a promotion into an unaudited table is the `audit-actor` hole this package exists to close.

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key. Not the grain — D5's signature, the same as the four lane tables: the row that means something is the supplier/upstream/material triple, and nothing enforces it.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this relationship belongs to. Set by the server from the selected project; the CSV never carries it (G1 — a project is referenced by uuid, never by a name the user typed).

columns.name: plant_name
columns.meaning: The project's plant, copied onto every row. A denormalization the schema has carried since 2025 and a trigger enforces: `ensure_dataset_plant_matches_project` refuses a row whose plant disagrees with its project's.

columns.name: supplier_id
columns.meaning: The DOWNSTREAM party of this relationship, as the user's own systems spell it — the direct supplier whose own supplier is named beside it.

columns.name: upstream_supplier_id
columns.meaning: The UPSTREAM party — who supplies `supplier_id`. The direction is what makes the row a tier-2 fact rather than a tier-1 one, and it is the column a reader most often has backwards.

columns.name: material_id
columns.meaning: What flows along the relationship. NULLABLE, and the NULL is meaningful: it says the relationship is known but what it carries is not.

columns.name: relationship_type
columns.meaning: How the two parties are related, in the user's own vocabulary. NOT a closed set: no CHECK constrains it and no code branches on it, so it is a label a person reads and nothing else.

columns.name: volume
columns.meaning: How much moves along the relationship over one `time_unit`. A RATE, like the lane tables' `volume`, and comparable across rows only after both are converted to the same period.

ingest.validate: numeric >= 0; blank lands no value, never 0 (D7)

columns.note: NOT TRACED into the simulation engine. `scsim` models one tier of supply; these rows are read by the network pages, not by `project_map.py`. Recorded so that nobody reads the shared column name as a shared code path.

columns.name: unit_price
columns.meaning: Price per unit of `material_id` along this relationship, in the project's own currency — which no column names anywhere in this schema.

columns.name: lead_time
columns.meaning: How long the upstream party takes to deliver. WEEKS by omission rather than by contract — unlike `inbound_logistics`, this table has NO `lead_time_unit` column, so there is nothing to say otherwise (the D9 shape, one table later).
columns.note: NOT TRACED into the simulation engine. It is a number the network pages display and nothing computes with — which is worth saying plainly, because a column named `lead_time` beside one the engine DOES read (`inbound_logistics.lead_time`) invites the assumption that both are inputs.

columns.name: time_unit
columns.meaning: The period `volume` is quoted over — day, week, month, quarter or year. It describes the VOLUME only and has never applied to `lead_time`.

tier3_suppliers.tier_name: canonical — the only tier humans edit
tier3_suppliers.grain: One tier-3 supply relationship: a tier-2 supplier and the supplier BEHIND it, for one material. The row is an EDGE, not a party; the schema is the same as `tier2_suppliers` because the fact is the same fact one hop further out.

governance.note: Two policies, both routed through the project's organization — `org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization)` for SELECT and the same predicate plus modeler-or-admin for writes. It is the dual-read shape WP 3.0 made uuid-only at the predicate (D29); the one remaining text branch is `organizations`' own read policy (D47, WP 6.2), not this one. `audited: true` SINCE WP 3.2, and the sequence is worth keeping. WP 2.3 instrumented twelve tier-2/3/4 tables and this was not among them, because nothing in the contract described it: `dataPlaneAudit.test.ts` requires the three triggers on every tier-2/3/4 table IN THE CONTRACT, so a table with no sidecar was outside the rule and nobody could see that its writes were unattributable. Writing this sidecar turned that gate red in the same session, and `20260916000016` is the gate being obeyed rather than a decision taken. It matters here more than most: `ingest_apply_run` promotes a CSV into this table, and a promotion into an unaudited table is the `audit-actor` hole this package exists to close.

policies.name: Tier3: organization access view
policies.using: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = tier3_suppliers.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) )
policies.with_check: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = tier3_suppliers.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) )

policies.name: Tier3: project access modify
policies.using: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = tier3_suppliers.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) AND (p.modeler_id = get_current_user_id() OR ( SELECT user_role FROM get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1 ) = 'admin') )
policies.with_check: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = tier3_suppliers.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) AND (p.modeler_id = get_current_user_id() OR ( SELECT user_role FROM get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1 ) = 'admin') )

columns.name: material_id

columns.name: relationship_type

columns.name: volume

user_ai_permissions.grain: One user's AI entitlements — which models they may reach, which one they get by default, and how the request is shaped. One row per user, or none.

governance.note: Read by `capabilities_for_user()` into the `models` block of its result, which is what the chat surfaces use to decide what to offer. Not part of the four capability layers — a capability answers "may you", this answers "with what".

columns.name: user_id
columns.meaning: The user these entitlements belong to. PK, so a user has at most one row.

columns.name: allowed_model_ids
columns.meaning: The models this user may use, as `ai_models.id`. An allow-list, but read as one only when it is non-empty.

substitutions.when: the array is empty, or the user has no row at all
substitutions.visible_as: nowhere, and it is worth stating plainly: EMPTY MEANS EVERYTHING here, not nothing. The resolver sets `all_allowed` true when the array is empty or absent, which preserves the behaviour that existed before the column did. An administrator clearing the list to revoke access would grant all of it instead.

columns.name: default_model_id
columns.meaning: The model a new conversation starts on. Nullable — the app falls back to its own default.

columns.name: fallback_model_id
columns.meaning: The model used when the default is unavailable or over budget.

columns.name: temperature
columns.meaning: Per-user sampling temperature override. Dimensionless and NOT a physical quantity — it is a model knob, recorded here so nobody mistakes it for one of the platform's measured values.

columns.name: max_context_override
columns.meaning: A per-user cap on context window size, in tokens. Nullable — the model's own limit applies.
columns.note: NOT TRACED into the simulation engine and never will be: `scsim` has no concept of a language model. This is an AI-plane setting that happens to live in the governance tier.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was created. Server-stamped.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When it was last changed. Server-stamped.

user_ai_permissions.note: The empty-array-means-everything rule in `allowed_model_ids` is the one thing a reader of this table must not get wrong. It is deliberate — it preserves the pre-column behaviour for every user who has no row — but it inverts the usual reading of an allow-list, and nothing at the point of display says so (§5 T2).

user_capabilities.grain: One grant or denial, for one user_id and one capability. The INNERMOST layer: an explicit per-person answer that beats every other.

governance.note: One of the four layers `capabilities_for_user()` resolves, in the order role -> org -> project -> user, most specific winning. `audited: false` and it matters here more than on most tables: these rows ARE the permissions, and a change to one currently leaves no record of who made it (§2.1 `audit-actor`, WP 2.3).

columns.name: user_id
columns.meaning: the user the row grants for.

columns.name: capability_key
columns.meaning: The capability, naming a row in `capabilities`.

columns.name: allowed
columns.meaning: Whether this layer grants the capability. TRI-STATE in effect: a missing row means "inherit from the next layer out", `false` means "deny here". They are different answers and the resolver's COALESCE depends on the difference.

substitutions.when: no row exists at this layer
substitutions.value: the next layer out decides; the chain ends in false
substitutions.visible_as: capabilities_for_user returns the resolved boolean; which layer decided is not reported

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was created. Server-stamped.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When it was last changed. Server-stamped.

user_capabilities.note: WP 2.2 seeded `data_edit_inputs` and `data_edit_policies` into this table from whatever `data_editing` already said, so effective access on the day of deploy was identical to the day before. `data_editing` is deliberately still here: it is removed when the last call site has moved to one of the new keys, not before.
